questions.question_text: In this verse, is the characteristic predicated of God or otherwise related to God; if so, in what relation (God as the one who bears it, acts, gives it, or is its object)? Record the relation, or record that it is not related to God here.

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence directly and explicitly names forgiveness as an attribute of God's character. Three data points converge:

1. **H5546 (sal.lach — Psa 86:5):** "You, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you." Group 5380-001 description names this as "forgiveness as a characteristic attribute of God's inner being — the disposition of readiness to pardon that belongs to his essential goodness and steadfast love." This is the most direct single-verse attribution of forgiveness to divine character.

2. **H5547 (se.li.chah — Psa 130:4):** "With you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared." Group 880-001 names this as "forgiveness as a divine attribute and possession — a quality that belongs to God's character, that grounds the possibility of the human-divine relationship, and that evokes reverential fear."

3. **H5545 (sa.lach) — divine exclusivity:** OBS-064-003 establishes that the entire Hebrew salach root is exclusively divine in subject — no human ever forgives with salach in the OT. This lexical restriction embeds in the vocabulary itself the theological claim that forgiveness at its deepest level belongs to God's nature.

The character of God revealed: forgiveness is not an occasional divine act but a settled disposition belonging to his essential goodness (Psa 86:5), located structurally with him as a divine possession (Psa 130:4), and exercised exclusively by him in the OT register (salach-root). The nature reflected is: God is the one whose character is constitutively oriented toward releasing the legitimate debt-claim against the sinner.

findings.session_b_note:
Rom 8:32 (anchor 888-001) reveals God as one who does not spare his own Son but gives — giving at supreme personal cost as the defining expression of divine character. Eph 2:8 establishes grace as sovereign, unmerited divine disposition. Exo 33:17 (anchor 889-001) reveals grace grounded in prior divine knowing and personal address. The divine character reflected: one who gives freely to the undeserving, whose giving is not exhausted by cost, and whose favour is rooted in personal knowledge of the recipient.

*Consistent with prior analysis. Adds structure: the prompt clarifies that what is reflected is not merely generosity but the combination of sovereign freedom, personal knowing, and uncaused bestowal.*

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence for compassion reveals God's character with unusual explicitness and density. Several distinct qualities emerge from the data:

**God is constitutively compassionate — not occasionally so.** The Exodus 34:6 formula (rachum ve-channum — "merciful and gracious") is a divine self-declaration, not a description of a particular act. It names God's character before and apart from any specific occasion. This formula is cited or echoed across the entire OT corpus: Neh 9:17; Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jon 4:2 (SD-017). God's compassion is not a response contingent on circumstances — it is what God is.

**God's compassion is visceral and somatic in its scriptural description.** The RACHAM/SPLANCHN root families describe divine compassion in the language of bodily inner movement. Hos 11:8 uses the most striking formulation: "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (ni.chum). The divine inner life is described as deliberative — God's compassion contends with and overcomes the competing inner disposition of judgment (Pass 2, FRAMEWORK SIGNAL on ni.chum). This is not the language of detached decree; it is the language of felt, warm, bodily-imaged inner experience.

**God's compassion has a maternal character.** H7356A ra.cham (group 729-001) grounds divine compassion in the image of the womb: "carried from the womb" (Isa 46:3). The womb is the space of origination, protection, and intimate care. God's compassion is described in terms of what a mother's body does for the child she carries — the most interior, involuntary, and complete form of care the vocabulary has access to.

**God's compassion is temporally asymmetric with judgment.** Isa 54:8 establishes an explicit temporal contrast: a moment of anger versus everlasting chesed/racham. Judgment is temporary; compassion is permanent (SD-019). This asymmetry is not incidental — it is a structural statement about which characteristic is more fundamental to God's inner nature.

**God's compassion is sovereignly free.** Rom 9:15 (oikteirō) — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion" — grounds compassion in divine sovereignty, not in human condition or merit. Compassion flows from what God is, not from what the recipient has done or become.

**God's compassion is deep beyond ordinary range.** The NT hapax legomenon polusplanchnos (Jas 5:11) — "very compassionate" — was coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name the depth of God's compassion at the point of maximum permitted suffering (SD-014). The intensity of the coinage is itself data about the character being named.

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence for contrition reflects two aspects of divine character simultaneously, and the relationship between them is theologically precise.

First, **divine holiness as the generative context**: Isa 57:15 opens with an extended divine self-identification — "the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy." It is this God — the utterly holy, transcendent, eternal one — who dwells with the contrite. The holiness of God is not incidental framing; it is the very quality whose encounter produces contrite collapse in the human inner being. The crushing vocabulary of the registry (dkh, ktt, nkh) images what happens to the human inner being when it genuinely encounters the reality of divine holiness: it is brought low, broken, reduced.

Second, **divine attentiveness to lowliness**: The pattern across all five Dependence/Creatureliness groups is that God actively moves toward the contrite — nearness (Psa 34:18), dwelling (Isa 57:15), looking (Isa 66:2), non-despising (Psa 51:17). The divine character reflected is not indifference to inner posture but a specific, consistent orientation: God is drawn toward the inner being that has been brought low. This is not a mechanical trigger but a relational disposition — divine character expressed as attentiveness to vulnerability.

The nature of God reflected is therefore: holy (transcendent, set apart, causing the contrite to collapse) and simultaneously near to the low (dwelling, attending, reviving). Contrition in the human being images this double divine reality — the creature that is genuinely before the holy God cannot maintain self-elevation; the one who is genuinely low finds divine nearness. The divine character that contrition images is the holiness that does not consume the lowly but revives them.

*New finding: The double divine quality — holy and near-to-the-low — has not been assembled as a single characterisation in the prior analysis. The registry data names these separately across multiple observations; this prompt assembles them into a unified characterisation of what divine character contrition reflects.*

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence reveals three dimensions of God's nature that fellowship images in the human person.

**First: God as the initiating giver of participation.** 2Pe 1:4 presents God as the one who grants precious and very great promises specifically so that human beings may *become partakers of the divine nature*. The initiative is entirely God's — he grants, humans receive and become. This images a God whose nature is not self-enclosed but self-communicating: he opens his own nature to creaturely participation. Fellowship, at its highest expression, is therefore not a human social arrangement but an analogue to a divine self-giving that precedes it.

**Second: God as the one who actively joins what is divided.** Eze 37:19 presents God as the agent who takes the stick of Ephraim and the stick of Judah and makes them one in his hand. The action is direct divine joining — God himself performs the act of unification. This images a God whose nature includes active relational restoration: the divided does not remain divided when God acts. Fellowship is the inner-relational participation in a divine nature that is itself unifying.

**Third: God as witness and guardian of covenant fellowship.** Mal 2:14 presents God as witness to the covenant between husband and wife — specifically to the companion bond (*chaverah*) that faithlessness violates. God cares about the relational bond at the level of covenant. This images a God whose nature includes attentiveness to relational faithfulness: the covenantal companion-bond is not merely human but is held by God as witness.

Together, the data reveals that God's nature reflected in fellowship is: self-communicating (he shares divine nature), unifying (he joins the divided), and covenant-attentive (he holds relational bonds in witness). Human fellowship, at its best, images all three.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence reveals that goodness is constitutive of God's character at its most fundamental level. Psa 119:68 ("You are good and do good") establishes an ontological prior — God's being-good precedes and grounds his doing-good. This is not goodness as one attribute among many but as a character description. The doxological assertion group (884-001) — "the Lord is good, his steadfast love endures forever" — names goodness as the summative confession of who God is in his covenantal relationship to creation. Gen 1:31 (884-007) extends this: the Creator's evaluative pronouncement declaring creation "very good" is an expression of his own goodness — he can only declare good what coheres with his character. God's goodness thus images itself in the human person as the capacity for moral assessment, relational orientation, and ontological alignment with what genuinely benefits. The human image-bearer who is good reflects the same character that God is, not by self-generation but by derivation. (OBS-067-OBS-001, OBS-067-OBS-026, OBS-067-OBS-036, OBS-067-OBS-037)

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence reveals that love is not merely an attribute God exercises but a characterisation of what God is. The divine self-declaration formula at Exo 34:6 (OBS-103-069) names rachum (compassionate) + chesed (steadfast love) as the first two inner attributes God proclaims of himself — love leads the divine self-portrait. Jer 31:3 names God's love as 'everlasting' (ahavat olam) — a qualifier that exceeds any human love-form (OBS-103-093). Song 8:6 names love's flame as 'the very flame of the Lord' (shalhevetyah) — grounding love's intensity in the divine nature itself (OBS-103-096). The data culminates in the NT claim (1Jo 4:8 — God is love), carried in the registry as PH2-103-004 and evidenced structurally by the entire divine love vocabulary across the data. The characteristic being imaged in the human person is therefore not a quality God has alongside others but God's own constitutive being-as-love.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence names divine mercy as the character of the Father (Luk 6:36 — "Be merciful as your Father is merciful"), as the inner compassion of the Lord (*polysplanchnos/oiktirmōn*, Jam 5:11), as the defining inner disposition ("Father of mercies," 2Cor 1:3), and as the ground of divine action (Psa 78:38 — "being compassionate, he atoned"). God's mercy is not incidental to his character — it is named as his defining disposition and as the motivation for his most significant acts (atonement, forgiveness, comfort). OBS-111-030, OBS-111-031, OBS-111-052, OBS-111-068.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence reveals God as the holy One who dwells with the crushed. Isa 57:15 names God as "the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy" and then declares his dwelling with the contrite and lowly spirit. This is not God's mercy or grace in the abstract — it is specifically the divine character of holiness generating a preferential dwelling with the crushed. Isa 66:2 confirms the pattern: "this is the one to whom I will look — he who is humble and contrite in spirit." God's character as holy-and-attentive-to-the-crushed is what contrition reflects or images in the human person. OBS-030-045, OBS-030-062.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence reveals God as the one who initiates and defines the highest fellowship. 2Pe 1:4 grounds divine nature participation in God's own "precious and very great promises" — the divine character and promise are the origin of the fellowship. 1Jo 1:3 presents the human-horizontal fellowship as derived from the vertical: "our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ." God's character as the one who shares himself — who opens his own nature to creaturely participation — is what fellowship at its peak reflects. The divine image expressed in fellowship is the communicative, self-sharing character of God. OBS-062-058, OBS-062-056.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence reveals that covenant-making and covenant-keeping are primary attributes of God's nature. God is "the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Deu 7:9 — OBS-034-039). He swears by himself because there is no greater (Heb 6:13, inferred from 3308-001 — OBS-034-052). He "remembers" his covenant (Gen 9:15 — OBS-034-038) — covenant-keeping is an act of God's own inner memory and faithfulness. The divine nature that covenant reflects is: faithfulness (keeping commitment across time), initiative (God cuts the covenant — OBS-034-046), and the capacity for binding self-commitment. In God, covenant is not a response to external pressure but an expression of who he is — his relational disposition toward his creation.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence reveals that kindness (chesed) is God's defining relational attribute — not one quality among many but the one he most characteristically names when he identifies himself. Exo 34:6 establishes the canonical self-disclosure: God is "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness." The superlative grammar ("abounding") signals that chesed is characteristic of him in excess [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-089]. Lam 3:22 further establishes that God's chesed "never ceases" — permanence and inexhaustibility are definitional [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-085]. In the NT, chrēstotēs (G5544) is attributed directly to God in Rom 2:4 and Rom 11:22, where divine kindness is paired with severity as two expressions of the same covenantal faithfulness [XREG: G5544, OBS-099-091]. The character of God revealed: one whose inner disposition toward the creature is constitutively kind — stable, inexhaustible, and covenantally faithful.

findings.session_b_note: The peace registry reveals that shalom is constitutive of God's identity, not merely a condition he produces. Three data points establish this: (1) YHWH-Shalom (Judg 6:24, OBS-117-148) — the altar name declares God IS peace, not that God has or gives peace; (2) H7965G group 2508-002 (Isa 54:10, OBS-117-145) — "my covenant of peace shall not be removed" — the eternality of the peace-covenant is grounded in God's own unchangeability; (3) DIM-117-001 (OBS-117-019): LORD of Hosts appears throughout the corpus, establishing that the God of peace is simultaneously the God of eschatological power — peace is not weakness but the sovereign rest of the one whose power is uncontested. The theological anchor terms (H3073 YHWH-Shalom, H3071 YHWH-Nissi, H3072 YHWH-Tsidkenu) further confirm: God names himself by his characteristic acts and identities, and peace is one of those constitutive names.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence reveals that giving (na.tan) is constitutive of God's character in multiple modes: God gives from covenantal faithfulness (OBS-060-018, OBS-060-035, OBS-060-036), from compassion responding to suffering (OBS-060-037, OBS-060-038), from anger in moral judgement (OBS-060-043), and from eschatological generosity (OBS-060-048, OBS-060-049). The anchor verses disclose that divine giving is never transactional — it is always the expression of an inner-being orientation. God gives land as the enactment of his covenantal word (Gen 12:7, Gen 15:18); God gives Spirit to instruct as the expression of his formative care (Neh 9:20); God gives eschatological transformation from depletion to praise (Isa 61:3). The character of God reflected in this registry is: a God whose inner commitments, compassions, and purposes necessarily express themselves as giving. Giving is the outward form of God's inner faithfulness.
findings.finding_value: The verse evidence reveals that giving (na.tan) is constitutive of God's character in multiple modes: God gives from covenantal faithfulness (OBS-060-018, OBS-060-035, OBS-060-036), from compassion responding to suffering (OBS-060-037, OBS-060-038), from anger in moral judgement (OBS-060-043), and from eschatological generosity (OBS-060-048, OBS-060-049). The anchor verses disclose that divine giving is never transactional — it is always the expression of an inner-being orientation. God gives land as the enactment of his covenantal word (Gen 12:7, Gen 15:18); God gives Spirit to instruct as the expression of his formative care (Neh 9:20); God gives eschatological transformation from depletion to praise (Isa 61:3). The character of God reflected in this registry is: a God whose inner commitments, compassions, and purposes necessarily express themselves as giving. Giving is the outward form of God's inner faithfulness.

The verses reveal that God himself is extensively the subject of hatred. Psa 11:5 locates it in his soul: "his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence." Isa 1:14 records God saying "my soul hates" disordered worship. Hos 9:15: "there I began to hate them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds." The pattern is consistent: God's hatred is a real inner-being disposition, located in his soul, always directed at wickedness and covenant violation — never arbitrary. This reveals that in God, hatred is the other side of his absolute commitment to righteousness. What he loves perfectly, he opposes perfectly. When the human person hates what God hates (Pro 8:13, Psa 97:10, Psa 139:21), they are aligning their inner being with God's own.

God holds minimal contempt as an originating characteristic. The two instances where na.ats is attributed to God (Deu 32:19 — "the Lord saw it and spurned them"; Lam 2:6 — "the Lord has spurned king and priest") are judicial responses to Israel's prior contempt of him, not an independent divine disposition. God does not regard his creation as beneath regard; he takes his own name, covenant, word, and people with full weight and seriousness. The relative silence is structurally significant: contempt — the posture of treating what is sacred as worthless — is not a characteristic of God toward his creation.

God is extensively the subject of abhorrence. Psa 106:40: "he abhorred his heritage." Psa 5:6: "the Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man." Amo 6:8: "I abhor the pride of Jacob." The ta.av root carries physical resonance — the sense of something that cannot be tolerated in one's presence. God's abhorrence reveals that he is not indifferent to evil but constitutionally repelled by it at the level of his inner being. When the righteous person abhors falsehood (Psa 119:163), they are participating in God's own inner-being reality.

Cruelty and ruthlessness are not characteristics God possesses by inner nature. Isa 13:9 uses akh.za.ri to describe the day of the Lord's judgment in its severity ("the day of the Lord comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger"), but this describes the unsparing quality of the judgment, not a settled disposition of God's character. God is never named as cruel or ruthless by inner character in the way he is named as a hater of evil. Cruelty is defined by the absence of what God characteristically has — mercy, restraint, purposive care. It is therefore an anti-divine characteristic, naming the condition of persons in whom image-bearing capacities for restraint have been removed.

God's character is revealed in M06-E primarily through his response to the reproached, not through God being a subject of the characteristic. The dominant divine movement is removal: Gen 30:23 (God takes away Rachel's reproach), Jos 5:9 (God rolls away the reproach of Egypt), Isa 25:8 (God will take away the reproach of his people from all the earth). God also imposes reproach as covenantal judgment (Eze 5:14, Jer 23:40) — but even this is reversible. What the corpus reveals: God is constitutionally oriented toward the dignity and honour of persons made in his image. Reproach violates something God takes seriously enough to act to reverse.

Exo 23:22 is decisive: "I will be an enemy (a.yav) to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries." God explicitly adopts the adversary posture on Israel's behalf. This reveals that the adversary structure is not intrinsically wrong — God can take it up. What makes an adversary relationship godly or ungodly is not the structure of opposition but what is being opposed and why. God's adversary posture is covenantal, responsive, and purposive — adopted in service of his people's protection.

Malice is never attributed to God in the verse evidence. In Eze 25:6-7, 25:15, 36:5, God appears only as the one who names and judges the malice of the nations. The divine response to malice is judgment — not possession of the characteristic. Malice is the compound of enmity, contempt, and soul-level pleasure in another's destruction. None of these, in their compound form, is a characteristic God possesses. The absence is absolute and significant.

Within M06, the characteristics divide into those God shares with the righteous person (hatred of evil — M06-A; abhorrence of evil — M06-C; adversary posture in covenant faithfulness — M06-F) and those that are exclusively creaturely conditions of disorder (contempt — M06-B; cruelty — M06-D; malice — M06-G) or conditions God removes rather than holds (reproach — M06-E).

God's constitutive being is love — the divine self-disclosure formula at Exo 34:6 (Group 1583-a/b) names chesed as his defining inner attribute; 1Jo 4:8 establishes that God is love ontologically. Love is not one attribute among many but the characterisation of what God is. The specific love-forms (chesed, agapē, rachamim) all name God before naming the human: the divine instance is the original; the human instance is participatory.

God is constitutively compassionate — ra.chum in Exo 34:6 (Group 1594) names his compassion alongside chesed in the divine self-disclosure formula. The maternal imagery of Isa 49:15 (Group 1596) — "can a woman forget her nursing child?" — establishes that God's compassion exceeds the most reliably tender human compassion. The character revealed: one who is moved by the encounter with his people's suffering as a mother is moved by the cry of her infant.

God is "rich in mercy" (Eph 2:4 — Group 1632) — mercy is a constitutive divine abundance, not a reluctant concession. The Lukan birth narrative deploys eleos as the content of God's covenant-faithfulness in action (Luk 1:50, 54, 72, 78 — Group 1632). The character revealed: one whose authority is exercised as merciful toward the lesser party who stands in guilt or helplessness.

"No one is good except God alone" (Mar 10:18 — Group 1096) — goodness is God's exclusive constitutive attribute from which all creaturely goodness is derivative. God's kindness is purposive and active: "God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance" (Rom 2:4 — Group 1111). The character revealed: one whose inner disposition is generative gracious goodwill that is not passive but transformatively directed.

God's gentleness makes the person great — "your gentleness made me great" (Psa 18:35 / 2Sa 22:36 — Group 1271). Christ's meekness and gentleness are named as the ground of apostolic appeal (2Cor 10:1 — Groups 1102, 1104). The character revealed: one who holds all coercive power and chooses not to exercise it destructively — the stooping of the infinite toward the finite that produces greatness in the recipient.

God names himself as comforter — "I, I am he who comforts you" (Isa 51:12 — Group 1742). He is the "Father of mercies and God of all comfort" (2Cor 1:3 — Group 3073). The maternal comfort image (Isa 66:13 — Group 1742) identifies his comforting with the most instinctive human tender care. The character revealed: one who actively moves toward the distressed with the specific intent to relieve — not passively available but initiatorily present.

The "fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2Cor 13:14 — Group 1055) names koinōnia as a quality of the divine inner life. God is "faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son" (1Cor 1:9 — Group 1055). He initiates katallagē — "God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself" (2Cor 5:18 — Group 2069). The character revealed: a God whose inner communal life (Trinitarian fellowship) overflows into restoration of broken relationships and constitution of a shared community.

Across all seven sub-groups, the verse evidence establishes God as the constitutive origin of every characteristic in M05. Not one characteristic is presented as naturally human or autonomously generated: love is what God is (M05-A); compassion is his defining attribute (M05-B); mercy is his inexhaustible richness (M05-C); goodness is his exclusive quality (M05-D); gentleness is his mode of exercising power (M05-E); comfort is his self-identification (M05-F); fellowship is his Trinitarian inner life (M05-G). The cluster as a whole images a God of relational, gracious, generous, non-coercive engagement with his creation.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** God's righteousness is not derived from anything external to himself — it is declared foundational and permanent across all his ways and all his works (Deu 32:4; Psa 145:17; Psa 111:3). The verse evidence reveals that righteousness in God is not a quality he exercises when appropriate; it is the constitutive character of everything he does. He cannot act unrighteously — not by constraint but by nature: "he does no injustice" (Zep 3:5). His righteousness is structural: it is the foundation of his throne (Psa 89:14; Psa 97:2). This reveals a God whose essential nature is moral order, truth, and right — not as principles he follows but as what he is.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The verse evidence shows human righteousness positioned consistently as derived from and answerable to God's righteousness. God's righteousness is the standard against which human standing is measured — "you are righteous; we have acted wickedly" (Neh 9:33; Ezr 9:15; Lam 1:18; Dan 9:7). In the NT, human righteousness is explicitly a participation in God's nature: the person is "born of him" who is righteous (1Jo 2:29), and the believer is constituted as "the righteousness of God" in Christ (2Cor 5:21, VSG M26-A2-008). The characteristic in the human images the character of God precisely because it is not self-generated but received.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** The uprightness sub-group (yo.sher, me.shar, ne.kho.chah) reveals that straightness and level-ness are qualities God possesses and expresses: "I the Lord speak the truth; I declare what is right" (Isa 45:19, VSG 1212-001). The Messianic scepter of uprightness (Heb 1:8, VSG 1218-001) reveals uprightness as a divine-royal quality. The path of the righteous is "level" because God makes it so (Isa 26:7). What is straight in God becomes the ground for what is straight in the person.

**[C — Justification]** The verse evidence reveals a God who is simultaneously just and the justifier — this pairing in Rom 3:26 (VSG 3194-001) is the theological core of justification. God's nature as righteous judge is the same nature that makes his justifying act possible. Justification is not God setting aside his righteousness — it is God expressing his righteousness through Christ. The term dikaiōsis (justification) in Rom 4:25 (VSG 3203-001) names the restoration of right standing as flowing from God's own righteous nature.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The verse evidence reveals that God's avenging justice flows from the same righteous character that grounds all his other acts. "Vengeance is mine; I will repay" (Rom 12:19; Heb 10:30, VSG 6841-002/004) names God as the exclusive legitimate possessor of retributive authority. His judgments in their most severe expressions are declared "just and true" (Rev 19:2, VSG 944-002). Divine retribution is not rage — it is the expression of a nature that cannot permit wrong to remain unaddressed.

**[E — Condemnation]** The verse evidence reveals that God's condemnation is an expression of the same nature that makes his justification significant. Condemnation is the negative judicial verdict of a God whose righteousness is real — "he condemned sin in the flesh" (Rom 8:3, VSG 4846-002). The ministry of condemnation exists because God is just (2Cor 3:9, VSG 738-001). The self-condemned person (Tit 3:11, VSG 4848-001) reveals that the moral structure God has built into persons includes the capacity for conscience to echo divine judgment.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The verse evidence reveals a God who reckons — who counts, credits, regards, and assigns moral standing. "It was counted to him as righteousness" (Rom 4:3–11, VSG 3410-001). This divine reckoning is not arbitrary; it is the act of a God whose nature is truth and right. The term kardiognōstēs — heart-knower (Act 1:24; 15:8, in VSG M26-A1-002) reveals that divine reckoning penetrates to the actual inner state, not mere appearances. God's moral reckoning images perfect knowledge joined to perfect justice.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The structural opposites (ra.sha, a.val) reveal God's character by contrast. He does no a.val — no injustice (Deu 32:4; Zep 3:5). The very existence of the wicked category (ra.sha) assumes a God against whom wickedness is defined. The wicked are "not so" (Psa 1:4) — they are the negative image of what God is. The opposites exist in the cluster specifically because God's righteousness needs a contrast by which its absolute character becomes visible.

**[CLUSTER]** The cluster as a whole reveals a God whose essential nature is righteousness — not as one attribute among others but as the architectonic quality of his being from which all the sub-groups derive their coherence. A1 names what God is; A2 shows the human person as derived image; C, D, and E are the modes in which God's righteousness acts in history; F is the faculty by which God's righteousness assesses; B qualifies the inner texture of righteous character; G defines the boundary. Every sub-group traces back to one source: the nature of God.

Wisdom is explicitly and repeatedly attributed to God as an essential, not merely distributed, attribute. VCG01 (Dan 2:20 anchor): "to whom belong wisdom and might" — wisdom as divine possession. Rev 7:12 ascribes wisdom to God in doxology. Rom 11:33 names "the wisdom of God" as depth beyond human comprehension. The evidence reveals: wisdom characterises what God IS, not merely what he gives. The human characteristic therefore images a constitutive divine attribute.

God's planning nature is what the human capacity for counsel and deliberate intent reflects.

findings.finding_value: E — Across all sub-groups, there is a consistent pattern: each characteristic has an explicit divine version (God's wisdom, God's understanding, God's knowledge, God's counsel, God's thoughts, God's word) that precedes and grounds the human version. This is a cluster-level finding: M15 is not primarily a cluster of human capacities that happened to be attributed to God — it is a cluster of divine attributes that the human person is created to image and participate in. Dan 2:21: "he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding" — the giving structure assumes prior divine possession. The cluster's governing narrative is: divine attribute → human imaging.

findings.finding_value: The anxiety-faculty is shown as the capacity for directed attentive concern — the inner ability to fix attention on something of value and be troubled by its welfare. 1Pe 5:7 reveals God's character most directly in relation to this: "he cares for you" (merimna cast onto God) — the command to transfer anxiety is grounded in God's active, attentive care. The same term (merimna) that names human anxiety about valued things names God's disposition toward the human person. This suggests the anxiety-faculty at its root images God's caring attentiveness — anxiety is the misdirected form of a faculty whose proper direction is the same as God's own orientation toward what he values.

findings.finding_value: 2Cor 4:8 — "perplexed but not driven to despair" — is grounded in the whole Pauline argument that the treasure is in jars of clay, showing that God deliberately places his power in weak vessels. The implication: God is never in despair about the outcomes his word will achieve. The cluster's despair vocabulary has no divine counterpart — God does not despair. The evidence reveals this characteristic as the antithesis of divine faithfulness, not its image.

findings.finding_value: 2Cor 4:1 — "having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart" — grounds the absence of discouragement in God's mercy. The implied divine character: God's mercy is the inexhaustible resource that makes sustained inner resolve possible. Luk 18:1-8 (the widow and the judge) presents God as the one who will "give justice speedily" — the parable grounds not-losing-heart in God's character as a just, attentive, and responsive Father who is not indifferent. God does not grow weary in his purposes.

findings.finding_value: Mat 14:31 — Jesus directly addresses Peter's doubt, then grasps his hand — revealing that God in Christ does not condemn the doubter but reaches toward them. Jam 1:5 (context for Jam 1:8 dipsuchos) presents God as giving wisdom "generously to all without reproach" — his character is characterised by single-minded generosity that does not withhold from those who are double-minded.

findings.finding_value: Across all sub-groups, the cluster's vocabulary is uniformly negative in the divine portrait — none of the M20 characteristics are attributed to God. Instead, each sub-group reveals God's character as the structural opposite: attentive care (against anxiety), faithful forward-orientation (against despair), inexhaustible mercy (against discouragement), single-minded generosity (against indecision).

findings.finding_value: God's character as gracious is constitutive, not episodic. The Exo 34:6 formula — "the Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" — is not a description of what God does on occasion but of what God is by self-declaration. Group 2330-001 (all 13 chan.nun verses) sustains this portrait: the formula recurs in Psa 86:15; 103:8; 111:4; 116:5; 145:8; Joe 2:13; Jon 4:2, naming graciousness as the stable identity of God across narrative, prophetic, and psalmic contexts. Within M39-A, ba.rakh group 1299-001 (Gen 1:22; 1:28; 2:3) shows that blessing is the first outward act of this character — God blesses at creation before any human need arises. Charis group 888-001 (Eph 2:8; 2Cor 12:9) locates this character in its NT fullness: grace is sovereign, transforming, and sufficient in weakness. The character of God reflected here is: initiating, abundant, undeserved, personally engaged, and structurally prior to any human response.

findings.finding_value: The goodness characteristic also reflects divine character, but in its evaluative and moral register. The verse evidence in M39-B names goodness as what God affirms and approves: 1Ki 8:18 ("you did well that it was in your heart") shows God recognising and endorsing the quality of inner goodness before the act. The divine goodness-affirmation is morally precise — God evaluates the heart, not merely the outcome. The character reflected: God as moral evaluator whose own goodness sets the standard for what is affirmed as good.

findings.finding_value: Both sub-groups converge on a single underlying divine character truth: God is constitutively good and constitutively gracious. These are not two separate attributes but two aspects of the same inner divine character — the one gracious toward the lesser (M39-A) and the one who is and affirms the good (M39-B). The verse evidence does not separate them: Psa 116:5 pairs "gracious" and "righteous"; Psa 145:8 pairs "gracious" with "steadfast love"; Gen 4:7 connects doing well with being accepted.

findings.finding_value: The sub-group does not evidence God's nature in a reflective mode. What it evidences is the divine negative — God using the prosperity-fatness mechanism as judgment (Isa 6:10: "make the heart of this people fat"). This is not a reflection of divine character in the human person but divine judicial action on the human person. No positive divine-nature reflection is evidenced in M46-A.

findings.finding_value: The sub-group evidences how wealth produces failures of pity and satisfaction in the human person. No divine-nature reflection is evidenced — the hardness toward Lazarus (Luk 16:19-21), the contempt in the assembly (Jam 2:2-3), and the deceitfulness of riches (Mat 13:22) all describe human inner failure, not divine character.

findings.finding_value: Pro 8:18 evidences Wisdom claiming "riches and honour are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness." The divine nature reflected here is the integration of material abundance with righteousness — in God (through Wisdom), prosperity and moral integrity coexist without conflict. Isa 33:6 extends this: "the fear of the Lord is Zion's treasure (cho.sen)" — God himself is identified as the source and substance of what true wealth is. The cluster's M46-C evidence suggests that God's nature is one in which material goodness and moral goodness are unified, not opposed.

findings.finding_value: 2Cor 8:9 evidences the most explicit divine-nature statement in the cluster: "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich." God's nature — specifically Christ's divine richness — is the origin point of the Christological wealth-exchange. God is rich (plousios) in a way that enables voluntary impoverishment for others' enrichment. Eph 2:4 adds "God, being rich in mercy" — divine richness as inexhaustible generosity. The plousiōs provision of 1Ti 6:17 ("God who richly provides all things for enjoyment") names the quality of divine provision as abundant, generous, and purposefully enabling human flourishing.

findings.finding_value: M01-A reveals that God is himself the supreme object and generator of reverential fear: his holiness, incomparable greatness, awesome acts, and sovereign authority are what produce the reverential posture in the human person. The character of God that M01-A reflects is his absolute worthiness of awe — he is not merely powerful but uniquely holy, so that fear-of-God is the only fitting inner response to who he is. The anchor Exo 15:11 names this directly: "awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders," with the fear arising from witnessing God's incomparable holiness. The Proverbs wisdom cluster (M01-A-VCG-02, anchor Pro 1:7) reveals that the fear God generates is epistemologically constitutive — he is the ground of all genuine knowledge. The covenant dimension (M01-A-VCG-03, anchor Psa 25:14) reveals that God is a relational being who offers friendship and covenant intimacy to those whose inner posture is reverential. The Mal 2:5 material reveals that God structured an entire covenant relationship around this response.

M01-B reveals God's majesty through the terror encounters produce. The repeated pattern of angelic appearances followed by "do not be afraid" (Luk 2:9-10; Luk 1:12-13; Mat 17:6-7; Rev 1:17) shows that divine presence is intrinsically overwhelming — God's holiness, mediated through angels or through Jesus's own acts, produces fear as an involuntary reflex. The Transfiguration (Mar 9:6) and the storm-calming (Mar 4:41) reveal that Jesus's character includes the same awe-inducing dimension as the OT God of Sinai. The pattern of Jesus addressing fear with self-disclosure ("it is I") reveals God's disposition toward the frightened person: he does not leave the fear unaddressed but names himself as the ground of release.

M01-C reveals God as the sovereign deployer of terror as a covenantal instrument. The Exo 23:27 anchor ("God's terror is sent as an advance weapon") shows God deploying dread purposively, not arbitrarily — it is a feature of his governance of history. The Ezekiel 32 corpus (M01-C-VCG-03) shows that God alone controls the terror that nations deploy: "God himself declares he spread terror in the land of the living" (Eze 32:32), so even imperial terror is ultimately under divine authority. This reveals God as the final sovereign over all fear-inducing power.

M01-D reveals God as one who both produces and commands dismay. He dismays rebels and enemies as a judicial act (Psa 2:5; Jer 49:37 anchor), but he also directly commands against dismay in his people (Jer 1:17 anchor D-VCG-04). This double agency — causing dismay in enemies, forbidding it in his servants — reveals a God who governs inner composure as part of his covenantal relationship. The Job corpus (M01-D-VCG-01, anchor Psa 6:3) shows that even God's hidden face produces dismay, revealing that divine presence is constitutive of inner stability in the human person.

M01-E reveals God as the source of the trembling that creation instinctively enacts before holiness. The Sinai material (Exo 19:16 anchor, E-VCG-01) shows that God's presence produces involuntary whole-body trembling even in a community of people — the mountain itself trembles (Exo 19:18). This reveals God's holiness as a reality that the physical world registers. The E-VCG-02 corpus (anchor Isa 66:2) shows that God actively looks for a specific kind of person: one who trembles at his word, paired with humility and contrite spirit. This reveals God's character as responsive to reverential somatic gravity in the human person.

M01-F reveals God as judge and as the ground of freedom from anxiety. The dread-of-judgment corpus (M01-F-VCG-04, anchor Heb 10:27) reveals God's absolute judicial authority: "fearful expectation of judgment" is a real inner experience grounded in God's actual judgment-power. The 1Jo 4:18 material (fear rooted in punishment-anticipation, expelled by perfect love) reveals that God's own character — love perfected — is the counter to fearful anticipation. The M01-F-VCG-05 pastoral anxiety material (anchor 2Cor 12:20) shows that concern for God's people, modeled by Paul, participates in God's own pastoral character.

M01-G reveals God by contrast: the spirit God gives is not timidity but "power, love, and self-control" (2Ti 1:7 anchor). Timidity as inner constitutional failure reveals by negation what God's character is — generative, courageous, loving. The Rev 21:8 material, listing cowardice alongside idolatry and murder, reveals that God's character is definitively non-cowardly: he is the one who acts, sustains, and does not shrink from judgment or from love.

Across M01, fear as a human inner-being characteristic reflects and images the holiness, sovereignty, and relational depth of God. The cluster reveals that God is: (1) the supreme object of reverential fear by virtue of his holiness and incomparability (M01-A); (2) one whose presence is intrinsically overwhelming (M01-B, E); (3) sovereign over all terror as a historical instrument (M01-C); (4) the ground of inner stability whose withdrawal produces dismay (M01-D); and (5) the final judge before whom anticipatory dread is rational (M01-F). The characteristic images God not as a property God shares with the human person (God does not fear — see T0.1.2) but as the One before whom the human person rightly orients in fear.

The judicial-wrath corpus reveals God as a moral agent for whom wrongdoing cannot pass unmarked. Wrath is not arbitrary emotion but a structured response to moral violation: Rom 1:18 names it as revealed against those who suppress the truth; Heb 3:11 shows it as the ground of a binding oath; Rom 4:15 frames it as the judicial product of law meeting transgression. The characteristic images God as the one who holds the moral order with weight — what is wrong incurs consequence.

The burning-rage corpus reveals God as a being of intense moral passion who takes covenant betrayal with consuming seriousness. Cha.rah and che.mah across M02-B-VCG-01 depict God's incensed anger as reactive to specific acts of faithlessness (Num 25:3; Jos 7:1; Judg 2:14). The fire/heat vocabulary images a God who is not indifferent — a being whose inner state is genuinely engaged by the moral condition of those in covenant with him.

The indignation corpus (M02-C-VCG-01) reveals God as one whose moral displeasure is principled and sustained: Psa 7:11 names indignation as a constant, daily disposition — "a God who feels indignation every day." This images a God whose moral character is not episodic but enduring.

The provocation corpus (M02-D-VCG-01) reveals God as a relational being who can be genuinely affected by the behaviour of those in covenant with him. Jer 11:17 names Baal worship as the specific act provoking God's anger; Jer 7:19 introduces the question whether provocation truly wounds God or rebounds on the provokers. Together these reveal God as genuinely responsive — not impassive — to human covenant action.

The jealousy-as-identity corpus (M02-E-VCG-01) reveals God as a being of exclusive passionate devotion: Exo 34:14 names jealousy as God's own name — not a description of God but a claim about what he is constitutionally. The characteristic images a God for whom exclusive devotion is not a preference but an identity-level reality.

Across the cluster, the verse evidence reveals a God whose character includes genuine, structured, morally calibrated anger. He is not the unmoved mover of philosophical abstraction but a being who burns with moral passion, holds wrath as judicial verdict, maintains indignation as a standing moral stance, and jealously protects exclusive covenantal relationship. The cluster as a whole images God as the one in whom moral seriousness is constitutively absolute.

The M03 corpus reveals a God who himself grieves, is moved by grief, records grief, and responds to it. God hears Israel's groaning under slavery and remembers his covenant (Exo 2:24, Exo 6:5 — M03-E-VCG-01). God sees Hezekiah's tears and responds with healing (2Ki 20:5 — M03-A-VCG-02). God collects the psalmist's tears in a bottle and records them in a book (Psa 56:8 — M03-A-VCG-02). In all their distress God himself was afflicted (Isa 63:9 — M03-D-VCG-03). In the New Testament, the Spirit's grief at sin (Eph 4:30 — M03-C-VCG-02) and Jesus's Gethsemane soul-sorrow (Mat 26:37-38, Mar 14:34 — M03-C-VCG-03) reveal that grief is not peripheral to divine nature but deeply embedded in it. The grief M03 describes in the human person therefore images a God who is moved by loss, responsive to suffering, and capable of entering into and participating in the grief of his creatures.

The same pattern is distributed across sub-groups. In M03-A, God hears the sound of weeping (Psa 6:8) and commands its cessation as promise (Isa 30:19; Jer 31:16). In M03-B, God governs mourning — commanding it, withholding it, and reversing it (M03-B-VCG-03). In M03-C, godly grief produces repentance (2Cor 7:9, 7:11) — a pattern that mirrors God's own grief over sin (Eph 4:30). In M03-D, the psalmist's cry from distress is met by God's answering voice from his temple (Psa 18:6), showing God as attentive to grief-distress. Across sub-groups, the characteristic is consistently shown as something God observes, responds to, participates in, and governs.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The verse evidence directly attributes exultation to God himself, revealing it as a genuine divine characteristic before it is a human one. God rejoices over restored Israel with gladness (Zep 3:17 — su.s and gil_verb: "he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will exult over you with loud singing"), takes delight in prospering his people (Deu 30:9 — su.s), rejoices in Jerusalem (Isa 65:19 — gil_verb and su.s), delights in doing Israel good with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41 — su.s), and rejoices over Zion as a bridegroom over a bride (Isa 62:5 — su.s). This evidence reveals God as a being whose inner life includes triumphant, exultant delight — his exultation is not incidental but flows from his relational investment in his people and the restoration of right order. The human capacity for exultation reflects this divine character: the person who exults in YHWH images the God who exults over his people.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence explicitly attributes Joy to God across multiple registers. God is named as the one who produces and multiplies Israel's joy (Isa 9:3 — "you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you"); creates Jerusalem to be a joy and her people a gladness (Isa 65:18 — gi.lah); rejoices in his people's festive songs (Judg 9:13 — "wine that cheers God and men"); rejoices over his people with gladness (Zep 3:17 — sim.chah); rejoices in Jerusalem (Isa 65:19 — sa.mach); and rejoices over the repentant sinner (Luk 15:7 — "more joy in heaven"; Luk 15:10 — "joy before the angels of God"). In the Johannine corpus, Jesus has his own joy (Joh 15:11 — "my joy may be in you") and declares his joy fulfilled in the disciples (Joh 17:13). The evidence reveals God as a being whose inner life participates in Joy — he rejoices over his people, over restored covenant, and over recovered sinners. Joy is not merely a human response to God but a divine inner state that God himself inhabits and directs toward his creation.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Two primary evidences for the divine dimension of Suffering-Joy: (1) **Jesus' agalliao in the Holy Spirit** — Luk 10:21 ("In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father...'") — this is the clearest instance of the characteristic operating in the divine-human person; Jesus' exultation occurs in the context of the disciples having been exposed to opposition and the suffering of itinerant ministry; his Spirit-located rejoicing is not despite the context of difficulty but in and through it; (2) **Heb 12:2** — "for the joy that was set before him [he] endured the cross, despising the shame" — the cross is the suffering context; the joy set before Christ is the eschatological ground that enabled endurance of suffering. Together these reveal God's own inner life as encompassing the capacity to hold joy and suffering together without the suffering cancelling the joy. The characteristic reflects the divine image as the capacity to inhabit genuine rejoicing when circumstances press against it, because the inner being is grounded in a reality that transcends circumstances.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The M04-L-VCG-01 corpus (32 verses) is the most concentrated evidence for Gladness as a divine attribute. God's evaluative-goodness declarations across Gen 1:4–31 (seven "God saw that it was good / very good" appraisals) reveal God as a being whose inner life includes the capacity to perceive, assess, and register gladness/satisfaction in what is genuinely good. Beyond creation: God is declared good in character ("good and upright" — Psa 25:8; "good and forgiving" — Psa 86:5; "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" — Psa 145:9; "The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble" — Nah 1:7). The ki-tov declarations throughout the Psalms (100:5; 106:1; 107:1; 118:1, 29; 135:3; 136:1) establish God's goodness as an intrinsic character attribute, not a situational response. Gladness is the inner state of one who recognises and inhabits what is genuinely good — and God's character is the archetype of that goodness. In M04-O: God's covenantal goodness produces Gladness in the people (Neh 2:18 — God's good hand upon Nehemiah becomes the testimony that stirs communal resolve; Ezr 6:22 — "the Lord had made them joyful" at the Feast of Unleavened Bread). God is the origin and exemplar of the Gladness the characteristic describes.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence reveals Delight as a profoundly divine characteristic across three registers: (1) **Volitional-sovereign delight** — M04-H-VCG-01 establishes that God's delight is his sovereign will operating without external constraint: "Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases" (Psa 115:3); "whatever the Lord pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth" (Psa 135:6); Isa 46:10 — "My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose" (che.phets); Isa 55:11 — God's word accomplishes what he purposes. Divine delight and divine sovereignty are identical: God's inner pleasure is the operative principle of all his acts; (2) **Relational delight in persons** — M04-H-VCG-02 shows God's delight directed personally and redemptively: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psa 18:19; 2Sa 22:20); God delighted in Solomon and set him on the throne (1Ki 10:9; 2Ch 9:8); Isa 62:4 — God's delight in Zion becomes her new name; "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn and live" (Eze 18:23; 33:11); God delights in steadfast love, justice, and righteousness (Jer 9:24); "he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18); (3) **Affective delight in God's own word and wisdom** — Pro 8:30–31 — Wisdom was daily God's delight before creation; Jer 31:20 — Ephraim is God's "darling child," sha.a.shu.im, his cherished treasured one; Mat 3:17; 12:18; 17:5; Mar 1:11; Luk 3:22; 2Pe 1:17 — "this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (eudokeo at baptism and transfiguration); Mat 12:18 — "my soul is well pleased" — delight located in God's own soul directed toward the Son.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Three divine registers: (1) **Divine beauty as Pleasure** — Psa 27:4 names the no.am (beauty/pleasantness) of the Lord himself as the supreme object the psalmist seeks — "to gaze upon the beauty of the Lord and to inquire in his temple"; the pleasantness is an intrinsic quality of God's own being, not merely of his acts; (2) **Divine responsive Pleasure at worship** — M04-K-VCG-01 (the ni.cho.ach corpus, 38 verses) reveals God as one who receives the soothing aroma of correctly-offered sacrifice with inward satisfaction; Gen 8:21 — "the Lord smelled the pleasing aroma, the Lord said in his heart" — God's inner response to Noah's offering is a settling, calming pleasure that moves him to covenant resolve; Num 28:2 — "my pleasing aroma" — God describes the offering as his own food, claiming the pleasure-relation personally; (3) **Divine covenantal pleasantness as character** — Psa 36:8 names "the river of your delights" as flowing from God himself; Psa 90:17 — "the favor/pleasantness of the Lord our God be upon us" — divine pleasantness as gracious character directed outward toward the community; Zec 11:7, 10 — the shepherd's staff named No'am (Pleasantness/Favour) representing the quality of divine covenantal grace toward the flock.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder is the most explicitly theocentric characteristic in M04 — virtually the entire M04-I-VCG-01 corpus (61 verses) is a catalogue of divine acts that produce wonder. The evidence reveals three dimensions of God's character: (1) **God as the exclusive worker of wonders** — Psa 72:18 ("who alone does wondrous things"); Psa 86:10 ("you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God") — Wonder is not a response to a powerful class of beings but is uniquely and exclusively evoked by the one God; (2) **God's acts exceed human comprehension** — Job 5:9; 9:10 ("great things and unsearchable, marvellous things without number"); Job 37:5 ("God thunders wondrously… great things that we cannot comprehend"); Psa 40:5 ("they are more than can be told") — the incomprehensibility of God's acts is constitutive of Wonder; (3) **God's name as Wonderful** — Isa 9:6 ("his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor") — the coming child's identity inherently evokes awe; Wonder is an essential quality of Christ's being, not merely a reaction to his deeds.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across the seven characteristics, two structural categories emerge: (1) **Characteristics attributed to God fully** — Exultation (Char 1), Joy (Char 2), Gladness (Char 3), and Delight (Char 4) are all explicitly attributed to God with the same vocabulary terms used for both divine and human instances. Delight is the most fully attributed of all, spanning five distinct divine registers (sovereign will, relational, moral, trinitarian, and creative). Joy is directly located in God's inner being (Zep 3:17; Joh 15:11). Exultation uses the same su.s/gil terms for both divine exultation (Jer 32:41; Zep 3:17) and human exultation. Gladness establishes the divine evaluative-cognitive act ("God saw that it was good" — Gen 1:4–31) as the archetype of all human evaluative gladness; (2) **Characteristics partially attributed or not attributed** — Pleasure (Char 5) is attributed to God partially (ni.cho.ach divine reception; Psa 27:4's no.am as God's own beauty), but with more restriction than Chars 1–4. Wonder (Char 6) is strikingly the one characteristic Scripture does not attribute to God — Zec 8:6 explicitly distances God from the wonder-response; instead God's character is wonder-inducing rather than wonder-experiencing. Suffering-Joy (Char 7) is attributed to God only in the incarnate Christ (Luk 10:21; Heb 12:2) — it is not a divine-attribute in the same register as Chars 1–4. The cluster therefore reveals a spectrum: from fully-shared divine characteristics (Exultation, Joy, Gladness, Delight) through partially-shared (Pleasure) through creaturely-response-only (Wonder) through incarnation-specific (Suffering-Joy). This spectrum is analytically significant — the more fully a characteristic is shared with God, the more it belongs to the original created design; the less shared, the more it is a response to creaturely finitude or fallen condition.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Shame as an experienced inner state reflects God's moral seriousness and his investment in the dignity of persons. The evidence from M07-C is most direct: the God who receives Ezra's shame-before-holiness (Ezr 9:6 — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you") is a God before whom exposure is real and moral standing matters. The repeated Psalm promise that those who trust in God "will not be put to shame" (Psa 22:5; 25:2; 31:1; 119:31; Rom 5:5; 9:33; 10:11) reveals that God is the guardian of the inner dignity of those who rely on him — he takes personal responsibility for protecting them from shame's inner collapse. The M07-B evidence shows God actively deploying shame as a moral verdict (putting enemies to shame; exposing idol-makers' inner bankruptcy), revealing that shame participates in divine judgment and justice. Shame also reflects God's holiness — the fact that coming into his presence without atoned sin produces the inability to lift one's face (Ezr 9:6; Eze 36:32) reveals a God whose holiness generates the experience of shame in the morally uncleansed.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The dominant revelation in CHAR-2 is divine sovereignty over human standing. M07-D-VCG-03 (27 sha.phel verses) shows God as the primary agent of abasement: "God brings low and exalts" (1Sa 2:7, vc=21164); "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2Sa 22:28, vc=21165); "God alone executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:7, vc=21169). God's character revealed is a God for whom the proud inner disposition is intolerable, and who acts against it with terrifying sovereign force (Isa 10:33, vc=21178). Pride reaches for what belongs to God alone (Isa 2:11 — "the Lord alone will be exalted in that day"), and God's enforcement of that boundary is the judicial expression of his holiness.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 reveals God as the one who assigns and guards worth — the one whose evaluation of persons is authoritative and cannot be overridden by human contempt-judgments. Joh 8:49 (vc=35000) — "I honor my Father, and you dishonor me" — places dishonour as a relational act directed at Jesus personally, revealing a God whose worth is real and whose engagement with persons is worthy of honour. Rom 9:21 (vc=34960) — the potter's sovereign right to assign vessels for honourable or dishonorable use — reveals God as the primary worth-assigning agent; human dishonour-assignments are derivative and fallible.

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 reveals God as the standard against which moral shamefulness is measured. Paul's renunciation of "shameful, underhanded ways" (2Cor 4:2, vc=34972) is grounded in conduct that must bear "open scrutiny before God" — God's sight is the evaluative standard. Eph 5:12 (vc=34985) — deeds done in secret so morally degraded "it is shameful even to speak of them" — presupposes a moral standard before which certain conduct cannot stand. The conscience recognising shamefulness reflects God's own moral judgment about what violates the propriety of created existence.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 reveals God as the one who reverses contempt-verdicts. Act 4:11 (vc=54638) — "the stone rejected by the builders has become the cornerstone" — God overturning the contempt-verdict of the builders and establishing the rejected as the foundation. 1Cor 1:28 (vc=54643) — "God chose what is low and despised in the world to nullify things that are" — God deliberately selecting what contempt has marked as of no account, thereby exposing the contempt-assessments of the world as false. This reveals a God who specifically positions himself against contempt-generated shame by choosing, accepting, and vindicating the despised.

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 reveals God as both the standard and the source of moral innocence. The inner moral purity that CHAR-6 names — the clean conscience, the blameless will, the hands free of deliberate wrongdoing — reflects God's own moral purity in its creaturely form. Gen 20:5 (vc=22817/22821) — Abimelech's claim to have acted "in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands" — presupposes a moral standard (heart-integrity and hand-cleanness) that is real and assessable before God, who responds by acknowledging the claim (Gen 20:6). The God who can verify and acknowledge innocence is the God whose own character makes moral innocence a meaningful category.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Read across six characteristics, the cluster reveals six distinct angles on God's character — none duplicating another. Char 1 (shame as experienced inner state) reveals God as the guardian of creaturely dignity who takes personal responsibility for protecting those who trust him from shame's inner collapse (the Psalm supplication formula "let me not be put to shame" — Psa 25:2; 31:1 — presupposes this guardianship). Char 2 (enforced abasement) reveals God as the sovereign agent who corrects pride with terrifying force — "God alone executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:7). Char 3 (dishonour as worth-denial) reveals God as the authoritative worth-assigner whose evaluation of persons cannot be overridden — the potter's sovereign right (Rom 9:21) is the supreme statement of this. Char 4 (shamefulness as moral-evaluative judgment) reveals God as the moral standard: "open scrutiny before God" (2Cor 4:2) is the test against which all conduct stands. Char 5 (contempt-produced shame) reveals God as the contempt-reverser — choosing the despised to nullify the world's confident worth-assessments (1Cor 1:28; Act 4:11). Char 6 (innocence as structural counter) reveals God as the confirmer of genuine moral innocence — the one who verifies and acknowledges the innocence-claim (Gen 20:5-6). The cluster-level convergence: God operates simultaneously as guardian (Chars 1, 5), sovereign agent of correction (Char 2), authoritative worth-assigner (Chars 3, 5), moral standard (Char 4), and innocence-confirmer (Char 6). No single angle exhausts what M07 reveals about him.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The verse evidence reveals that God alone holds the prerogative of genuine exaltation, and that CHAR-1 is the creature's usurpation of that singular divine position. The structural logic is stated explicitly in the day-of-the-Lord material: Isa 2:11 (vc=34601, M08-A3-VCG-04) — "the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day"; Isa 2:17 (vc=34602, M08-A3-VCG-04) — "the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day." **[CHAR-2]** E — The verse evidence reveals that CHAR-2 (Presumptuous defiance) reflects the divine nature by standing in direct opposition to it: CHAR-2 is the creature's will asserting itself against the very limits God has established, and the evidence consistently frames God as the one who establishes those limits and judges their violation. **[CHAR-3]** E — The verse evidence reveals that CHAR-3 reflects and distorts the divine nature as the ultimate and only legitimate ground of boasting. **[CHAR-4]** E — The verse evidence reveals that CHAR-4 (vain conceit — the mind's inflated false self-picture) reflects, by inversion, God's nature as the one who gives the accurate measure by which the mind should assess itself. **[CHAR-5]** E — The verse evidence reveals that CHAR-5 reflects, by usurpation, God's nature as the sole and genuine source of all power and might. The Eze 30 corpus (vc=33996, 33997, 33998, M08-E-VCG-01): God repeatedly declares he will bring down Egypt's "proud might" — the reversal evidences God as the one who holds the genuine power that CHAR-5 misattributes to the nation. 1Ti 6:17 (vc=60878, M08-E-VCG-02): the wealthy are warned not to "set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides everything" — God as the genuine provider of all material goods is what CHAR-5 ignores in claiming wealth as a self-exaltation ground.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across all five characteristics, the cluster reveals a single structural logic: each characteristic reflects, by inversion or usurpation, a divine attribute that belongs to God alone. What surfaces when the five are compared is the graduated scope of the usurpation. CHAR-1 (Arrogant self-elevation) usurps God's prerogative of genuine exaltation — "the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" (Isa 2:11, M08-A3-VCG-04) names the eschatological resolution that CHAR-1 has deferred. CHAR-5 (Pride of power and position) usurps God's status as the sole genuine source of all power and might, with Isa 47:8 (M08-E-VCG-02) taking this to its theological extreme — the creature declaring "I am, and there is no one besides me," claiming the divine I-am. **[CHAR-2]** E — The corpus reveals God as a sovereign authority who requires and receives the inner yielding of the will from persons he has created and redeemed. The gospel-obedience cluster (M09-D-VCG-01 — Rom1:5; Rom16:26; Rom10:16; 2Th1:8) frames obedience of faith as the telos of divine disclosure — the mystery now revealed demands and elicits the will's submission. **[CHAR-3]** E — Both verses locate God's response to contrition as nearness, saving action, and indwelling presence: Psa34:18 — "the Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit"; Isa57:15 — "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite." **[CHAR-4]** E — Heb5:2 — the high priest who "can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness" — images a God who, in the institution of the Aaronic priesthood, designed a mediator whose gentleness is grounded in shared vulnerability. **[CHAR-6]** E — The corpus reveals God as one who both calls for and restores the freely-moved willing spirit. **[CHAR-1]** E — The corpus reveals that God himself is the perceiver and responder to humility in the inner person, suggesting that humility corresponds to something in the divine nature that recognises and honours it. In the ka.na evidence, God repeatedly observes the inner act of humbling (2Ch12:7 — "they have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them"), responds to it with mercy (1Ki21:29; 2Ch12:12; 2Ch34:27), and explicitly contrasts it with proud self-assertion as the posture he opposes (Jam4:6 — "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble"; 1Pe5:5). **[CLUSTER]** E — The six characteristics together image a God whose character is neither self-promoting nor coercive. Four of the six directly establish this by contrast or reflection: Humility (CHAR-1) most fully, through Christ's kenotic self-lowering in Phili2:8, images a God whose movement is downward toward the creature rather than upward in self-assertion; Submission (CHAR-2) images a God who desires the inner allegiance of the will, not only outer compliance — the gospel calls for obedience of faith as the culminating response to divine self-disclosure; Contrition (CHAR-3) images a God who is constitutionally drawn toward the broken inner state, simultaneously inhabiting transcendence and the crushed spirit (Isa57:15); Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6) images a God who calls for freely-given devotion over coerced contribution and actively restores the willing capacity when it is lost. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4) and Dignity (CHAR-5) image God more obliquely — CHAR-4 through the priestly mediator's calibrated compassion (Heb5:2), CHAR-5 through the settled moral gravity that belongs to holiness without performance. The cluster-wide pattern is: M09 images the divine character through six variations on a single theme — *God neither asserts himself through force nor receives forced returns; he moves freely toward the creature and calls for freely-offered response*. The structural opposite of the cluster (M08 Pride/self-assertion) thus images the inversion of the divine character.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Wilful sinning reveals the character of God negatively: it is the one thing the verse evidence consistently shows God holding the person morally accountable for, which illuminates God as the moral reference point against whom all wilful sin is ultimately directed. Psa 51:4 states the paradigmatic formula — "Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight" — locating God as the primary party offended by every act of wilful sinning, even sins with human victims (David's sin against Bathsheba and Uriah). Gen 39:9 (Joseph) frames the refusal to sin as inseparable from reverence for God: "How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" — implying that God's moral character defines the boundary the sinning will crosses. The characteristic thus reflects God's holiness by negation: wilful sinning is the inner act that violates what God is.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The three mechanisms reveal God's character through contrast and implication. (1) *God as the one who does not entice through desire*: Jam 1:14 — "each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire" — the verse is set within a context (Jam 1:13 — not quoted but implied) that explicitly distinguishes God from the enticement mechanism: God does not entice toward evil. The mechanism of desire-enticement is constitutively not-God's mode of operation. (2) *God as the ground of covenantal identity*: Act 21:21 — the apostasy charge describes forsaking Moses — the covenantal framework given through Moses is the gift of God's self-revelation; forsaking that covenantal identity is a defection from what God established. (3) *God as the one whose image requires authenticity*: Gal 2:13 — sunupokrinomai (collective hypocrisy) falsifies identity and corrupts community integrity; authenticity before God and in community is what the characteristic destroys.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The 112-verse corpus reveals God's character through five distinct dimensions. (1) *God as the one whose glory constitutes the standard from which sin's universality is measured*: Rom 3:23 — "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" — God's glory is the normative standard; sin is defined as the universal human falling-short of that glory, revealing God as the one in whose image humanity was made to live but from whose likeness all have departed. (2) *God as the one who alone can forgive sins*: the VCG-02 forgiveness register — Mar 2:7; Luk 5:21 — "who can forgive sins but God alone?" — God's exclusive authority to forgive is what makes Jesus's forgiveness-declarations a claim to divine identity. The character of God as the exclusive forgiver is the foundation on which the entire VCG-02 corpus rests. (3) *God as the one who condemns sin in the flesh through the Son*: Rom 8:3 — "he condemned sin in the flesh" — God's active judicial movement against sin through the incarnation reveals his moral seriousness and salvific intent simultaneously. (4) *God as the one whose holiness requires propitiation and purification*: Heb 2:17; Heb 1:3 — sin creates an offense requiring propitiation and a defilement requiring purification; both reveal God as holy in a way that cannot simply absorb sin's presence. (5) *God as the one whose new-covenant promise is specifically the removal of sin*: Rom 11:27 — "when I take away their sins" — God's covenantal commitment is defined by what he will do about sin.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Sin as enslaving power reveals God's character primarily through the liberation it requires. (1) *God as the liberator from sin's mastery*: Joh 8:34 — "everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin" — Jesus names the slavery as the condition requiring the freedom that the Son can give (the broader Joh 8:36 context: "if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed" — implied by the slavery statement). (2) *God as the source of the indwelling seed that prevents sin's dominion*: 1Jo 3:9 — "no one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him" — the divine birth and the indwelling seed are the counter-powers to sin's enslaving function; these are God-given. (3) *God as protector against sin's dominion*: 1Jo 5:18 — "he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him" — God actively protects the born-of-God person from sin's re-enslavement; the protecting agent (born of God — Christ) is the divine counter to the enslaving power.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The 205-verse corpus reveals God's character across five dimensions. (1) *God as the one who sees and records*: Exo 32:33 — "whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book" — God maintains a divine register; Gen 18:20 — "the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave" — the sin has reached God as a measurable, audible reality. (2) *God as the one who remembers sin precisely*: Jer 14:10 — "he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins"; Hos 13:12 — "his sin is kept in store" — the divine memory is reliable and permanent. (3) *God as the one who searches for sin*: Job 10:6 — "that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin" (VCG-03) — God actively investigates and scrutinises the person. (4) *God as the one who blots out the record*: Isa 43:25 — "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" — God can erase the divine record as a sovereign act. (5) *God as the one who bears the burden of his people's sin*: Isa 43:24 — "you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities" — the accumulated record is experienced by God as a burden on the divine-human relationship.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The 34-verse corpus reveals God's character across four dimensions. (1) *God as the one who provides the means of atonement*: Exo 29:36 — the daily sin offering is God's prescribed institution; Lev 23:27/28 — the Day of Atonement is God's appointed holy convocation; he has established the framework within which forgiveness is available. (2) *God as the one who does not count trespasses*: 2Cor 5:19 — "in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them" — the divine disposition is toward non-imputation, not toward accumulating the record against the person. (3) *God as the one who provides blood-atonement*: Mat 26:28 — "my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" — God himself provides the atoning blood rather than requiring the creature to supply it. (4) *God as the one whose forgiveness has eschatological scope*: Mar 3:28 — "all sins will be forgiven the children of man" — God's forgiveness has universal potential scope, with only one exception (Mar 3:29 — blasphemy against the Holy Spirit).

**[CHAR-15]** E — The 8-verse corpus reveals God's character across three dimensions. (1) *God as the one who holds generations accountable to the ancestral record*: Isa 43:27 — "your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me" — God addresses present Israel through the lens of ancestral failure; the present generation is addressed as the inheritors of what the first father began. (2) *God as the one who responds to prolonged corporate sin with judgment*: Jer 8:14 — "the Lord our God has doomed us to perish... because we have sinned against the Lord" — the corporate sinning of the present generation in continuity with the past produces divine doom; (3) *God as the redeemer who saves from ancestral backsliding*: Eze 37:23 — "I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God" — God's redemptive purpose addresses the inherited sinning pattern from outside it.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The 64-verse corpus reveals God's character across four dimensions. (4) *God as the one who constitutes sinner-status through Adam*: Rom 5:19 — "by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners" — God's judgment of Adam's act imputes the sinner-identity to all.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The 97-verse corpus reveals God's character across four dimensions. (1) *God as the one who sees guilt when the person cannot hide it*: Jer 2:22 — "though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord God" — divine omniscience makes guilt permanently visible regardless of the person's concealment effort; Psa 69:5 — "the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you" — the divine gaze penetrates guilt's concealment. **[CHAR-18]** E — The 162-verse corpus reveals God's character across four dimensions. (1) *God as moral auditor who measures and tracks iniquity to completion*: Gen 15:16 — "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" — God tracks iniquity as a measurable quantity with a threshold; Hos 13:12 — "the iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is kept in store" — God maintains a sealed record; Psa 90:8 — "you have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence" — nothing is hidden from his omniscient gaze. **[CHAR-19]** E — The 147-verse corpus reveals God's character across five dimensions.
