**[CHAR-2]** E — Unintentional sinning reveals the character of God primarily through the remedial system God established to address it — a system that reflects God's moral seriousness about sin at every intentionality level, and his provision for the person who has sinned without knowing. Lev 4:2 — "if anyone sins unintentionally in any of the Lord's commandments about things not to be done" — presupposes a God who holds commandments whose violation is real even without deliberate defiance. The prescribed remedy (Num 15:28 — "the priest shall make atonement before the Lord for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally... and he shall be forgiven") reveals a God who is both morally exacting (even inadvertent violation requires remedy) and graciously provident (a remedy is prescribed and forgiveness follows). The character of God visible here is *holy and merciful simultaneously*: the holiness requires that inadvertent sin be addressed; the mercy ensures that address is available.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The 101-verse corpus reveals God's character across five dimensions. **[CHAR-21]** E — The 64-verse corpus reveals God's character across four dimensions. **[CHAR-3]** E — Confession reveals God's character in two directions. (1) *God as the one to whom confession is rightly directed*: throughout the corpus, genuine confession is oriented toward God as the primary offended party — "I have sinned against the Lord" (1Sa 7:6; Jer 14:20; Dan 9:11; Luk 15:18/21). God's moral authority as the standard against which sin is measured makes him the proper recipient of confession — which reveals him as *holy and morally sovereign*, the reference point of all moral reality. (2) *God as the one who cancels sin upon genuine confession*: Eze 33:16 — "None of the sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him" — reveals God as a God who holds a moral record but is prepared to erase it when the person turns. The characteristic exists in a landscape where confession is heard and responded to by a God who both takes sin seriously and provides for its cancellation.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Conscience suppression reveals the character of God primarily through contrast and consequence. Jer 2:35 — God declares: "Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned'" — God's response to the false innocence claim reveals him as a God who sees through self-deception and judges not only the sin but the denial of it. God's moral omniscience is the implicit premise: the person may suppress awareness of their sin, but God's awareness is undiminished. Jer 16:10 — the people ask "what sin have we committed?" in the face of declared judgment — God's announcement of judgment presupposes his accurate moral knowledge even when the persons themselves lack it. The characteristic thus reveals God as the one whose perception cannot be suppressed: what the conscience suppresses in the human, God sees clearly and will bring to judgment.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Refusal to repent reveals God's character primarily through the expectation it violates and the response it draws. Neh 9:29 — "you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey" — reveals God as a God who warns before judging, who desires turning, and who regards the refusal to turn as a presumptuous overriding of his patient initiative. The God who warns is a God of moral patience and persistent invitation; the human refusal to turn is the creature's rejection of that invitation. Heb 10:26 — "if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins" — reveals that God's provision of sacrifice presupposes the creature's willingness to engage it; refusal to turn after knowing the truth closes off the divine provision. The characteristic reveals God as one whose moral provisions (sacrifice, warning, the turn) are refused by the creature that should receive them.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Habitual defection reveals God's character through two lenses. (1) *God as the one who is sinned against habitually*: 2Ki 17:7 — "the people of Israel had sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt" — God is the covenant Lord whose redemptive action is the context against which habitual sinning occurs. The relationship God established is the relational framework within which the recurring defection takes place. (2) *God as the one whose patience is provoked for an extended period*: Heb 3:17 — "with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned?" — God's provocation over forty years reveals his holiness responding to sustained rebellion — not immediate termination but prolonged moral witness sustained across a whole generation's habitual sinning. The character revealed is: morally serious toward sustained defection, patient in the sense of bearing it over time, and ultimately resolute in consequence (the bodies fell in the wilderness).

**[CHAR-7]** E — Contagious sin reveals the character of God through three lenses. (1) *God as the one who warns in advance*: Exo 23:33 and Deu 20:18 are preventive commands — God specifies before entry into Canaan that foreign nations will "make Israel sin" and that being taught their abominable practices will result in sinning against the Lord. God's foreknowledge of the contagion mechanism and his preventive instruction reveal him as a God who sees the transmission pathways of sin before they operate. (2) *God as the one who holds leaders accountable for what they transmitted*: 1Ki 16:2 — God directly charges the king: "you have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger" — naming the contagious transmission as the specific indictment. 1Ki 21:22 — God declares Ahab's house will be destroyed "because you have made Israel to sin." (3) *God as the one who is provoked through transmitted sin*: 1Ki 14:22; 1Ki 16:13/26 — Israel's sins (transmitted from the leader) provoke God to anger through their idolatrous objects. The communal sin that leaders generate reaches God as a relational offence from the community.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Political revolt reveals God's character primarily through one distinctive verse: 2Ch 21:10 — "So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day... At that time Libnah also revolted from his rule, *because he had forsaken the Lord, the God of his fathers*." The causal connection — Jehoram forsaking the Lord producing Libnah's revolt — reveals God as the constitutive source of covenantal-political order. When the king abandons God, the political coherence that God's covenantal relationship sustained begins to fragment. God's character is revealed as the foundation of ordered authority: his being forsaken produces political disorder; his presence maintains the relational-political structure. The remaining verses address political revolt at the human-authority level without explicit God-reference, but 2Ch 21:10 establishes that God is the ultimate ground of the authority structure from which revolt breaks.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Sinful speech reveals God's character through three lenses. (1) *God as the exclusive holder of divine prerogatives*: Mar 2:7 — "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" and Joh 10:33 — "you, being a man, make yourself God" — blasphemy is defined as the improper claiming of what belongs exclusively to God. The characteristic reveals God as the one whose authority, identity, and prerogatives are absolute and non-transferable. (2) *God as the one whose Spirit cannot be blasphemed without eternal consequence*: Mat 12:31 — "the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" — God's Spirit is the one reality against which blasphemous speech carries irreversible moral weight. (3) *God as the one against whom the beast's constitutive speech is directed*: Rev 13:6 — "It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven" — God's name, presence, and people are the targets of the most extreme form of sinful speech.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Wickedness as settled person-identity is definitionally structured against the divine nature rather than derived from it. Job 34:10 states explicitly that it is "far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong" (re.sha) — God's nature is declared the absolute structural opposite of what wickedness names. This structural opposition is the primary theological datum: wickedness does not reflect or image any divine attribute; it reveals the divine character by negation and contrast. Psa 11:5 reinforces this — "his soul hates the wicked" — establishing that wickedness is specifically the object of divine loathing, not a divine attribute. What the evidence reveals about God through this characteristic is therefore apophatic: God's righteousness, justice, and wholeness are defined in part by their absolute incompatibility with the inner orientation that wickedness describes. The wicked person is the anti-image of what God is, and the universe of 190 verses sustains this polarity throughout.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Evil as constitutional inner nature is definitionally opposed to God's nature rather than derived from it. Rom 9:14 (vc=65872 — VCG-06) poses and immediately rejects the charge of unrighteousness (adikia) against God — divine sovereign choice is explicitly not constitutionally evil. The verse establishes that God's nature is the structural antithesis of constitutional inner evil. Rom 12:9 (vc=14417 — VCG-06) commands the community to "abhor what is evil" — this command reflects the divine moral character that stands against evil as constitutional nature. 1Cor 13:6 (vc=14341 — VCG-06) frames love (the divine character) as refusing to "rejoice at wrongdoing" — unrighteousness is what love's opposite produces. The evidence collectively reveals God as constitutionally righteous and the human constitutional evil as an inversion of that righteousness.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic reveals God's nature primarily through the divine response: active revulsion, loathing, and rejection directed at specific inner moral conditions. Pro 6:16 (vc=65952 — VCG-05) frames God as the one who "hates" and finds "abomination" in seven specific attitudes and acts — establishing that God's holiness is not merely a passive state of purity but an active repugnance toward moral corruption. Pro 3:32 (vc=1686 — VCG-02) contrasts the abomination of the devious person with divine intimacy: "the devious person is an abomination to the Lord, but the upright are in his confidence" — revealing that God's moral character involves both rejection of the crooked and intimate sharing with the upright. Pro 11:20 (vc=1677 — VCG-01) and Pro 16:5 (vc=1689 — VCG-02) confirm that God's revulsion is specifically directed at inner-being conditions (crooked heart, arrogant heart). Luk 16:15 (vc=21 — VCG-02) reveals that what humans exalt as admirable is an abomination in God's sight — God's evaluative standard is categorically different from human social evaluation. The evidence collectively reveals God as morally sensitive at the inner-being level, responding to the quality of the heart with either revulsion or delight.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Idolatrous abomination reveals God's character primarily through the divine-jealousy and divine-exclusivity dimensions: God is a moral being whose holiness cannot coexist with false devotion. Deu 32:16 (vc=65938 — VCG-02): "They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger" — the divine response is jealousy and anger, revealing that God's character includes a morally serious covenantal exclusivity that is violated by idolatrous attachment. Eze 5:11 (vc=65969 — VCG-05): because the sanctuary was defiled with abominations "I will withdraw. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity" — God's holiness is incompatible with idolatrous defilement; the divine presence is forced to withdraw. Jer 44:4 (vc=65966 — VCG-04): "do not do this abomination that I hate" — God's character involves intense moral hatred of idolatrous devotion. The evidence reveals God as a relational being whose holiness is covenantally exclusive — he cannot share devotion with idol-objects without responding with jealousy, anger, and withdrawal.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic reveals God's nature primarily through the divine response to iniquity as an active inner process: God perceives, hates, and judges it. Psa 5:5 (vc=38237 — VCG-03): "you hate all evildoers" — God's active moral hatred is directed at those whose inner character is constituted by the working of iniquity; the hating is not passive disapproval but a settled divine stance toward those who persistently generate evil from within. Job 11:11 (vc=38206 — VCG-04): "For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it?" — God perceives and registers iniquity even when hidden from others, revealing his character as omniscient moral witness. Psa 94:23 (vc=38249 — VCG-03): "He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness" — God's character includes active retributive justice that returns the inner scheming of iniquity upon those who practise it. The evidence reveals God as the moral pole against which active inner scheming is measured and judged.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic reveals God's nature primarily through what the characteristic attacks: God's name, his dwelling, and his glory — the very realities that blasphemy targets. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): the beast "opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven" — God's name and dwelling are the specific objects of blasphemous contempt, revealing God as a named, dwelling, glory-bearing being whose character and presence are the pole against which defiant speech defines itself. Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): "they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory" — the withheld glory reveals that God's character warrants and invites glory; blasphemy is precisely the refusal to render what is due. Rom 2:24 (vc=14357 — VCG-02): God's name is "blasphemed among the Gentiles" — his name exists to be honoured and known, not dishonoured. The characteristic reveals God as the morally serious, glory-bearing, name-holding personal being whose honour is the target of evil expressed through speech.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across all six characteristics, God's nature is revealed apophatically — the M10b cluster defines the divine character by its absolute incompatibility with every form of inner evil it names. The cluster reveals five distinct divine properties through the six characteristics' evidence: (1) God is structurally incapable of wickedness (Char 1: Job 34:10 — "far be it from God that he should do wickedness") — the moral order itself presupposes divine righteousness as its ground; (2) God is constitutionally righteous — the opposite of constitutionally evil (Char 2: Rom 9:14 rejects divine unrighteousness; Mat 7:11 frames human evil against divine goodness); (3) God is actively revulsed by corrupt moral character — his holiness responds to inner moral corruption with active revulsion, not passive disapproval (Char 3: Pro 6:16 — "hates"; Pro 11:1 — "abomination to the Lord"); (4) God's holiness is covenantally exclusive — he cannot share devotion with idol-objects without responding with jealousy and withdrawal (Char 4: Deu 32:16 — jealousy provoked; Eze 5:11 — withdrawal); (5) God perceives, hates, and judges active iniquity-scheming as an omniscient moral witness who returns iniquity upon its practitioner (Char 5: Psa 5:5; Psa 94:23). The cluster's sixth characteristic (Char 6) reveals God as the glory-bearing, name-holding personal being whose honour is the specific target of blasphemous evil speech. The cluster collectively reveals God as: righteous-not-wicked, constitutional-goodness-not-constitutional-evil, revulsion-at-abomination, covenantally-exclusive, omniscient-moral-witness, and glory-bearing — six faces of the divine character disclosed by what M10b opposes.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The ritual defilement-state reflects, by structural contrast, the holiness and categorical purity of God. The characteristic operates as the condition that is incompatible with the divine presence, and this incompatibility is theologically explicit in the evidence. Lev 15:31 names the stakes directly: the people's uncleanness must be kept separate from them "lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst." The divine dwelling cannot coexist with the defiled state — the defilement-state reflects God's character by being precisely what God is not. Lev 11:44 makes the positive mirroring equally explicit: "I am the Lord your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing." Ritual purity is the creaturely image of divine holiness; the defilement-state is its direct contradiction. The characteristic thus reveals that God's nature is one of absolute categorical distinction — holy/unclean are not merely labels but ontological realities before him.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The moral-inner defilement-state reveals God's character primarily by contradiction: the characteristic is what God is not, and its presence in the inner person marks the distance between the creature and the Creator. The most direct evidence is Isa 6:5 (M10c-C-VCG-01): confronted by divine holiness ("my eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts"), the prophet's immediate response is the recognition that his lips — his inner-moral organ — are unclean. The holiness of God is the revealing force; the defilement-state is what that holiness exposes. Similarly, 1Th 4:7 (M10c-C-VCG-02): "God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness" — the divine calling is defined as holiness, and the moral-inner defilement-state is named as what the divine calling opposes and moves the person away from. God's character — as holy, as morally pure in all inner motivation — is the standard that makes the moral-inner defilement-state visible as a condition of the inner person.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The corporate/covenantal defilement characteristic reveals God's character primarily through the categories of divine holiness, covenantal faithfulness, and the sanctity of the divine name. The characteristic operates as what violates these divine realities. Num 35:34 (M10c-D-VCG-04): "you shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the Lord dwell in the midst of the people of Israel" — God's dwelling presence establishes the boundary that defilement violates; his holiness requires a clean habitation. Eze 43:7 (M10c-D-VCG-03): "the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name" — the divine name is a reality that can be defiled, revealing that God's name is a sacred relational extension of his person that the covenant people's conduct either honours or degrades. Eze 5:11 (M10c-D-VCG-03): defilement of the sanctuary provokes divine withdrawal — "I will withdraw; my eye will not spare" — revealing that God's covenantal presence is not unconditional and responds to covenantal defilement with withdrawal. The characteristic thus reveals God as one whose holiness, name, and dwelling presence constitute real relational vulnerabilities that the covenant people's corporate conduct directly affects.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Characteristic 4 (Defilement by external spiritual agency) reveals God's character primarily through the dynamics of authority and restoration. The characteristic reveals what God is not (the source of defiling agency) and what God does (exercise sovereign authority over defiling agents and restore the defiled person). Mar 3:11 (M10c-E-VCG-03): unclean spirits "fell down before him and cried out, 'You are the Son of God'" — the spirits' recognition of divine identity reveals God as the one before whom every defiling spiritual force is compelled to bow. Luk 4:36 (VCG-03): "with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!" — God's authority over the defiling agents is sovereign and effective. Luk 6:18 (VCG-02): "those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured" — restoration of wholeness is the divine act. The characteristic reveals a God whose authority is supreme over all defiling forces and whose disposition toward the defiled person is one of restorative power.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across all four characteristics, the cluster reveals God's nature through a single convergent logic: every form of defilement is what God is not, and the revelation of his holiness is what makes the defilement visible. Characteristic 1 surfaces this through the incompatibility of the ritual state with divine habitation (Lev 15:31 — "lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle") and through the positive mirroring of Lev 11:44 ("I am holy... you shall not defile yourselves"). Characteristic 2 surfaces it through the moral standard that exposes the condition: God's holiness as the revealing force at Isa 6:5 and the divine calling defined as holiness at 1Th 4:7. Characteristic 3 extends the revelation to the sacral relational extensions of God's person — his name (Eze 43:7), his sanctuary (Eze 5:11), his land (Num 35:34) — showing that defilement harms what God has extended of himself into the covenant community's life. Characteristic 4 adds the dimension of authority: the spirits' involuntary prostration before Christ (Mar 3:11) reveals God as the sovereign before whom every defiling force must bow. The cluster as a whole thus surfaces a God whose holiness is positively expressed as authority (Char 4), as sacral personal extension (Char 3), as moral-calling standard (Char 2), and as categorical cleanness (Char 1) — and the defilement cluster is the negative space that makes all four dimensions visible.

questions.section: T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
questions.question_text: Across the characteristic's verses, is it ever borne by God himself or only by the creature, and what does that pattern of presence or absence indicate for its place in the human person and in the divine image?

findings.session_b_note:
Yes. Scripture attributes forgiveness to God explicitly and in multiple registers:

- As **disposition** (sal.lach — the adjective: God is "forgiving" as a character description, Psa 86:5)
- As **possession** (se.li.chah — abstract noun: "with you *there is* forgiveness," Psa 130:4; Dan 9:9)
- As **exclusive act** (sa.lach — the verb: God alone forgives with this root; Mar 2:7 in the NT: "who can forgive sins but God alone?")
- As **declared NT authority** (G0863H — Jesus claiming and exercising the divine act, Luk 7:47-48; Joh 20:23 — the Spirit-given authority to forgive extended to the disciples)

What this reveals about significance in the human person: the human capacity to forgive is a derived capacity — it mirrors and participates in something that originates in God. OBS-064-003 notes: "The spirit-level origin of forgiveness (divine disposition, divine act) is not merely theological framing but is embedded in the lexical restriction of the OT salach vocabulary." The significance for the human person is therefore: when a human forgives (using G0863H in the NT), they are exercising an act whose deepest structural origin is divine. The human act of forgiveness is an imaging of divine character, not a purely natural or social capacity.

Yes — extensively. G5485 charis in group 888-001 names grace as "sovereign, unmerited divine disposition." H2580 chen in 889-001 names "divine relational favour." G5487 charitoō (Luk 1:28 anchor) names God's act of bestowing grace as a completed act that transforms the recipient's standing. findings.session_b_note:
Scripture attributes compassion to God with unusual directness, frequency, and vocabulary density. The GOD_AS_SUBJECT flag is warranted for H2587 chan.nun (13 occurrences, almost exclusively divine epithet), H2617B che.sed (predominant divine referent across Psalter, prophets, and historical books), H5150 ni.chum (2/3 occurrences divine), H7358 re.chem (God as actor over the womb in ~9/25 occurrences), H2551 chem.lah (Gen 19:16), G3627 oikteirō (Rom 9:15, exclusively divine sovereignty), G4697 splanchnizō (Jesus as primary subject in Gospels), and G4184 polusplanchnos (Jas 5:11) — as confirmed in the Pass 2 God-as-Subject table.

What does this attribution reveal about the significance of compassion in the human person?

Two implications follow from the data:

First, compassion in the human person is a reflection of something that belongs primarily and essentially to God. The attribution of compassion to God is not metaphorical embellishment — it is the primary usage, and human compassion is derivative. The human person's capacity for compassion is therefore not merely a natural emotional response but a participation in the character of the one in whose image the person is made. This is reinforced by the fact that the RACHAM root is anatomical (re.chem, womb) — the human person's body is the ground from which the vocabulary of divine compassion is drawn. The direction of meaning flows from the human body to the divine inner life, but the direction of significance flows the other way: what the human experiences somatically, God possesses constitutively.

Second, the divine character formula of Exod 34:6 (rachum ve-channum) functions as the standard of inner being that human compassion aspires to reflect. Joel 2:13 explicitly deploys this formula as the ground for human repentance and heart-rending ("return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful" — SD-029). The divine character is not merely the source of compassion but the norm against which human compassion is measured.

findings.session_b_note:
Scripture does not explicitly attribute contrition to God as a divine characteristic. The vocabulary of this registry (dkh, ktt, nkh — crushing, being broken, being smitten) is consistently applied to human subjects or to the Servant (Isa 53:5), not to God as the one who is contrite. God is the subject who crushes (Psa 44:19 — "you have broken us"; Psa 51:8 — "the bones that you have broken"), not the one who is crushed.

The structural logic runs in one direction: divine holiness produces contrite collapse in the human; divine nearness responds to that collapse. Contrition is not a divine attribute in the verse evidence — it is the characteristically creaturely response to the holy God.

This directional asymmetry is analytically significant. It means contrition does not image God by resembling God in this quality (as, for example, love images a God who is love). Rather, contrition images God by imaging the *right creaturely response* to divine reality — the appropriate form of human inner being before the holy God. The significance for the human person is that contrition is not optional piety but the structurally correct inner posture for a creature before the Creator-God. Its absence (Jer 44:10) is not merely a personal failing but a failure of creaturely orientation.

findings.session_b_note:
Scripture does not use the explicit vocabulary of fellowship (koinōnia, chavar, chaver) to describe God's own inner life or inter-Trinitarian relations within the verse evidence of this registry. However, God is represented as the *source and enabler* of fellowship in the highest register (2Pe 1:4 — divine nature participation) and as the *agent of fellowship-action* (Eze 37:19 — active joining). The attribution is functional rather than direct: God does not describe himself as a *fellow* or participant in the same way he describes himself as loving or merciful, but his actions constitute fellowship at its deepest level.

This has a significant implication for the human person: if fellowship in its highest form is what God grants access to (his own nature), and what God enacts (joining of the divided), then the human capacity for fellowship is not merely a social faculty. It is the creaturely analogue of a divine activity. The human person who participates genuinely in fellowship is doing something that structurally resembles what God does when he joins the divided into one.

**Observation:** The NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 13 of 15 terms means that detailed theological analysis of the Hebrew and Greek vocabulary in divine-attribution contexts is not present in the data. This is a limitation on what can be said with precision here. The claim above is grounded in verse observation, not word-level analysis.

findings.session_b_note: Scripture attributes goodness to God extensively and explicitly. Psa 119:68 ("You are good"), Psa 34:8 ("the Lord is good"), Psa 100:5 and Ps 106:1 / 107:1 / 118:1 (doxological refrain "for he is good"), Lam 3:25 ("the Lord is good to those who wait for him"), Rom 11:22 (God's chrēstotēs), Eph 2:7 (God's chrēstotēs in Christ). The attribution reveals that goodness in the human person is not an independent achievement but a participation in and reflection of an attribute that originates in God. Human goodness is derivative by design — it is what being made in the image of the good God looks like in a creature. This has direct significance: the human person who embodies goodness is expressing their created nature; the human person who fails to do so is in a condition of departure from original design. (OBS-067-OBS-001, OBS-067-OBS-006)

findings.session_b_note: Scripture attributes love to God across both testaments and with unprecedented density in R103 — 14+ GOD-dominant groups (OBS-103-034). The attribution operates at three levels: (a) love as God's relational disposition toward persons (chesed-GOD group 536-001; agapaō-GOD group 571-002; rachamim-GOD group 544-001); (b) love as God's inner-being experience — God's soul has a beloved (Jer 12:7, OBS-103-086), God's inner organs move with compassion (Jer 31:20, Isa 63:15, OBS-103-106, OBS-103-117), God grieves the withdrawal of his love; (c) love as what God is ontologically (1Jo 4:8 — held via PH2-103-004). The significance for the human person: because love is constitutive of God's being, it is the primary characteristic through which the human person bears the divine image. A human person who loves is not merely imitating a divine behaviour but reflecting the divine nature. The love-capacity is the image-capacity.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — Scripture explicitly and repeatedly attributes mercy to God. **[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes, explicitly and repeatedly. "The Lord is righteous in all his ways" (Psa 145:17); "just and upright is he" (Deu 32:4); "righteous Father" (Joh 17:25). The attribution reveals that righteousness in God is prior to and constitutive of everything else — before law, before covenant, before creation. This means righteousness in the human person is not an achievement but a participation in something that already fully exists in God. The human instance is always secondary and derivative; its significance in the person is precisely that it reflects and images what is primary in God.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — "born of him" who is righteous (1Jo 2:29); "the righteousness of God" in Christ (2Cor 5:21, VSG M26-A2-008). The attribution of righteousness to God reveals that when the human person possesses it, they are participating in something of transcendent origin. In the OT, this explains why the righteous person can appeal to God on the basis of their righteousness (Psa 7:8; 18:20, VSG 942-001) — the appeal works because righteousness in the person reflects and aligns with righteousness in God.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — "I the Lord speak the truth; I declare what is right" (Isa 45:19); the Messianic scepter of uprightness (Heb 1:8). That God possesses and expresses uprightness reveals that straightness/level-ness in the human person is not a merely human virtue — it is an imaging of divine character. The human who "walks in uprightness" (Pro 14:2) is walking in alignment with the directional quality of God himself.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — God is "just and the justifier" (Rom 3:26). The dual attribution is crucial: God does not set aside his justice to justify — he is the righteous one who justifies. This reveals that human justification is not God relaxing his standards but God expressing his righteousness through a new mode. The significance for the human person: justification is not a legal fiction but a genuine moral transformation grounded in the one who is himself righteous.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Rom 12:19; Heb 10:30). The exclusive attribution of retributive authority to God reveals that avenging justice in the human is always derivative, commissioned, and bounded. The magistrate is "God's servant, an avenger" (Rom 13:4) — not an autonomous agent of retribution. The significance: human retributive action is legitimate only when it images and serves divine retributive justice, not when it expresses personal vengeance.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — God condemns sin (Rom 8:3); his judgments are just (Rev 15:3; 19:2). The verse evidence attributes condemnation to God as a judicial act expressing his righteousness. The significance for the human person: condemnation is a real and serious verdict because the God who passes it is genuinely righteous. The freedom from condemnation (VSG 4846-002) is therefore a profound inner-being reality — not merely an administrative acquittal but a status secured before the actually-righteous God.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — God counts faith as righteousness (Rom 4:3–11); God is heart-knower (Act 1:24). The attribution of reckoning to God reveals that the human capacity for moral reckoning images a divine faculty. The significance: the human inner act of moral reckoning (logizomai in Rom 6:11; 8:18) participates in a mode of knowing and assigning worth that God himself performs. Human reckoning is an image of divine reckoning, which is why Paul can instruct believers to "count yourselves dead to sin" as a spiritually real act.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Scripture does not attribute wickedness or injustice to God — precisely the opposite: "without iniquity" (Deu 32:4); "he does no injustice" (Zep 3:5). The significance of this non-attribution: wickedness in the human person is not a divine quality distorted — it is the absence of a divine quality. Wickedness is not an alternative to righteousness; it is the failure of righteousness. The human who is ra.sha is a person in whom the image is broken at the righteousness point.

**[CLUSTER]** Scripture's explicit attribution of righteousness to God is the single most theologically significant fact about this cluster. It means that every sub-group is not studying a human quality that God happens also to possess — it is studying a divine quality that humans participate in, image, fail to image, or need to receive from outside themselves.

findings.finding_value: Yes — extensively and with unusual directness. The attribution is explicit in at least five distinct registers: (1) the divine character formula (Exo 34:6 and its 7+ echo verses); (2) divine self-declaration in blessing (Gen 12:2; 22:17 — "I will bless"); (3) the divine inner pleasure as the ground of blessing (eudokia — Luk 2:14; Phili 2:13); (4) the NT grace-theology corpus (charis — Rom 3:24; Eph 2:8; Gal 1:15); (5) the divine acceptance and delight vocabulary (ra.tsah — 1Ch 29:17; Isa 42:1). findings.finding_value: M01-A does not attribute reverential fear to God. The set-aside of Deu 32:27 (divine apprehension) was confirmed at Phase 7 — outside programme scope. The Fear of Isaac (Gen 31:42; 31:53, M01-A-VCG-06) uses "fear" as a divine name, signifying that God is the object of the fear, not its subject. No M01-A verse attributes God-fearing to God himself.

M01-B's acute fear is not attributed to God. The Mar 14:33 material (Jesus in Gethsemane, ekthambeo) describes Jesus experiencing anguished horror at approaching suffering — this is the nearest evidence, though the term there names awe-laden distress rather than fear of threat. It is routed to M01-B-VCG-01. Its significance is noted: if authentic, it suggests acute alarm is not alien to the incarnate Son, but the evidence is a single instance of the ekthambeo term and warrants caution about over-reading.

Terror as a quality is attributed to God's acts (e.g. Exo 23:27 "God's terror") but as an instrument God deploys, not a state God experiences. The characteristic is God's weapon, not God's experience.

Scripture does not attribute fear as an inner experience to God within M01's evidence base. The set-aside of Deu 32:27 removed the one possible instance of divine inner apprehension. Fear is consistently and exclusively a creaturely response — to divine holiness, to threat, to judgment. This silence is itself significant: it establishes fear as definitively creaturely in structure. The significance for the human person is that fear is the appropriate posture of the creature before the Creator — not a shared property between them, but the asymmetrical relational posture that marks the creature's proper position.

Scripture explicitly and pervasively attributes anger, wrath, indignation, burning rage, and jealousy to God. The attribution is so dominant across M02 that the human instances are the minority. Specific attributions: wrath (orgē) to God at Rom 1:18; burning anger (cha.ron) to God at Exo 15:7; indignation (za.am noun) to God at Psa 78:49; provocation of God to anger (ka.as) from Deu 4:25 through Hos 12:14; divine jealousy (qan.na) at Exo 20:5; Exo 34:14; divine jealousy (qin.ah) at Eze 36:5. The significance for the human person is that anger/wrath in the human inner being is not a regrettable infirmity but an image-bearing capacity — the human person is designed to bear, in creaturely form, something that God himself constitutionally is. When a human is rightly angry at injustice, they reflect the moral seriousness of God.

The cluster's preponderance of divine-subject verses is itself a finding about significance. Anger is not primarily framed in Scripture as a human problem to be solved but as a divine attribute to be respected and, in the human person, rightly ordered. The frequency of divine attribution places this characteristic at the centre of Scripture's portrait of God's moral nature.

Scripture does explicitly attribute grief to God. Three evidences stand out across the corpus. First, the Spirit's grief at sin is named directly: "grieve not the Holy Spirit" (Eph 4:30 — M03-C-VCG-02); the Spirit is personally affected by the community's choices, showing grief as an appropriate responsive inner-being state in the Spirit's person. Second, Jesus's Gethsemane grief is soul-located at maximum depth ("very sorrowful, even to death" — Mat 26:38, Mar 14:34 — M03-C-VCG-03); this is the characteristic in Jesus's own inner being as he faces the cross. Third, God's solidarity in distress: "in all their distress he was afflicted" (Isa 63:9 — M03-D-VCG-03). The divine attribution reveals that grief, sorrow, and anguish are not constitutional weaknesses to be overcome but appropriate relational responses to loss, sin, and suffering — which is why the human capacity for grief is not a mark of the fall alone but reflects the responsive relational nature God himself possesses.

The most explicit divine attributions are concentrated in M03-C-VCG-02 (Eph 4:30 — Spirit's grief) and M03-C-VCG-03 (Mat 26:37-38, Mar 14:34 — Jesus's grief in Gethsemane). These two VCGs carry the most theologically dense evidence for grief as a divine characteristic.
