**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, explicitly and repeatedly. Deu 28:63 shows God taking delight in ruin as he formerly took delight in doing Israel good (su.s); Deu 30:9 shows God again taking delight in prospering the restored (su.s); Isa 62:5 portrays God's delight in Zion as a bridegroom's delight (su.s); Isa 65:19 has God rejoicing in Jerusalem (gil_verb + su.s); Jer 32:41 locates God's rejoicing in doing good "with all my heart and all my soul" (su.s); Zep 3:17 pairs God's rejoicing (gil_verb) and exulting (su.s) over his restored people with gladness and loud singing. The attribution reveals that exultation is not a merely creaturely emotion but participates in the divine life — when the human person exults in God, they are responding with the same category of inner state that God exercises toward them. This makes exultation a fundamentally relational and reciprocal characteristic: God exults over his people; his people exult in him.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, explicitly and extensively. Beyond the references in T0.1.1: God gives joy directly into the heart (Psa 4:7 — "you have put more joy in my heart"); makes people joyful (Ezr 6:22 — "the Lord had made them joyful"); is himself the source of fullness of joy (Psa 16:11 — "in your presence there is fullness of joy"); commissions Jesus to carry joy (Heb 12:2 — "for the joy that was set before him"); and God as the master whose joy the faithful servant enters (Mat 25:21, 23). The attribution reveals that Joy is not incidental or peripheral in God's inner life but is bound up with his covenantal relationship with his people, his redemptive purpose, and his own eschatological gladness at restoration. For the human person, this means Joy is not merely an emotional bonus but an image-bearing capacity — the person who rejoices genuinely participates in a mode of being that God himself inhabits.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, most fully in the person of Christ. Heb 12:2 names the joy set before Christ as the ground of his endurance of the cross — the divine-human person exercises Suffering-Joy in its purest form: suffering as extreme as crucifixion held alongside and through joy set before him. Luk 10:21's Jesus rejoicing in the Holy Spirit acknowledges the hiddenness of kingdom realities from the world (a form of the disciples' vulnerability/suffering in the mission context) while exulting. The attribution reveals: Suffering-Joy is not merely a human coping mechanism for unfortunate circumstances but participates in the divine inner life as Christ exercised it — the capacity to hold eschatological joy as more real and determinative than present suffering. For the human person, Suffering-Joy is an image-bearing participation in Christ's own suffering-to-glory pattern.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, explicitly and foundationally. Gen 2:18 — "it is not good that the man should be alone" — God evaluates and declares a deficiency; this is the evaluative-gladness faculty operating in its negative register: the good that is absent is recognised and named. The Gen 1 series (VCG-01) is the positive register: God perceives and declares goodness in what he has made. Psa 119:68 — "you are good and do good" — explicitly joins divine being-good (ontological Gladness-quality) and doing-good (action arising from it), a model the programme observation OBS-026 identifies as the being/doing pattern. Neh 9:20 — "you gave your good Spirit to instruct them" — the Spirit's quality of goodness is an attribute of the divine Gladness-character extended outward. The attribution reveals: Gladness in its evaluative-cognitive form (the recognition and declaration of what is truly good) is first God's own inner act before it is the human person's. The human capacity for Gladness-as-evaluative-recognition is an image-bearing participation in God's own goodness-perceiving inner life.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, more extensively and programmatically than any other M04 characteristic. The attributions span five different registers: (1) God's sovereign volitional delight (Psa 115:3; 135:6; Isa 44:28; 46:10; 53:10; 55:11; Ecc 8:3; Jon 1:14) — his pleasure is his will; (2) God's relational delight in persons (Psa 18:19; 22:8; 37:23; 41:11; Num 14:8; 1Ki 10:9; Isa 62:4; Deu 30:9) — his pleasure motivates rescue, exaltation, and restoration; (3) God's moral delight — what he takes pleasure in and what he does not: "you delight in truth in the inward being" (Psa 51:6); "God does not delight in wickedness" (Psa 5:4); he takes no pleasure in sacrifice without inner transformation (Psa 40:6; 51:16; Isa 1:11; Heb 10:6, 8); he delights in steadfast love rather than sacrifice (Hos 6:6; Jer 9:24; Mic 7:18); (4) God's trinitarian delight — the Father's soul well pleased with the Son (Mat 12:18; eudokeo — the most explicit soul-location of divine Delight in Scripture); (5) God's creative delight — Wisdom as God's daily delight before creation (Pro 8:30); Jer 31:20's cherishing of Ephraim as a darling child. The breadth of attribution reveals: Delight is not incidental to God's character but is the integrating inner disposition that drives his will, his relational choices, his moral preferences, and his creative pleasure. Human Delight is a participation in the most comprehensive and fundamental feature of the divine inner life evidenced in M04.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes, in two primary registers: (1) **God's being as pleasant/beautiful** — Psa 27:4 (no.am as God's own character-quality perceptible in worship); Psa 36:8 (river of delights flowing from God); (2) **God's inner responsive pleasure at worship** — Gen 8:21 (God's heart moved by the soothing aroma); the entire ni.cho.ach corpus of M04-K-VCG-01 names an inner divine state of calmed, settled reception — God experiences the pleasing aroma as genuinely soothing to his regard. The attribution reveals: human Pleasure as the soul's positive receptive response to what is pleasant is grounded in a God who himself experiences pleasantness in his own being and in rightly-directed worship. The human capacity for pleasure in beautiful persons, agreeable speech, and material goodness images back the divine pleasure in his own beauty and in worship that is rightly offered.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder is not directly attributed to God as a characteristic God himself possesses in this corpus — rather, God's deeds and character are the objects that produce Wonder in those who encounter them. The partial exception: Zec 8:6 ("if it is marvellous in the sight of the remnant… should it also be marvellous in my sight, declares the Lord?") — God distances himself from the wonder-response, implying his own perspective transcends wonder rather than experiencing it. Isa 9:6's "Wonderful" (pe.le) as a name/title for the coming child is closest to attributing Wonder-quality to God, but this names his character as wonder-inducing rather than as one who experiences wonder. The attribution reveals: in Scripture, Wonder is primarily a human response to God rather than a divine characteristic — it belongs to creatures confronting the incomprehensible Creator.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The attribution pattern across the seven characteristics reveals a hierarchy of divine-human sharing. (1) **Delight** (Char 4) is the most comprehensively attributed divine characteristic in M04 — more extensively and in more registers than any other. This places Delight at the centre of God's inner life as evidenced in this cluster; (2) **Joy and Exultation** (Chars 2 and 1) share the same vocabulary with the divine instances and are explicitly located in God's heart (Jer 32:41 — "with all my heart and all my soul") — making them genuinely shared inner-being states; (3) **Gladness** (Char 3) establishes the divine evaluative act (Gen 1:4–31) as the archetype from which human evaluative gladness flows; (4) **Pleasure** (Char 5) is attributed more partially — the no.am of God's own beauty and the ni.cho.ach divine inner response to worship are real, but the full human range of pleasure (sensory, luxury, relational) is not mapped onto God; (5) **Wonder** (Char 6): its near-non-attribution is the most analytically significant silence in the cluster. Zec 8:6 is an explicit marker: Wonder is characteristically creaturely; (6) **Suffering-Joy** (Char 7): attributed only in the incarnate Christ — making this the one M04 characteristic whose divine grounding is entirely christological rather than divine-nature grounding. The cumulative pattern reveals the cluster's theological centre of gravity: the inner positive characteristics of the cluster are most fully divine when they involve directed pleasurable orientation toward what is genuinely good (Delight, Joy, Gladness, Exultation), less divine when they are primarily receptive-sensory (Pleasure), and not properly divine at all when they are specifically creaturely-perceptive-cognitive (Wonder) or incarnation-requiring (Suffering-Joy).

**[CHAR-1]** S — The evidence does not directly attribute shame as an experienced inner state to God himself. Psa 113:6 (sha.phel, set aside at Phase 8.5) uses sha.phel for God's own "stooping down" to behold creation, but this is God's condescension rather than shame. No verse in the 224-verse CHAR-1 corpus attributes shame as a felt inner experience to the divine person. The analytical significance of this silence is considerable: shame as experienced here is the product of exposure, inadequacy, or moral failure — none of which can characterize God. The characteristic is distinctively creaturely. The one asymmetry is that the evidence shows God *producing* shame in others as a moral and judicial act, which is a function of his holiness and justice rather than an experience he shares with the human person.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God is the primary agent of CHAR-2 in VCG-03: he brings low (1Sa 2:7), brings down haughty eyes (Psa 18:27, vc=21168), casts the wicked to the ground (Psa 147:6, vc=21171). The attribution is not that God experiences humiliation but that he exercises it as a judicial act — revealing CHAR-2 as a morally ordered phenomenon: God's deployment of it is the appropriate leveling of what has elevated itself beyond its proper place.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Within the CHAR-3 corpus, God is the ultimate arbiter whose dishonouring of a vessel or person (Rom 9:21) is the authoritative assignment, contrasted with human worth-denial which may be arbitrary or unjust. God does not dishonour unjustly; human dishonour-extension frequently does.

**[CHAR-4]** S — Scripture does not explicitly attribute CHAR-4 to God — God does not engage in moral-evaluative judgment from within his own experience of shamefulness. God is the standard against which shamefulness is assessed, not one who possesses the characteristic himself. Silent on God possessing CHAR-4.

**[CHAR-5]** S — Scripture does not explicitly attribute CHAR-5 — shame as the received experience of being treated with contempt — to God himself. Jesus receives contempt and mockery (Luk 23:11, vc=54640) — but this is God incarnate in the creaturely condition, not God in his eternal nature receiving contempt from equals. God as such is not susceptible to the experience of being treated as of no account by a more powerful agent, because no such agent exists. Silent on God possessing CHAR-5.

**[CHAR-6]** S — Scripture does not explicitly attribute the experience of innocence-as-structural-counter-to-shame to God in the way CHAR-6 is defined — as an inner state that protects against guilt-shame. God has no guilt-shame to be protected against. God is holy; the innocence of CHAR-6 is a creaturely moral state that reflects, imperfectly and derivatively, what God is by nature. Silent on God possessing CHAR-6 in its M07-H form.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The six characteristics divide cleanly into two groups. Char 2 alone is explicitly attributed to God as agent: he brings low, casts the wicked down, changes glory into shame (1Sa 2:7; Psa 147:6; Hos 4:7). God exercises enforced abasement as a judicial act. The remaining five (Chars 1, 3, 4, 5, 6) are all explicitly silent on God possessing the characteristic: shame as felt experience, dishonour as received, shamefulness as conscience-judgment, contempt-produced shame, and innocence-as-shield are all exclusively creaturely states. Char 3 partially bridges this — God assigns dishonour-standings (Rom 9:21) — but does not undergo worth-denial from another. The cluster's pattern is therefore asymmetric: God is the primary actor within M07's field (abasing, assigning worth, reversing contempt, confirming innocence) but does not experience M07's characteristics as the creature does.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Scripture does not attribute arrogant self-elevation to God. The 174 Phase 5.5 set-aside verses (the M22-register rum, ga.on, ga.vah material) carried divine-majesty content that belongs to God's own register and was correctly excluded from CHAR-1's corpus. What the remaining §3 evidence consistently shows is CHAR-1 as the creature's counterfeit of what God legitimately holds: Dan 11:36 (vc=34235, M08-A1-VCG-02) — the king "exalts himself and magnifies himself above every god" by his own will, explicitly placing CHAR-1 as a movement against God's divine position; Eze 28:2 (vc=34040, M08-A1-VCG-02) — "your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods'" — the creature claiming divine status is what CHAR-1 names at its sharpest. The silence of the evidence regarding God possessing CHAR-1 is itself the finding: arrogant self-elevation is exclusively creaturely, a distortion that competes with the divine rather than reflecting it.

**[CHAR-2]** S — Scripture does not attribute presumptuous defiance to God within the 45-verse §3.A corpus. God is consistently evidenced as the one who establishes the authority and revealed commands that CHAR-2 transgresses, and as the one who judges CHAR-2. Deu 18:20 (vc=34119, M08-B-VCG-01): "the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak" — God is the source of the command that the presumptuous prophet violates. The evidence is entirely silent on God possessing the boiling inner self-will that defines CHAR-2.

**[CHAR-3]** S — Scripture does not attribute CHAR-3 (self-directed boasting) to God within §3.B. The God-directed boasting of M08-C-VCG-03 (Rom 5:2, vc=33874; 1Cor 1:31, vc=33878; Phili 3:3, vc=33879) is not God boasting about himself but the believer glorying in God — a human act directed toward God. God as the subject of self-directed boasting is not evidenced. The evidence is silent on God possessing CHAR-3.

**[CHAR-4]** S — Scripture does not attribute vain conceit to God within the 12-verse §3.C corpus. God is the one who assigns the proper cognitive measure (Rom 12:3, vc=60866) against which CHAR-4 is the transgression. God possessing an inflated false self-picture is constitutively impossible — his self-knowledge is perfect and cannot exceed what he actually is.

**[CHAR-5]** S — Scripture does not attribute CHAR-5 to God within §3.D. The verse evidence consistently positions God as the one who judges and breaks structural power-pride (Lev 26:19; Eze 7:24, vc=33993; Eze 30:6, vc=33996) rather than as a possessor of CHAR-5. God's genuine strength and might belong to M23 (strength/power/dominion) and M22 (divine majesty), not to M08-CHAR-5.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Scripture does not attribute any of the five M08 characteristics to God. The cluster-level finding is uniform: all five characteristics are evidenced as exclusively creaturely distortions. The analytical significance of this unanimous silence varies by characteristic. For CHAR-1, CHAR-4, and CHAR-5, the silence is definitionally necessary — each presupposes a gap between actual worth and claimed worth (CHAR-4: fusioō, inflation beyond actual substance; CHAR-5: structural goods claimed as self-sufficient basis) that cannot exist for God. For CHAR-2 and CHAR-3's VCG-01 form, the silence reflects structural asymmetry: CHAR-2 requires an authority to defy that is external to the self; CHAR-3's self-directed boasting presupposes misattribution of received goods as self-generated. What the cluster-level comparison surfaces is that this uniform silence is not incidental — it is the cluster's systematic confirmation that M08 names distortions of the created order rather than creaturely analogues to divine attributes.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The corpus attributes submission explicitly to Christ: Heb5:8 — "although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered" — the incarnate Son experiences submission as something acquired through costly suffering. Rom5:19 — Christ's obedience as the redemptive act that makes many righteous — positions the Son's will-submission as the structural pivot of salvation history. The attribution to Christ reveals that submission of will is not a deficit forced on the creature by divine power but a posture the Son himself takes in relation to the Father. In the human person, the characteristic therefore carries Christological dignity: the one who submits participates in the inner-relational posture of the Son toward the Father, not merely in a social compliance structure.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The corpus does not explicitly attribute contrition to God. In both verses, God is the responsive agent — the one who draws near, saves, and revives — rather than the one who is contrite. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely in its direct attribution within this corpus: contrition is the inner state of the person; God is the one who responds to it with saving nearness.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The corpus does not explicitly name God as possessing metriopatheō or okneō. However, Heb5:2 is part of the Hebrews argument leading to Christ as the superior high priest (Heb4:15 — "we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses" — outside corpus but the structural context). The implication is that Christ's compassionate gentle-dealing (the antitype of the Aaronic priest's metriopatheō) reflects the divine character toward erring humanity. The attribution is indirect but structurally present: the Christological high priest carries this characteristic as a quality of the divine mediator.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The three-verse corpus does not explicitly attribute semnotēs to God. The characteristic is named as a quality of human persons (believers in 1Ti2:2, the overseer in 1Ti3:4, Titus in Tit2:7). The pairing with godliness (1Ti2:2) implies an orientation toward God but does not directly attribute semnotēs to him.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The five-verse corpus does not explicitly attribute willing-heartedness to God. In all five verses, the characteristic is a quality of human persons (the willing-hearted givers in Exo35; the willing craftsmen in 1Ch28:21; the penitent psalmist in Psa51:12). God is the recipient and restorer of the characteristic rather than its primary bearer. The implicit direction of attribution is that God values and can restore the characteristic, but is not described as having it himself.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Scripture attributes humility to the incarnate Son explicitly and personally: Jesus names himself "gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat11:29) and the Phili2:8 passage depicts his self-humbling as a willed, downward movement of the self taking on creaturely form and accepting death. This attribution is remarkable: the characteristic most often associated with creaturely dependence is owned by the one who has no need of dependence. That the Son takes on humility voluntarily rather than by necessity elevates the characteristic's significance — in the human person, humility is not merely an appropriate response to creatureliness but a participation in the self-giving movement that characterises the Son's own inner life. The Phili2 context frames the human call to humility (v.3 — "count others more significant") explicitly as imitation of Christ's pattern (v.5–8), establishing a direct connexion between the divine attribution and the human calling.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster divides cleanly on this question. Only CHAR-1 Humility and CHAR-2 Submission have explicit divine attribution — and exclusively through the incarnate Son: Mat11:29 (CHAR-1 — Jesus names himself "lowly in heart"), Phili2:8 (CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 jointly — the Son "humbled himself by becoming obedient"). CHAR-3 Contrition and CHAR-5 Dignity are not attributed to God directly; CHAR-4 Meekness and Gentleness is attributed obliquely through the high priestly type (Heb5:2). CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness is attributed only in the direction of God-toward-creature (God restores willing-heartedness in Psa51:12) but not as a quality God possesses. The cluster-level finding: M09 is the cluster in which the incarnate Son is the primary locus of divine attribution — the Christological concentration is the distinctive feature of the cluster's divine-attribution evidence. Characteristics without Christological attribution (CHAR-3, CHAR-5, CHAR-6) are exclusively creaturely in their direct evidence, grounding the cluster's dual structure: Christological core (CHAR-1, CHAR-2) surrounded by exclusively creaturely expressions.

---

**[CHAR-1]** S — The verse corpus for CHAR-1 contains no attribution of wilful sinning to God. This absence is analytically significant: the entire 98-verse corpus is structured around human sinning against God (VCG-01, 32V), human sinning against persons (VCG-02, 18V), and human sinning requiring restraint or remedy. God appears throughout as the offended party, the restraining agent (Gen 20:6 — "it was I who kept you from sinning against me"), and the judge (Eze 18:4 — "the soul who sins shall die"), but never as a sinning subject. The silence establishes wilful sinning as an exclusively creaturely phenomenon — something that arises from the constitution of the creature, not from the nature of God.

**[CHAR-10]** S — No verse in the 5-verse corpus attributes enticement (deleazō), collective hypocrisy (sunupokrinomai), or apostasy (apostasia) to God. God does not entice through desire (Jam 1:13–14 context), does not act hypocritically (whose nature is consistent and true), and does not defect from his own covenantal commitments. All three mechanisms are exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Partially — in an inverse form. Joh 8:46 — "Which of you convicts me of sin?" — and Heb 4:15 — "tempted as we are, yet without sin" — and 2Cor 5:21 — "him who knew no sin" — all confirm that the sinless state is attributable to God (in Christ), which is the structural opposite of the universal sinful condition. God does not possess the condition; God's sinlessness is the standard against which the universality of human sin is measured and from which all humanity has fallen (Rom 3:23 — "fall short of the glory of God"). The explicit divine sinlessness functions as the positive ground of the characteristic's definition.

**[CHAR-12]** S — No verse in the 9-verse corpus attributes sin's enslaving power to God. God appears as the liberator (1Jo 3:9 — God's seed; 1Jo 5:18 — the born-of-God protects) and as the one against whom the enslaved person sins (the broader biblical framework), but not as the enslaving power itself. The characteristic is exclusively a fallen-condition creaturely reality.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Partially — in the positive keeping-record mode. God is the keeper of the book from which sinners are blotted (Exo 32:32/33) and the one who searches for sin (Job 10:6; 14:16 — VCG-03). God maintains the record; he does not bear the sinful-record status. Exo 32:33 — "whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book" — God is the author of the record, not a participant in the condition recorded in it. The characteristic thus reveals God as the moral-record keeper rather than as the one who carries a sin-record before another.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes — on the giving side. God is the one who forgives: 2Cor 5:19 — "God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses"; Col 2:13 — "God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses"; Eph 1:7 — "the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace." The seeking side is human (the person seeks forgiveness); the granting side is divine. The characteristic thus involves both divine action (granting) and human action (seeking); Scripture attributes the granting explicitly to God.

**[CHAR-15]** S — No verse in the 8-verse corpus attributes the inherited sin-condition of generational sin to God. God appears as the one who addresses the condition (Isa 43:27 — naming the ancestral origin; Eze 37:23 — promising redemption from the backslidings) but not as the source or bearer of the condition. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-16]** S — No verse in the 64-verse corpus attributes the sinner-identity to God. God appears as the one who names sinners (1Sa 15:18; Amo 9:8), instructs them (Psa 25:8), came to save them (1Ti 1:15), and is separated from them (Heb 7:26 — "separated from sinners"). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-17]** S — No verse in the 97-verse corpus attributes the inner experience of guilt to God. God appears as the one who sees guilt (Jer 2:22), responds to it with judgment or mercy, removes it (Isa 6:7), and withholds until it is acknowledged (Hos 5:15) — but does not bear guilt as a subjective inner state. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-18]** S — No verse in the 162-verse corpus attributes the iniquity-as-crime condition to God. God appears as the one who measures iniquity (Gen 15:16), remembers it (Hos 13:12; Eze 21:24), punishes it (Isa 26:21), bears its weight vicariously through the servant (Isa 53:6 — "the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all"), and removes it (Zec 3:4). God does not bear iniquity as a personal moral crime; the characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-19]** S — No verse in the 147-verse corpus attributes transgression to God. God appears as the one who establishes the boundaries crossed (Rom 4:15), counts transgressions (Amo 1:3), withholds or grants pardon (Exo 23:21; Mic 7:18), and absorbs their cost through the servant (Isa 53:5/8). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The corpus contains no attribution of unintentional sinning to God. God appears in the CHAR-2 corpus as the standard-setter whose commandments are violated (Lev 4:2), the one whose altar requires purification (Exo 29:36; Eze 43:20), and the one whose forgiveness resolves the condition (Num 15:28; Lev 19:22). The absence is constitutive: God cannot sin unintentionally because he cannot be without knowledge of the moral reality of any act. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — it presupposes the limitation of creaturely knowledge that God does not share.

**[CHAR-20]** S — No verse in the 101-verse corpus attributes faithlessness to God. God appears as the one against whom faithlessness is directed (Lev 26:40; Dan 9:7), as the faithful witness (Mal 2:14), as the judge of treachery (Eze 17:20), and as the faithful standard against which Israel's unfaithfulness is measured. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-21]** E — One verse approaches this — Lam 3:9 — "he has blocked my ways with blocks of stones; he has made my paths crooked" — God is the subject of the crookedness-making action. However, the verse describes God's judicial action upon the sufferer (making their path crooked as discipline/judgment) rather than attributing moral perversity to God's character. God here acts as the one who twists the path, not as a morally perverted being. All other verses place perversity exclusively on the human side.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The corpus explicitly tests and denies this: Rom 3:5 — "That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.)" — the suggestion of divine injustice is raised as a rhetorical foil and immediately repudiated; Job 36:23 — "who can say, 'You have done wrong'?" — the question is rhetorical, implying the answer is no one. God's absolute freedom from injustice is one of the most densely evidenced theological claims in this corpus: five verses directly assert it (Deu 32:4; 2Ch 19:7; Psa 92:15; Job 34:10; Zep 3:5). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The corpus contains no attribution of confession to God. God does not confess sin because God does not sin. The entire 34-verse corpus is structured around human persons (individual and corporate) confessing before God — with God as the consistent recipient, never the confessor. The absence is constitutively significant: confession is exclusively a creaturely act, presupposing both the capacity to sin (which the creature has and God does not) and the relational standing before a holy God that requires acknowledgment of sin.

**[CHAR-4]** S — No verse in the 8-verse corpus attributes conscience suppression to God. God appears throughout as the one who sees, knows, and judges the moral reality that the human conscience fails to register. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — it presupposes the creaturely capacity to fail to perceive moral reality that God perceives fully. God cannot suppress awareness of moral reality because he is its author and standard. The absence is constitutive.

**[CHAR-5]** S — No verse in the 18-verse corpus attributes refusal to repent to God. God appears throughout as the one whose law is not followed (2Ki 10:31), whose warnings are not heeded (Neh 9:29), and whose sacrifice is closed off by deliberate refusal (Heb 10:26). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely: it presupposes a will that can choose to turn but chooses not to — a freedom God possesses but in the opposite direction (God always acts in accordance with his own moral nature). God cannot refuse to repent because God does not sin and therefore has no turning to withhold.

**[CHAR-6]** S — No verse in the 14-verse corpus attributes habitual defection to God. God appears as the party against whom Israel habitually sins (2Ki 17:7), the one provoked by sustained rebellion (Heb 3:17), and the one who will redirect the sinner's wealth (Pro 13:22). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — it presupposes a creature whose will can establish a settled pattern of departure from God, which is structurally inapplicable to God himself.

**[CHAR-7]** S — No verse in the 19-verse corpus attributes contagious sin to God. God appears throughout as the one who warns against it (Exo 23:33; Deu 20:18), is provoked by it (1Ki 14:22; 16:13), and holds leaders accountable for it (1Ki 16:2; 21:22). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — it requires a human leader with a sinful inner commitment and a community that receives the transmitted direction. God does not sin, therefore cannot make others sin in the morally culpable sense the corpus describes.

**[CHAR-8]** S — No verse in the 9-verse corpus attributes political revolt (pa.sha — breaking submission) to God. God does not revolt against authority; God is the source and ground of authority. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — it is what subordinate parties do when they break submission to governing authority.

**[CHAR-9]** S — No verse in the 22-verse corpus attributes blasphemy or sinful speech to God. God appears as the target of blasphemy (Rev 13:6), the one whose authority blasphemy presumes to claim (Mar 2:7; Joh 10:33), and the one whose Spirit suffers the unforgivable form (Mat 12:31) — never as a blasphemer. The characteristic is exclusively creaturely in both its slander and its blasphemy registers.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Scripture explicitly and forcefully denies this characteristic to God. Job 34:10 declares God incapable of wickedness (re.sha); Psa 36:1 portrays transgression as speaking within the wicked person "deep in his heart" while "there is no fear of God before his eyes" — structuring the wicked person's inner life as the space where God is absent. The absence of attribution to God is analytically significant: it means wickedness as settled person-identity is a purely creaturely failure-mode, with no divine analogue. Its significance in the human person is therefore as a measure of departure from the divine pattern — the further the inner person is from God (Psa 36:1; Mal 3:18 defines the wicked as "one who does not serve him"), the more completely this characteristic defines them.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Scripture explicitly denies constitutional inner evil to God. Rom 9:14 (vc=65872 — VCG-06) raises and immediately rejects the charge: "Is there injustice on God's part? By no means!" The denial is forceful and categorical. Heb 8:12 (vc=14342 — VCG-06) contrasts God's mercy toward human iniquities ("I will remember their sins no more") with the human constitutional condition — God stands over against human constitutional evil as the one who covers it by grace, not as one who shares it. The evidence is entirely consistent: constitutional inner evil is attributed exclusively to humans (Mat 7:11: "you who are evil"; Luk 11:13: the same), never to God.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Scripture does not attribute the experience of being abominable to God — God is not the one who becomes an abomination. But Scripture does explicitly attribute the response-side of the characteristic to God: God is the primary agent of the revulsion that names and constitutes something as abominable. Pro 8:7 (vc=65953 — VCG-02): "wickedness is an abomination to my lips" — spoken in Wisdom's voice, implying a divine-moral faculty of revulsion. Pro 11:1 (vc=65954 — VCG-01): "a false balance is an abomination to the Lord" — God's reaction is the defining standard. The divine attribution reveals that the characteristic's constitutive element (the revulsion response) is divine in origin: what makes something an abomination is specifically God's active moral response to it. This is analytically significant — the characteristic is not self-certifying in the human sphere but is defined by reference to the divine inner response. God's revulsion is the measure.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Scripture explicitly denies this characteristic to God: the divine cannot become an idolater or be abominable. However, Scripture does attribute God's intense revulsion-response to the characteristic: Jer 44:4 (vc=65966 — VCG-04): "this abomination that I hate" — God's hatred of idolatrous abomination is directly stated. Deu 12:31 (vc=1683 — VCG-02): "every abominable thing that the Lord hates they have done for their gods" — the Lord's hatred is the defining relational context within which idolatrous abomination is identified. Deu 7:25 (vc=1682 — VCG-02): idols are "an abomination to the Lord your God" — the relational identity of God is the standard. The non-attribution of the characteristic to God reveals that idolatrous attachment is exclusively a creaturely failure — the creature who was designed to give exclusive devotion to God has redirected that devotion to created objects. God's own character (exclusive, morally serious, jealous for undivided allegiance) is the positive standard against which idolatrous abomination is measured.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Scripture explicitly denies iniquity to God. Isa 55:7 (vc=38200 — VCG-02): the unrighteous man is called to forsake "his thoughts" and "return to the Lord" — the Lord is the party toward whom the iniquity-shaped person must turn; God is the structural opposite of the iniquity-scheming inner life. Psa 66:18 (vc=38182 — VCG-04): "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened" — the conditional structure implies that God, as the one who listens, is characterised by the absence of cherished iniquity. Psa 5:5 (vc=38237 — VCG-03): God hates evildoers — the hating posture is the divine stance against what God does not possess. The non-attribution reveals that iniquity as active inner scheming is exclusively a creaturely failure — specifically, the misuse of the mind, heart, and will faculties that God designed for generation of good.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Scripture does not attribute blasphemy or defamatory evil speech to God. God is consistently the object of blasphemy (Rev 13:6; 16:9; 16:11; 16:21 — VCG-01) and the one whose name is blasphemed by others' conduct (Rom 2:24 — VCG-02), never its subject. The non-attribution is emphatic: the entire VCG-01 corpus (6V) positions God as the one against whom defiant blasphemy is directed. This active non-attribution reveals that the characteristic is the polar inversion of the speech that God's nature calls forth — which is worship, glory, and honest testimony. Attributing evil speech to God would be a logical impossibility in the evidence's framework: God cannot blaspheme himself. The silence reveals the characteristic as exclusively creaturely, specifically as the misuse of the creaturely speech-faculty that was designed for truthful testimony about and toward God.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across all six characteristics, the pattern is unanimous and structurally consistent: no M10b characteristic is attributed to God; God is universally positioned as the moral authority against, over, and opposite to every form of inner evil the cluster names. Two distinct denial-patterns emerge across the cluster. The first is active denial: Job 34:10 (Char 1), Rom 9:14 (Char 2), and the VCG-01 corpus of Rev 16 (Char 6 — God as target of blasphemy, never its source) all make the non-attribution explicit and forceful. The second is structural-by-design: Chars 3 and 4 note that God attributes the response-side of the characteristic to himself (the revulsion response — Pro 8:7; Pro 11:1 for Char 3; Jer 44:4 for Char 4) while not possessing the state that triggers it. This second pattern is analytically distinctive: God owns the moral revulsion but not the abominable condition. Chars 1, 2, 5, and 6 attribute only the divine opposite: God judges, hates, perceives, and returns iniquity (Chars 1, 5), stands as the one who must be turned toward (Char 2: Act 3:26), and is the target whose glory is withheld (Char 6: Rev 16:9). The cluster's unanimous denial reveals the six characteristics as mapping the territory of what cannot be in God — the negative space that defines the divine character by its absolute incompatibility with every inner-being form of evil.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The verse evidence does not attribute the ritual defilement-state to God. The 133 verses show the characteristic operating exclusively in the human person and in objects/spaces in relation to the human person. God does not become ritually unclean; he is the standard against which the clean/unclean distinction is measured (Lev 11:44-45). The significance of this absence: the defilement-state is a specifically creaturely vulnerability — a condition that arises from embodied life in contact with death, discharge, and disease. God, being without body and without limitation by death, cannot bear this condition. The absence thus locates the defilement-state within the creaturely domain of finitude and mortality, and signals that the human person's susceptibility to it is part of their created embodied constitution, not a moral failure of the image per se.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The 26-verse corpus does not attribute the moral-inner defilement-state to God. No verse in §3 portrays God as possessing impurity, defiled conscience, corrupted will, or heart allegiance disorder. The characteristic is exclusively a condition of the human (and, in the Revelation apocalyptic register, of spiritually corrupted beings — Rev 16:13, 17:4, 18:2, VCG-04). The absolute absence of divine attribution confirms the significance: the moral-inner defilement-state is a departure from divine character, not an expression of it. Its significance for the human person is that it marks the inner person's failure to image God — the condition where the interior life has moved from conformity to divine holiness toward conformity to corrupted desire.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, uniquely at Eze 20:26 (M10c-D-VCG-02): "I defiled them through their very gifts in their offering up all their firstborn, that I might devastate them. I did it that they might know that I am the Lord." God defiles Israel through their own defiant gifts as a judicial act — using the instrument of their own self-defilement against them as a form of punitive desolation. The attribution is judicial and singular: God does not normally possess or generate defilement, but he can deploy it as an instrument of wrath when the people's defiant self-defilement reaches the point of idolatrous child sacrifice. This attribution reveals the characteristic's most extreme form — when the community's defilement is used by God himself as the mechanism of its own devastation.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The 21-verse corpus does not attribute the defilement-by-external-spiritual-agency condition to God. God is not a subject of this characteristic; he is its sovereign counterforce — the one whose authority commands the unclean spirits and whose power restores the defiled person. The absence of divine attribution confirms the characteristic as a condition that God opposes and reverses, not one he possesses or generates.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's pattern on divine attribution is 3 S : 1 E — three characteristics explicitly absent from God's possession (Chars 1, 2, 4) and one singular exception (Char 3: Eze 20:26 — God "defiled them through their very gifts" as a judicial act). The three S characteristics reveal defilement as a creaturely condition that God cannot bear, does not generate, and actively opposes. The one E instance (Char 3) is analytically distinctive: it is judicial, not constitutive — God does not possess the corporate-covenantal defilement-state but deploys it as an instrument of punitive devastation against a community that has itself willfully defiled. The cluster pattern reveals: defilement is constitutively alien to God, but God can wield it as judgment — the condition that stands against divine holiness can be turned by divine sovereignty into an instrument of divine wrath. This judicial deployment is unique to Characteristic 3 precisely because that characteristic is the one whose domain is the covenantal community's shared life before God, the relationship in which judicial response takes its most direct form.

questions.section: T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
questions.question_text: Where Scripture is silent about God's possession of this characteristic, what does that silence suggest about the characteristic's place in the divine image?
questions.review_note: folded_into=T0.1.2 · tier-catalogue v2_1 refit 2026-06-19 · silence first-class (God-possession silence read in the presence/absence pattern)

findings.session_b_note:
The silence is noted above — Scripture does not attribute contrition to God. The instruction notes that for characteristics like forgiveness, grace, or mercy, this prompt will typically be N (not applicable) because Scripture *does* explicitly attribute them to God. For contrition, the silence is the data, and it is informative.

The silence suggests that contrition belongs to the exclusively creaturely aspect of the divine image rather than to the shared aspect. The divine image includes both what humans share with God (love, wisdom, creativity, moral character) and what is proper to creaturely existence before God (dependence, limitation, responsiveness). Contrition belongs to the second category — it is the appropriate inner-being posture of a creature who knows itself to be creature before a holy Creator. God does not and cannot occupy this posture because God is not creature before Creator. The silence of Scripture on divine contrition is therefore not a deficiency — it is structurally correct. Contrition expresses the creaturely dimension of the divine image: being made in God's likeness includes being constituted as a being that can and should know its own lowliness before God.

findings.session_b_note: Scripture is silent about God possessing contrition — explicitly so. The verse evidence consistently frames contrition as the human posture before God, and God as the one who responds to it (draws near, revives, saves). The holiness of God is precisely what produces contrition in the human; a holy God does not experience contrition before another. OBS-030-045, OBS-030-062.

Scripture is not silent — God's hatred is extensively attested. This prompt does not apply to M06-A in the sense of silence. The positive attribution is the finding.

The relative silence (only reactive, judicial uses of na.ats attributed to God) suggests that contempt as a settled inner posture of treating what is sacred as beneath regard is not a characteristic of the divine nature. Since human beings are made in God's image, and contempt is absent from God's originating character, contempt is a distortion of the image — an inversion of the reverence and honour-giving that belongs to the properly ordered creature.

Not applicable in the same sense — ta.av is extensively attributed to God. However, the silence on God abhorring persons gratuitously (his abhorrence is always grounded in what they have become or done) suggests that abhorrence, even in God, is always object-specific and morally grounded, never ambient or arbitrary.

The silence is total for cruelty as an inner-being characteristic. This suggests that cruelty is among the furthest conditions from the divine nature — the opposite of mercy, restraint, and purposive severity, all of which God characteristically possesses. Cruelty's absence from God's nature means it cannot be an expression of the divine image; it can only be its negation.

God does not inhabit the condition of reproach as one who is reproached (he imposes and removes it). The silence on God experiencing reproach as an inner-social condition suggests that reproach belongs to the creaturely register — it is a condition that arises in the relational vulnerability of creatures among creatures, and in the covenantal context of faithfulness and unfaithfulness. It is not a condition of the divine being as such, though Christ's bearing of it (Psa 69:9 → Rom 15:3) is the redemptive exception.

The silence on God inhabiting a perpetual state of enmity toward his creation suggests that the adversary posture, while God can take it up (Exo 23:22), is not his natural orientation toward his creatures. His originating orientation is love and covenant; the adversary posture is adopted in response to specific conditions, not as a baseline.

The complete silence on God possessing malice suggests it is as far from the divine nature as any characteristic in M06. Malice requires the coexistence of enmity, contempt, and pleasure in destruction — none of which characterises God's originating orientation toward his creation. The silence marks malice as an exclusively fallen and adversarial condition.

There is no silence on divine possession across any of the seven sub-groups. Every M05 characteristic is explicitly attributed to God in the verse evidence. This is itself a cluster-level finding: M05 is a cluster in which every characteristic is constitutively divine before it is humanly expressed.
**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Not applicable — Scripture is not silent here. God's righteousness is one of the most extensively and explicitly attested divine attributes in the entire biblical corpus.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The relevant silence is not about God lacking righteousness but about the specific mechanisms of human righteousness (hungering, forfeiting, accumulating) not being attributed to God. God does not hunger for righteousness — he is righteous. The developmental and conditional aspects of human righteousness (M26-A2-002; M26-A2-006) have no divine counterpart, which suggests these aspects are specifically creaturely — they belong to the nature of finite moral beings who must grow into what God simply is.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** The specific vocabulary of B (yo.sher, me.shar as human inner disposition) is not extensively attributed to God in its inner-disposition mode. The struggle toward uprightness — the human inner work of aligning with what is straight — is not a divine struggle. This silence suggests that uprightness in B is a specifically creaturely mode of relating to the divine quality: the finite person's inner work of conforming to what God simply is.

**[C — Justification]** God is not justified — he is the justifier. The complete absence of God as the recipient of justification confirms that justification is a relational act flowing from God toward the creature. Justification presupposes a gap between the standard and the one being assessed. No such gap exists in God.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The specific mode of petitioning for divine vengeance (944-001: the cry of the wronged) has no divine counterpart. God does not cry out to a higher authority for justice — he is the final authority. This silence places the cry for justice firmly in the creaturely domain.

**[E — Condemnation]** God is not condemned — he is the one who condemns. Self-condemnation (autokatakritos, Tit 3:11) is specifically a creaturely phenomenon: the conscience turned against the self. This has no divine analogue.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The inner struggle of reckoning — working out whether to count oneself dead to sin (Rom 6:11), weighing sufferings against future glory (Rom 8:18) — is specifically creaturely. God's reckoning is immediate and complete; the human reckoning is laboured and instructed. The silence on God struggling to reckon suggests that the faculty itself images a divine act but must be exercised in a creaturely mode.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The complete silence on God possessing wickedness or injustice is definitional. God's nature is the measure against which G-terms are defined as their opposite. The silence is the most important thing about G in relation to God.

**[CLUSTER]** The pattern of silence in T0.1.3 reveals a consistent structure: the divine-to-human direction is source-to-image, standard-to-measured, giver-to-receiver. The specific creaturely modes (struggling, petitioning, forfeiting, being condemned, working to reckon) have no divine counterpart because they arise from the gap between the creature and the standard — the gap that the cluster's narrative (from A1 through C) is designed to close.

findings.finding_value:
The silence is consistent and instructive. M20 names characteristics of the human person in their fragility, limitation, and fallenness — states that arise from finitude (not knowing the outcome, not having sufficient strength, not knowing which way to go) and from sin (using despair to justify rebellion, failing to trust what is reliable). God has none of these limitations. The silence suggests these characteristics are not part of the divine image in the sense of being reflected qualities — they are creaturely conditions that arise when the image-bearer fails to trust the one whose image they bear. The positive faculty underlying each (attentive care, hope, resolve, single-mindedness) is divine; the M20 forms are its failure or misdirection.

findings.finding_value: The silence across all sub-groups on God possessing fear (apart from the single set-aside) reveals that fear belongs to the creaturely dimension of the divine image rather than to the divine nature itself. It is not a characteristic the image-bearer shares with its Source, but one that marks the proper orientation of the image-bearer toward its Source. The significance: fear-of-God in the human person is the inner structural acknowledgment of the asymmetry between Creator and creature. It is the inner posture that orients the person rightly within that asymmetry. The M01-A material (Pro 1:7; Psa 111:10; Ecc 12:13) confirms this: fear is the foundational inner disposition from which all right knowing and living begin — not because God fears, but because the human person, made in God's image, exists in a constitutive relation of creaturely dependence that fear truthfully registers.
