The evidence is not silent; the corpus shows grief attributed to God in three distinct ways (Spirit's grief, Jesus's grief, divine solidarity in distress). However, some sub-groups within M03 contain no explicit divine attribution: M03-A (weeping and tears) does not attribute weeping to God directly, though God commands and promises to wipe away tears (Isa 25:8). M03-F (pain and inner ache) does not attribute bodily pain or ache to God. M03-G (bitterness) does not attribute bitterness to God. The absence of divine weeping (M03-A) and divine bodily pain (M03-F) may signal that the somatic-expressive registers of grief — tears, groaning, physical ache — are specifically creaturely modes of a grief that in God is real but expressed without the bodily limitations of mortal flesh.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Scripture is not silent; it is explicit. There is no silence to interpret. The opposite observation is more significant: the breadth and intensity of divine exultation in the evidence — spanning six distinct passages, employing two primary terms (su.s, gil_verb), and grounding the divine exultation in relational faithfulness and restorative action — suggests that exultation is among the most fully attested divine inner states across the characteristic's corpus.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Scripture is not silent — divine joy is extensively evidenced. The more significant silence is in the VCG-06 (inverted/corrupt/absent joy) register: God's withdrawal of joy from the community (Deu 28:47; Hos 2:11; Jer 7:34; 16:9; 25:10; Joe 1:16) is the silencing of what God himself possesses and intended — the removal of the community's joy is shown as the most complete act of covenantal judgment precisely because joy belongs to the life God designed. The absence of divine joy toward a people (Isa 9:17 — "the Lord does not rejoice over their young men") is itself a severe verdict. The evidence thus shows divine joy as the norm and its absence or withholding as the exception under judgment.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The silence in the M04-E-VCG-01 sa.s.von restoration corpus (which is primarily about God reversing suffering rather than God experiencing suffering-with-joy) is analytically significant: the OT does not primarily present God as experiencing suffering-that-he-rejoices-through; rather, God is the one who reverses suffering. The characteristic in its paradoxical form (joy through suffering, not merely after it) emerges most fully in the NT through Christ's incarnate suffering and the Spirit's enabling of the church under persecution. This is not silence about the characteristic's divine grounding but about its location — Suffering-Joy's divine archetype is the incarnate Christ, not the transcendent Creator.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Scripture is not silent on divine goodness — it is extensively evidenced. The more analytically significant observation is the asymmetry within the corpus: M04-L-VCG-01 (divine character goodness) has 32 verses, making God the subject of goodness more prominently than any sub-group's human subject. This dominance reveals that Gladness-as-evaluative-recognition of the good is not primarily a human characteristic that God also happens to possess; it is a divine attribute that humans reflect. The human evaluative-gladness of M04-L-VCG-02 (moral appraisal of persons and actions) is the image-bearing participation in what God first exercises. No silence; instead, a positive finding about origination.

**[CHAR-4]** S — Scripture is not silent; divine Delight is the most extensively attributed characteristic in this cluster. The analytically significant observation is not silence but selectivity: God explicitly withholds delight in specific contexts (ritual sacrifice without inner transformation, wickedness, faithlessness — Psa 5:4; 40:6; Isa 1:11; Mal 1:10; Heb 10:6–8) and explicitly directs it toward others (steadfast love, justice, righteousness, the Son, repentant persons). The pattern of divine delight and divine withholding-of-delight together reveal that Delight is a morally structured characteristic in God's inner life — not indiscriminate pleasure but directed toward genuine goodness and relational faithfulness.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The evidence is not silent about divine Pleasure — but the divine pleasantness is more restricted in scope than the human. God's ni.cho.ach pleasure at worship is bounded by covenant conditions: Lev 26:31 ("I will not smell your pleasing aromas") shows divine Pleasure withheld from disobedient worship; Eze 20:41's future-oriented "as a pleasing aroma I will accept you" shows it restorable. The bounded quality of divine Pleasure at worship reveals that divine pleasantness is morally structured — it responds to genuinely correct worship and withdraws from its corruption (M04-P-VCG-01's misdirected ni.cho.ach). The human capacity for Pleasure has the same bounded quality: genuine pleasantness is appropriate to right objects; misapplied, it becomes luxury-curse (Deu 28:54–56) or illicit indulgence (Pro 9:17).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The near-silence about God experiencing Wonder is analytically significant. Zec 8:6's rhetorical question ("should it also be marvellous in my sight?") implies God does not stand in wonder at his own deeds — he is their originator and therefore understands them fully. Wonder is the creature's response to encountering what exceeds its comprehension; God is not a creature and does not encounter incomprehensible reality. The silence reveals Wonder as characteristically creaturely: it is the inner response appropriate to finite beings encountering the infinite. The human person who wonders is exercising a characteristically creaturely capacity — the capacity to be genuinely overwhelmed by what is greater than oneself — which is an image-bearing capacity but not one God exercises in the same way.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Three categories of silence: (1) **Silence that reveals creaturely limitation** — Wonder (Char 6): the near-silence is the most theologically instructive silence in the cluster. Wonder is specifically the inner response of a finite being encountering the infinite. God does not experience Wonder because he does not encounter anything that exceeds his comprehension; he is the ground of all comprehension. This silence reveals Wonder as uniquely placed among M04 characteristics — it is the characteristic most fully dependent on creaturely finitude and therefore cannot be straightforwardly a "divine image" characteristic in the way that Joy or Delight are; (2) **Silence that is selective rather than total** — Pleasure (Char 5): God does not experience the full range of human sensory and luxury pleasure, but the divine pleasantness of his own character (no.am) and his responsive inner pleasure at worship (ni.cho.ach) are real. The silence on the material-luxury register of Pleasure is analytically significant: the dimension of Pleasure most tied to embodied creaturely existence is the dimension least attributable to God; (3) **Silence broken only by the incarnation** — Suffering-Joy (Char 7): the OT's relative silence on God's experiencing suffering-with-joy is not a silence about the characteristic's value but about its location. Its divine grounding is christological — it requires the incarnation to become fully visible as a divine inner-being characteristic. This silence reveals Suffering-Joy as the characteristic whose full theological meaning depends most directly on the NT's christological disclosure.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The silence confirms that shame as experienced inner state is a creaturely characteristic arising from moral vulnerability, exposure, and the gap between what the person is and what is required. God possesses no such gap. The characteristic's absence from the divine nature establishes it as a response-function rather than an originating-function — it is what happens to a morally situated creature when exposed before what is holy, when trust collapses, or when moral failure is uncovered. The creation-contrast is sharpest in Gen 2:25 (vc=34835): before the fall, the human pair "were not ashamed," evidencing shame as belonging to the fallen creaturely condition rather than the created design. This suggests shame is a post-fall reality that nonetheless reflects real moral structure (the capacity for guilt, the awareness of one's standing before God and community) that the divine image-bearer retains even in the fallen state.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God exercises CHAR-2 but does not experience it as a creaturely condition. The silence confirms CHAR-2 is a fallen-world phenomenon: it is what happens to the creature that has over-reached. God humbles; he is not humbled by another.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The CHAR-3 corpus is primarily silent on God experiencing relational worth-denial as something that falls upon him from another equal. The dishonour directed at Jesus (Joh 8:49) reveals that God-incarnate can be the recipient of unjust worth-denial — but this is the creaturely context. Silent on God experiencing CHAR-3 in his eternal nature.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The silence confirms that CHAR-4 is a creaturely characteristic: it is the conscience's recognition, from within creaturely existence, of what violates the moral propriety of that existence. God's own moral character is the standard; the creature's conscience is the faculty that registers when conduct departs from that standard. CHAR-4 is the inner registrar of moral propriety, not the standard itself.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The silence confirms that CHAR-5 is a creaturely characteristic arising from the vulnerability of created persons to the contempt-judgments of others. God's systematic reversal of contempt-verdicts (1Cor 1:28; Act 4:11) reveals that he takes the contempt-produced shame of his people seriously — he does not ignore it but acts against it. The characteristic belongs to creaturely moral vulnerability; its resolution belongs to divine sovereign counter-action.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The silence confirms that CHAR-6 is a creaturely moral state — the creature's approximation to, and protection by, the moral purity that characterises God. The innocence that protects the image-bearer against guilt-shame is a creaturely participation in the moral order that God himself constitutes. CHAR-6 is exclusively creaturely in its M07 function (as protection against shame), though it derives from and reflects the divine moral character.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The near-unanimous silence across five of six characteristics establishes a consistent theological signal: M07's domain is distinctively creaturely moral vulnerability — the vulnerability to exposure, failure, degradation, contempt, and the loss of standing before others. God does not share this vulnerability; he addresses it from outside it. Char 6 sharpens this: innocence as the creaturely approximation to God's holiness is exclusively creaturely in its M07 function (as protection against shame), even though the holiness it approximates belongs to God. The cluster-level implication: M07's inner-being domain is one of the most distinctively post-fall domains in the programme — the created-design dimension is limited to the moral capacities (conscience, moral integrity of will and heart) that underlie Chars 4 and 6. All other characteristics are fallen-condition responses. God's silence from the characteristics he does not possess is matched by his richly evidenced activity in correcting, reversing, and resolving them.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The silence is theologically load-bearing. The §3 corpus consistently deploys CHAR-1 as what stands against God — against his judicial authority (Psa 94:2, vc=33952, M08-A4-VCG-02: the proud "deserve" divine retribution), against his sole supremacy (Isa 2:11–12, M08-A3-VCG-04: "the Lord alone will be exalted"), against his revealed character (Isa 37:23, vc=34304, M08-A4-VCG-05: raising the voice against "the Holy One of Israel"). The fact that God is never the subject of CHAR-1 in this corpus — while God is consistently the one who opposes, humbles, and reverses CHAR-1 — places CHAR-1 outside the divine image as such. The characteristic is not an image-bearing quality distorted; it is the creature's attempt to occupy God's own position, which makes it categorically different from characteristics that are genuine creaturely analogues to divine attributes.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The silence is analytically significant: CHAR-2 (the will boiling over against divinely-established limits) is constitutively impossible for God to possess, since God himself establishes those limits. The characteristic requires an external authority to defy — there is no authority external to God against which God could presume. Deu 17:12 (vc=34110, M08-B-VCG-02) and Deu 18:20 (vc=34119, M08-B-VCG-01) both frame CHAR-2 as transgression of limits that God himself has ordained (the appointed judge, the commanded word). The silence confirms CHAR-2 as a characteristically creaturely distortion: only a creature who stands under authority can defy that authority presumptuously.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The silence is structurally significant: CHAR-3 (self-glorification) would require a subject who inflates their own standing beyond what they deserve or beyond proper creaturely acknowledgment. God, being fully what he is, cannot self-inflate — there is no gap between his actual worth and his self-presentation. 1Cor 4:7 (vc=33871, M08-C-VCG-01): "what do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" — the premise of CHAR-3 is misattribution of what was received as self-generated. God receives nothing from outside himself; all goods originate from him, making the logical structure of CHAR-3 (claiming as self-generated what was received) inapplicable to God.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The silence is definitionally necessary. CHAR-4 is the mind's false, inflated self-assessment — a gap between the person's actual worth/standing and their cognitive picture of it. God's self-knowledge is perfectly accurate; there is no gap between what God is and what God knows himself to be. The structure of CHAR-4 (inflation beyond actual measure — fusioō/tufoō: to puff up beyond actual substance) presupposes a creature with limited actual standing who overclaims; God cannot overclaim because he is the measure itself. The silence confirms CHAR-4 as exclusively creaturely.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The silence is theologically instructive. CHAR-5 arises when strength, authority, or wealth becomes the ground for self-exaltation and contempt of others. God's strength is genuine rather than inflated beyond what he possesses — there is no gap between his actual power and his self-presentation. The silence confirms CHAR-5 as exclusively creaturely: it is the creature's false claim to power-derived self-sufficiency ("I am, and there is no one besides me" — Isa 47:8, vc=9563, M08-E-VCG-02: Babylon's self-declaration) that CHAR-5 names, a declaration structurally inapplicable to God who actually is the sole ground of all being.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The uniform silence across all five characteristics, read together, establishes a cluster-level principle: M08 characteristics are not defective forms of something God possesses in a pure form — they are creatureliness-specific disorders. This distinguishes M08 from clusters whose characteristics have genuine divine analogues (love, wisdom, grief in God). The cluster-level comparison between CHAR-1 (usurping God's exclusive exaltation), CHAR-3's VCG-03 (where the glorying-impulse does have a divine analogue — God delights in his own glory), and CHAR-4 (whose cognitive self-assessment has no divine analogue) reveals an internal differentiation: CHAR-3 uniquely has a positive divine-analogue dimension (God-directed glorying), while CHAR-1, CHAR-2, CHAR-4, and CHAR-5 have no positive divine-analogue form whatsoever. The silence of the four, compared with CHAR-3's partial positive, reveals that M08 sits at the boundary between pure-disorder clusters (where all characteristics are exclusively fallen) and mixed clusters (where the same faculty has both a fallen form and a created/redeemed form). CHAR-3 pulls M08 toward the mixed end; the other four hold it at the pure-disorder end.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The corpus does not evidence the Father possessing submission in the sense the Son does — the Father is consistently the one to whom Christ submits (Heb5:8 — "in submission to the Father"; the gospel as his command in Rom16:26). This asymmetry — Son submits, Father receives — suggests that submission in its creaturely form is specifically the Son's characteristic as the one who takes on creaturely relation with the Father in the Incarnation. For the human person, the implication is that submission reflects the image not by mirroring the Father's posture but by participating in the Son's: the human creature before God occupies the position the Son voluntarily occupies, and the characteristic is thus genuinely image-bearing through union with the one who exercises it fully.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The silence on God's own contrition is analytically significant. Contrition is structurally the inner state of one who has confronted their own failure or the holiness of another — a posture that presupposes moral limitation or transgression. God's possession of this characteristic in its creaturely form would be constitutionally incoherent. The silence therefore reveals that contrition is an exclusively creaturely characteristic — uniquely belonging to the moral creature who exists in the tension between their own failure and God's holiness. It does not image God by mirroring a divine quality but by being the inner state through which the creature's moral reality is honestly confronted before God.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The two-verse corpus is primarily silent on direct divine attribution of meekness or gentleness to God himself. In Heb5:2, the high priest's gentleness is specifically grounded in his own shared creaturely weakness — a structural ground that does not apply to God in the same form. The silence suggests that meekness/gentleness in its specifically creaturely form (the capacity for measured restraint grounded in one's own vulnerability and limitation) is a uniquely creaturely characteristic — it is the image-bearing expression of something in God (compassionate restraint toward the erring) but its specific form (grounded in shared weakness) is exclusively creaturely and characterises the mediating human figure.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The silence on divine attribution suggests that semnotēs in its creaturely form is the image-bearer's participation in the quality of settled moral gravity that belongs properly to God's holiness, expressed in the form appropriate to creaturely existence. The dignity of the human person before God is the creaturely expression of the divine weightiness — not God's own attribute directly reflected but the creature's share in the ordering gravity that characterises created existence properly ordered toward God. The silence also reflects that semnotēs has a distinctly social-characterological expression (visible in public life, household governance, teaching) that requires the creaturely social context for its expression.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The silence on divine possession suggests that willing-heartedness in its creaturely form is specifically the inner posture of the creature *toward God* — the freely-moved heart offering to the one who calls. The characteristic presupposes an asymmetry: there is one who calls (God) and one who freely offers (the creature). God cannot be willing-hearted toward himself in the same structural sense; the characteristic is constitutively creaturely in its directional structure. However, the divine calling for free offering rather than coerced contribution (Exo35:5) and God's own free giving (Psa51:12 — upholding with a willing spirit) suggest that God's own liberality is the divine ground from which the creaturely willing-heartedness derives and which it reflects: the freely-giving God calls for freely-giving creatures.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence is not silent on this matter (see T0.1.2). However, where the corpus addresses humility in the Father rather than the Son, it is consistently indirect: God *responds to* humility, *requires* humility (Mic6:8 — "what does the Lord require of you but… to walk humbly with your God"), and *produces* humility in the person. The Father's own possessing of the characteristic is not directly asserted in the corpus — only the Son's. This asymmetry suggests the characteristic, while present in the divine life, takes its definitively creaturely form in the Incarnation: the form in which a being descends below its natural standing, which is structurally unavailable to the Father in the same way. The silence at the Father level is analytically significant: humility in the human person is imago Dei not by simple reflection of the Father's nature but by participation in the Son's kenotic movement.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The silences are analytically graduated across the cluster. CHAR-3 Contrition is necessarily silent — the characteristic structurally presupposes a being capable of moral failure before a holy God; divine possession would be constitutionally incoherent. CHAR-5 Dignity is silent because it names a creaturely social-ordering quality (character gravity in civic, household, and pedagogical contexts) that requires the creaturely social sphere for its expression. CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness is structurally asymmetrical — it is the creature's freely-moving will *toward* God; God cannot be willing-hearted toward himself in the same directional sense. CHAR-4 Meekness is grounded in shared creaturely weakness (Heb5:2) — a constitutional ground unavailable to God in the same form. The cluster-level inference: the characteristics' silences are not accidental but trace the contour of the imago Dei — what the human person images is not a simple mirror of divine qualities but the *creaturely analogue* of divine character in the form appropriate to creaturely existence, asymmetry, and limitation. CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 alone achieve direct divine attribution through the Incarnation, which is itself the most radical case of creaturely-analogue-becoming-genuinely-divine.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The structural silence on God possessing wilful sinning (see T0.1.2) combined with the corpus's consistent framing of God as moral standard and judge (Eze 18:4; Eze 18:20; Gen 20:6; Eze 3:21) suggests that wilful sinning belongs to the fallen condition of the image-bearer rather than to the original divine image. The capacity for moral choice — the will — is part of the image; sinning is what happens when that will is turned against its Maker. 1Jo 2:1 ("I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin") presupposes that sinning is avoidable — that believers retain moral agency — but it is something Scripture explicitly aims to prevent rather than express. The imago Dei includes the will; wilful sinning represents the will's defection from the direction the image was designed to express.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The silence confirms the nature of each mechanism as a perversion of a God-given inner capacity. (1) *Desire*: God gave the creature desire as a designed faculty; enticement exploits what God gave. (2) *Social identity*: God gave the creature communal identity; hypocrisy falsifies what God designed for authentic community. (3) *Covenantal identity*: God gave Israel its covenantal identity through Moses; apostasy abandons what God established. The silence on God possessing these mechanisms confirms: each mechanism is the fallen-condition corruption of a created capacity that God gave and does not himself corrupt.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The silence on God possessing sin as universal condition is absolute and explicit — reinforced positively by the sinlessness of Christ (Heb 4:15; 2Cor 5:21; Joh 8:46) and the requirement for propitiation and purification that implies God's own holiness is not under sin's dominion (Heb 1:3; 2:17). The silence suggests that sin as universal condition is precisely the condition that separates the creature from the Creator: it is the defining gap between the human being as made and the God in whose image the human was made. Gen 4:7 — sin "crouching at the door" — presupposes a moral agency that can resist (unlike God who does not face such a force); the addressability of the command ("you must rule over it") presupposes a creaturely confrontation with sin that is categorically absent from the divine nature.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The silence on God possessing sin's enslaving power is absolute and structurally significant: the characteristic presupposes a *master-slave relationship* in which sin is the master and the creature is the slave (Joh 8:34 — "a slave to sin"). God cannot be enslaved — God is sovereign; and God does not enslave through sin — his purpose is liberation (1Jo 3:9; 1Jo 5:18). The silence reveals that the enslaving-power characteristic is constitutively the anti-God power structure: sin enslaves by claiming the governing role that belongs to God. 1Jo 3:8 — "the devil has been sinning from the beginning" — names the adversarial spiritual ground of the enslaving power; it is not God's power but the devil's originary sinning that grounds the enslaving structure.

**[CHAR-13]** E — God does not carry a sin-record before anyone else. He is the moral record-keeper, the one before whom the human sin-record exists. The silence on God possessing the record-as-burden reveals: (1) the characteristic is constitutively relational — it is the condition of a creature standing before a perfectly righteous Creator whose memory is complete; (2) Isa 43:24 — "you have burdened me with your sins" — God is burdened by human sin but as the one receiving the offense, not as the one who has an offense-record of his own. The asymmetry is structural: God keeps the record; the creature is the subject of it.

**[CHAR-14]** E — God never seeks forgiveness — he has no offense-record requiring another's pardon. The silence confirms the asymmetry at the characteristic's core: the seeking is constitutively creaturely (the fallen creature's movement toward God), while the granting is constitutively divine. This asymmetry reveals that the characteristic cannot be abstracted from the God-creature relationship: it names a specific direction of moral movement (creature → God in seeking; God → creature in granting) that requires both parties to be what they are.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The silence on God possessing the generational sin condition confirms its entirely fallen-creaturely nature: generational sin is the moral weight that accumulates through creaturely failure across generations. God cannot inherit sin because he has no predecessors whose sinning he would receive. Isa 43:27's structure — "your first father sinned" — presupposes a beginning-point of sinning in the first human ancestor, which God by definition does not share. The silence reveals that generational sin is the specific form of moral inheritance that belongs to finite creatures embedded in lineages, families, and nations — not to the eternal God who stands outside such transmission chains.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The silence on God possessing the sinner-identity is absolute and defining: Heb 7:26 — "holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens" — Christ's high-priestly character is defined precisely by his total separation from and non-participation in the sinner-identity. The silence reveals that the sinner-as-moral-character is constitutively the anti-image: it is the condition that arises when the image-bearer's moral character becomes defined by what God is not (sinless, holy, righteous). The characteristic exists only in the contrast with God's character.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The silence confirms that guilt-as-inner-state is constitutively creaturely: it is the conscience's recognition of moral liability *before* God — a relational inner state that presupposes both an offender (the person) and the one before whom the offense exists (God). God cannot be guilty before another, having no superior moral authority. Ezr 9:15 — "we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this" — guilt is the condition of standing before God with an unresolved moral debt; God stands in no such relational position before another. The silence is structurally necessary.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The silence confirms iniquity-as-accumulated-crime is constitutively creaturely: it is the human moral account of wrongdoing accumulated before the one who measures and judges it. Isa 43:24 — "you have wearied me with your iniquities" — positions God as the one upon whom iniquity's weight falls relationally; he is not the one who carries it as personal crime but the one who absorbs its relational burden. The silence is structurally necessary: God cannot commit moral crimes against himself or a higher authority, nor can he accumulate iniquity within himself. The very act of God pardoning iniquity (Mic 7:18) presupposes his total absence of it.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The silence is structurally necessary: transgression requires a higher boundary to cross, and God stands as the boundary-setter. Rom 4:15 — "where there is no law there is no transgression" — God is the law-giver whose command makes transgression possible; God cannot transgress his own commands. The silence reveals that transgression is constitutively creaturely — it can only exist where a creature stands under divine authority and chooses to cross the known line. God's absolute holiness (Exo 23:21 — "my name is in him" as ground for no pardon) is what makes the crossing possible as transgression.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The silence on God's possession of unintentional sinning (T0.1.2) reveals that this characteristic is grounded in *creaturely epistemic limitation* — the capacity to act without full knowledge of the moral implications of the act. God's omniscience excludes this capacity entirely: no act of God can be unintentional in the sense of proceeding without knowledge of its moral reality. The silence confirms that unintentional sinning belongs to the human condition as a *creature* (limited knowledge, limited perception) rather than to the divine image as such. The human capacity for inadvertent sin is the negative imprint of the creature's finitude, not a reflection of the divine image directly.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The silence is definitionally necessary: faithlessness requires a covenant bond whose violation constitutes the betrayal. God is the faithful party (the covenant-initiator) whose faithfulness is the very standard that makes human faithlessness intelligible as betrayal. Mal 2:10 — "Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why then are we faithless to one another?" — the appeal to God as common Father is the reason faithlessness toward one another is wrong; God's faithfulness is the constitutive ground that makes human faithlessness a moral failure. God cannot betray himself.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The silence (apart from Lam 3:9's judicial use) confirms that moral perversity is constitutively creaturely. God's nature is the straight standard against which perversion is defined: Pro 8:13 — wisdom hates perverted speech; Deu 16:19 — God's justice is what bribery subverts. The characteristic requires a prior moral order (which God embodies) that can be twisted; God is the source of the moral order, not subject to its distortion. Isa 29:16's "you turn things upside down" implies a right-side-up that God's own nature constitutes.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The corpus is not silent — it is emphatically declarative. God's freedom from injustice is the defining standard against which all human injustice is measured. Deu 32:4's "without iniquity, just and upright is he" establishes the divine character as the ontological baseline for justice; Eze 18's detailed Ezekiel-chapters ground individual moral accountability in God's own justice. The repeated explicit denials confirm: injustice requires a moral order to violate, and God is that moral order's author and embodiment — he cannot violate what he constitutes.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The structural silence on God confessing (T0.1.2) reveals that confession belongs to the *fallen creature's response to God* rather than to the original divine image. It is not a capacity the creature exercises because it shares it with God, but a capacity the creature requires because it has sinned against God. The corpus does evidence that confession is *divinely designed for* — God hears it (Neh 1:6 — Nehemiah prays "day and night" and God's ear is invoked as "attentive"), provides for it (Eze 33:16 — sins cancelled upon turning), and responds to it (1Sa 7:6 — corporate confession at Mizpah precedes Samuel's judgeship and renewal). The silence on divine confession and the presence of divine response together suggest that confession expresses the image not by sharing a divine quality but by enabling the image-bearer's restoration toward the God in whose image they were made.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The silence on God possessing conscience suppression (T0.1.2) indicates that the characteristic belongs entirely to the fallen creature rather than to any dimension of the divine image. Conscience itself is an image-bearing faculty — the moral witness within the person that reflects God's own moral awareness. Conscience suppression is the malfunction of that image-bearing faculty — the image's moral-witness capacity turned off or refused. The silence on God's possession confirms: the image includes conscience; conscience suppression is what happens to the image when it is damaged by sin and sustained rebellion. The characteristic is not a reflection of the divine image but its negation.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The absence of any divine refusal-to-repent in the corpus (T0.1.2) combined with the evidence of God's persistent moral invitation (Neh 9:29 — warnings given to turn them back) reveals that refusal to repent belongs entirely to the fallen creaturely condition. The divine image includes the *capacity* to turn (genuine moral agency, genuine will) but the fallen creature's use of that capacity in the direction of refusal is not a divine image expression but its negation. The silence confirms: the image provides the capacity for moral turning, and refusal to repent is what the will does with that capacity when it is captured by sin.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The silence on God possessing habitual defection (T0.1.2) combined with 1Jo 3:6's positive statement — "no one who abides in him keeps on sinning" — reveals that habitual defection is definitionally opposed to the condition of abiding in Christ (who images God perfectly). Abiding in him and keeping on sinning are mutually exclusive (1Jo 3:6). Since God's character is perfectly expressed in the one who abides in him — "no one who abides in him keeps on sinning" — the silence confirms that habitual defection has no place in the divine nature. The characteristic is the negative inverse of the abiding relationship: where abiding produces freedom from habitual sinning, habitual defection is the condition of those who have "never seen him or known him" (1Jo 3:6).

**[CHAR-7]** E — The silence on God possessing contagious sin combined with his direct indictment of leaders who practise it (1Ki 16:2; 21:22) reveals that the characteristic represents an abuse of the God-given authority structure. Leaders are given authority so that their inner moral direction shapes the community toward God; contagious sin is what happens when that authority structure operates in the opposite direction — transmitting sin rather than righteousness. The silence confirms that the characteristic is the *perversion* of the image's authority-bearing capacity, not an expression of it. God-given authority is designed for moral formation toward God; contagious sin corrupts it into moral formation away from God.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The silence on God revolting combined with 2Ch 21:10's causal link (God forsaken → revolts occur) reveals that political revolt is the characteristic that emerges when the God-grounded authority structure is abandoned. God himself does not revolt because he is the source and legitimising ground of all authority — revolt against God is the primordial rebellion that the pa.sha register of the H6586 root names in other M10 contexts. The political-revolt register of pa.sha in this corpus applies the same root to the human-political level: just as theological revolt breaks the God-human covenantal relationship, political revolt breaks the authority-subject governing relationship. The silence on divine political revolt confirms: God is on the receiving end of revolt (covenantal-theological), not its practitioner.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The silence on God blaspheming reveals two things. (1) God possesses speech — he speaks, names, declares, and pronounces — but his speech is always aligned with his own nature and truth; the creature's sinful speech is the perversion of the speech-capacity God gave. (2) Even the highest creaturely agents — angels — restrain blasphemous speech: Jude 9 — "even the archangel Michael... did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment" and 2Pe 2:11 — "angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment." If angelic speech is constrained from blasphemy, God's speech is infinitely more so. The silence confirms: sinful speech is the perversion of the image's speech-capacity, a capacity God gave and cannot himself misuse.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Scripture is not silent but actively declarative on this point (Job 34:10). Nevertheless, the analytical question about the divine image remains important: because wickedness-as-settled-person-identity is constitutionally absent from God, it cannot be an aspect of the divine image that the human is designed to reflect. The verse evidence suggests that the human capacity for this characteristic represents a corruption or inversion of the image, not an expression of it. Psa 9:17 defines the wicked by their forgetting of God; Gen 18:23–25 presupposes that wickedness and righteousness are distinct moral statuses that map onto just and unjust outcomes respectively — the whole structure presupposes a divine moral order the wicked person violates. Wickedness-as-settled-identity is therefore the image-bearer in a state of image-corruption or image-inversion.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Scripture is not merely silent but actively declarative in opposing this characteristic to God (T0.1.2). The analytical significance: evil as constitutional inner nature belongs exclusively to the creaturely sphere as a post-creation failure-condition. Its absence from God is not accidental silence but the positive ground from which the characteristic's seriousness is assessed. That humans are "constitutionally evil" (Mat 7:11 — VCG-02) while God is not means the characteristic represents the precise site where creaturely nature has departed from its original orientation toward the divine. The silence about God's possession is the theological ground for why the characteristic requires transformation (Act 3:26 — VCG-05 — turning from wickedness through divine blessing).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Scripture is not silent but actively declarative: God is the one who reviles, not the one who is reviled. The relevant silence concerns the human experience of being abominable to oneself — the characteristic's subjective inner dimension is almost entirely framed from the divine-perspective side (what God finds abominable) rather than as a first-person inner experience of the abominable person. Where the human inner experience does appear — Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): "you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and your abominations" — it appears as an awakened human conscience finally registering the divine verdict. The silence about God possessing the experience of abomination (being repugnant) reveals the characteristic as a purely creaturely failure-condition: God has no moral corruption that would make him abominable. What God has is the morally sensitive faculty of revulsion that names and responds to abomination in the creature.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Scripture is not silent but actively declarative (T0.1.2): God hates idolatrous abomination rather than possessing it. The silence about God's possession reveals the characteristic as the inversion of the designed God-devotion faculty in the human person. The human person was created with the capacity for exclusive devotion — a capacity designed for God. When that capacity is attached to idol-objects, idolatrous abomination results. God's non-possession of the characteristic is the negative space that defines the characteristic: what makes idolatry an abomination is precisely that the devotion-faculty is attached to what is not God. The silence about God possessing false devotion confirms that CHAR-4 is constitutively a departure from the relational orientation the created human was designed for.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Scripture is actively declarative (T0.1.2) rather than merely silent. God is consistently positioned as the moral authority who perceives, hates, and judges iniquity rather than as one who possesses it. The silence about God scheming iniquity reveals the characteristic as the image-bearer's misuse of the generative inner capacities (mind devising, heart conceiving, will executing) that are meant to produce what is good. Isa 32:6 (vc=38181 — VCG-02): "his heart is busy with iniquity" — the heart's busyness with iniquity names the corruption of a generative capacity; the divine image designed human persons with generative inner faculties precisely so that good could be conceived and enacted from within. The silence about God plotting trouble on beds or conceiving mischief (Psa 7:14 — vc=38245 — VCG-02; Psa 36:4 — vc=38235 — VCG-02) names the characteristic as the inversion of what those faculties were for.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Scripture is not merely silent but actively declarative (T0.1.2): God is the target of blasphemy, not its agent. The silence about God speaking evil through speech reveals the characteristic as the inversion of the image-bearing speech-capacity. The human person as image-bearer was equipped with speech specifically to name, testify, and render glory to God and to represent reality truthfully. Evil expressed through speech — blasphemy, slander, false accusation — inverts every dimension of that design. Rom 14:16 (vc=14359 — VCG-02): "do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil" — the possibility of good being spoken of as evil presupposes that speech was designed to name good as good; the inversion is the failure of the image-bearing speech-function.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics note not silence but active declaration — God is positioned as the structural opposite and the moral judge of every characteristic. The cluster-scope pattern is: each characteristic's silence about God's possession reveals the specific image-bearing capacity that the characteristic corrupts. Char 1's denial reveals that wickedness corrupts the image's moral-directional capacity (the inner person oriented toward God). Char 2's denial reveals that constitutional evil corrupts the image's generative-nature (the inner nature designed to produce from its constitution what is right). Char 3's denial reveals that moral-character abomination corrupts the image's relational-moral alignment with God. Char 4's denial reveals that idolatrous abomination corrupts the image's devotion-capacity (designed for God, misdirected to idols). Char 5's denial reveals that iniquity-scheming corrupts the image's generative-inner-faculties (designed to conceive and produce good). Char 6's denial reveals that evil speech corrupts the image's speech-capacity (designed to name, testify, and glorify). The cluster's six silences collectively map the image-bearer's six primary inner capacities — moral direction, constitutive nature, moral-relational alignment, devotion, generative faculty, and speech — each of which has a corresponding M10b form of corruption.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The silence confirms that the ritual defilement-state is not an image-bearer expression in the sense of resembling God, but rather it functions within the image-bearing vocation by defining the boundary of access to divine presence. Lev 10:10 frames the priestly vocation: "to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean." The priest's calling is to hold the distinction God himself embodies. The defilement-state, by being what God is not, creates the space in which the image-bearing vocation is exercised: the human person is called to manage the clean/unclean boundary in imitation of divine holiness. The silence about God's possession of defilement means the human engagement with this characteristic is participation in a structure God establishes and maintains, not a reflection of a divine property.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The silence confirms that the moral-inner defilement-state is the condition of the image-bearer when the image is disrupted or distorted. It is not a divine property the person is created to reflect; it is the condition that emerges when the person ceases to image God's holiness. Isa 64:6 (M10c-C-VCG-01) makes this most stark: "we have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment" — the corporate confession of a community whose interior life no longer reflects divine moral purity. The silence about God's possession of this state positions the characteristic as the marker of image-disruption: the divine image in the person is in proportion to the absence of moral-inner defilement, and in inverse proportion to its presence.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The near-total silence about God's possession of this characteristic (the Eze 20:26 exception being judicial and unique) confirms that the corporate/covenantal defilement-state is a specifically creaturely-covenantal condition. God's silence as a bearer of this characteristic reveals its essential nature: it is the condition that arises when creaturely covenantal persons — whose inner will, shared life, and sacred stewardship are oriented toward God — turn away from him in unfaithfulness. The characteristic requires a covenantal community in relation with a holy God; it cannot exist in God himself, but it exists in the gap between what the covenantal community is called to be and what they have become through corporate moral defection.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The silence confirms that defilement by external spiritual agency is categorically alien to the divine nature. God is holy; the unclean spirits recognise this by their response to Jesus (Mar 3:11 — falling before him, confessing "Son of God"). The silence suggests the characteristic belongs entirely to the adversarial-creaturely domain: it arises from the action of spiritual beings in opposition to God's holiness, affecting human persons who are vulnerable to this external force. The characteristic's place in the divine image is entirely negative: it is the disruption of the image-bearer's proper constitution by an alien spiritual power.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's combined silence on divine possession reveals a differentiated picture of the characteristic's place in the divine image. Characteristic 1's silence places the defilement-state within the creaturely domain of finitude and mortality — God cannot bear the condition because he is without body and without limitation by death; the silence locates the human person's susceptibility as part of their created embodied constitution. Characteristic 2's silence places the defilement-state as the marker of image-disruption — the divine image in the person is in inverse proportion to its presence. Characteristic 3's near-silence (with the Eze 20:26 exception) places the condition as belonging to the gap between covenantal calling and covenantal betrayal — it requires both the covenantal relationship and the community's departure from it. Characteristic 4's silence locates the condition as categorically alien to the divine nature, belonging to the adversarial-creaturely domain. Across the cluster, the silence progressively confirms that defilement is a multi-dimensional marker of creaturely distance from God — bodily-mortal (Char 1), moral-interior (Char 2), covenantal-relational (Char 3), and adversarial-spiritual (Char 4).

questions.section: T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
questions.question_text: Does this verse state any purpose, role, or effect the characteristic serves in the person — what it leads the person to be, do, or become? Record it if stated; otherwise record none.

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses this partially. The verse evidence foregrounds the *relational* purpose of forgiveness in the human person rather than its created-design purpose specifically.

What the data establishes:
- Forgiveness equips the human person to **sustain horizontal relationships** that would otherwise collapse under the weight of accumulated offence (F-003; Mat 18:35; Luk 17:3-4)
- Forgiveness equips the person to **participate in the vertical relationship** with God — specifically, Mat 5:24 establishes that unreconciled relationships impair worship, implying forgiveness is the condition for full vertical access
- Forgiveness equips the person to **break the cycle of debt-accumulation** in community (Mat 18:27 — the parable logic: forgiveness given prevents a destructive spiral)
- OBS-064-029 notes that forgiveness received generates love-orientation — suggesting forgiveness equips the person to **become relationally disposed toward others**

What is not addressed: whether forgiveness belongs to the original created design (pre-fall) or is exclusively a response to the fallen condition. The data does not distinguish these. This is noted under Prompt 2 below.

The partial answer: forgiveness equips the human person to sustain, restore, and deepen relational bonds — both horizontal (human-human) and vertical (human-God). It is a relational-capacity enabler.

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses this prompt with evidence sufficient for several observations, though the question of original created purpose is not directly stated in the verse evidence and must be assembled from the data's implications.

**Compassion equips the person to face outward toward the suffering of others.** The registry description states: "Compassion always faces outward toward the one suffering and produces action." This is the functional description confirmed across the vocabulary. Splanchnizō (G4697) is consistently triggered by the sight of suffering — crowds without a shepherd, a widow's grief, a leper's condition, a wounded stranger (Pass 1, group 730-001). Compassion equips the person to be moved by what they see in another, not merely to observe it from a safe distance.

**Compassion equips the person to participate in another's experience.** The SYM-PATH root family (sumpatheō, sumpaschō, sumpathēs) names compassion as genuine entry into another's experience — suffering-with, not merely sympathising-from-outside. 1 Pet 3:8 places sumpathēs (sympathetic) as a defining character quality in the list of community virtues. This equips the person for genuine relational solidarity.

**Compassion equips the person to bear the image of God in concrete social and relational contexts.** The eleēmosunē vocabulary (G1654) shows how compassion arrives at its normative social form — almsgiving. Luke 11:41 grounds almsgiving in inner purity; Matt 6:2-4 addresses the manner of giving. The inner quality of compassion is what gives the outward act its validity (Pass 1, term 20 sense analysis). Compassion equips the person to embody in social practice what God is in his inner character.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not directly address whether compassion as created purpose is specifically oriented toward a pre-fall relational ideal or whether its current expression is already conditioned by the presence of suffering (i.e., whether compassion presupposes a fallen world). This is named explicitly at T0.2 Prompt 2.

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence speaks clearly to what contrition *does* in the post-fall condition — it produces the inner-being posture that draws divine nearness, revival, and acceptance (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15; Psa 51:17; Isa 66:2). But the question of *created purpose* — what contrition equips the human being for in their constitution as a creature — is only partially addressed.

What the data does support: contrition equips the human person for **genuine receptivity before God**. The contrite inner being is characterised by openness, lowliness, and absence of self-claim — it is constituted to receive rather than to assert. This receptivity is not merely a post-fall emergency measure; the three-fold posture of Isa 66:2 (humble, contrite, trembling at God's word) suggests an orientation of creaturely attentiveness that is constitutive of the right creature-Creator relationship. In this sense, contrition may belong to the *creaturely* dimension of the human design — the capacity for appropriate self-knowledge before a holy God.

What is missing: the data does not directly address whether contrition is part of the original created design (before moral failure) or whether it is specifically a response to the fallen condition. This is a genuine gap, addressed further at T0.2 Prompt 2.

*Partial: the data establishes the receptive-orientation function but does not definitively locate it within created design versus fallen response.*

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence establishes several purposes fellowship serves in the human person, though the data does not frame these explicitly in terms of *created design* — the evidential frame is primarily soteriological, moral, and covenantal rather than protological.

**What fellowship equips the person to become:** 2Pe 1:4 presents fellowship with divine nature as the mechanism by which persons *escape from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire* and *become partakers of the divine nature*. The telos is participation in the nature of God — fellowship equips the person for ontological transformation toward divine likeness.

**What fellowship equips the person to do:** Ecc 4:10 shows fellowship in its mutual-support function: *if they fall, one will lift up his fellow*. Fellowship equips the person for practical inter-relational action — lifting up the fallen. Psa 119:63 grounds companionship in moral alignment: fellowship with those who fear God equips the person for righteous life. 1Jo 1:3 shows fellowship equipping persons to extend the relational chain: hearing leads to fellowship, and fellowship is proclaimed to create further fellowship.

**What fellowship equips the person to be:** The co-occurrence with unity (R167), love (R103), and comfort (R192) suggests that fellowship is part of a cluster of characteristics that constitute the person's relational inner being. Fellowship equips the person to be a participant — not merely an observer or individual — in shared life.

**Gap identified:** The data does not directly address whether fellowship is part of the *original created design* or whether its higher registers (divine nature participation) are responses to the fallen condition. This is noted below in Prompt 2.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence indicates that goodness as a created characteristic equips the human person for three interrelated purposes: (1) Moral orientation — to recognise, assess, and align conduct with what is genuinely beneficial (884-002, 884-004, 884-006). Mic 6:8 defines this as doing justice, loving kindness, walking humbly — the equipped person has the capacity to live in right orientation toward God and others. (2) Relational connection — to receive God's goodness and extend it toward others (884-001, 884-002, 886-002). Rom 15:14 names the goodness-filled person as one "able to instruct one another" — goodness equips for community. (3) Volitional alignment — to prefer and choose what is genuinely good (884-008). The volitional-preference idiom's 40 verses show goodness functioning as the criterion of the will's proper operation. The three purposes converge: the person equipped with goodness has the capacity to be good (character), do good (conduct), and choose good (volition). (OBS-067-OBS-001, OBS-067-OBS-027, OBS-067-OBS-039, OBS-067-OBS-040)

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence points to love as the characteristic that equips the human person to participate in the relational structure of divine life — to enter and sustain the three directional axes identified in OBS-103-035 (vertical-descending, vertical-ascending, horizontal). Love of God with all heart, soul, and mind (Mat 22:37, OBS-103-139) equips the person to respond to the divine love that constitutes them. Love of neighbour (Lev 19:18, OBS-103-071) equips the person to bear the image of God toward other persons. Love in community (Joh 13:34, OBS-103-145) equips the person to live within the relational structure that constitutes the community of God's people. Together: love equips the person to be the image-bearer — to reflect God's own love outward in every relational direction. The great commandment (love God, love neighbour) implies that love is the purpose-function of the human person as created: the person is made to love, and love is what the person most fundamentally is for.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence suggests that the human capacity for covenant serves the purpose of structuring faithful, committed relationship — both vertically (with God) and horizontally (with other persons). The vocabulary of covenant spans marriage alliance (H1285 sub-sense 1a5 — OBS-034-009), friendship covenant (3304-004 — OBS-034-049), political treaty (1a1), and the divine-human bond (1b). The created purpose is the capacity to enter and sustain solemn, binding relational commitments — to be the kind of person who can make a promise and keep it, whose word is reliable, and who can be held in relationship through structured mutual commitment. This equips the human person for stable communal life, faithful marriage, and the particular form of relationship with God that Scripture calls covenantal.

findings.session_b_note: Peace serves as the integrative condition of the human person's existence — the state in which the person is whole, functional, and in right relation with God, self, and others. The evidence from OBS-117-144, OBS-117-149, OBS-117-156 establishes this: shalom as wholeness of person (Isa 26:3 — mind, trust, peace as an integrated state), welfare of the whole person (Jer 29:11 — future, hope), soul's rest (Psa 4:8). The purpose is not merely psychological comfort but existential integrity — peace is the condition in which the person fulfils their creaturely purpose of walking with God (Mal 2:6, OBS-117-146: walked with me in peace and uprightness). Lam 3:17 ("my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is") shows by negation: without shalom, the soul loses access to its own flourishing.

findings.session_b_note: The human giving group (872-005) shows that inner-being giving equips the human person for: (a) receptive relinquishment — accepting that all possessions are gifts held on loan from God (Job 1:21, OBS-060-044); and (b) active covenantal self-offering — giving the body in obedient service grounded in trust (Isa 50:6, OBS-060-045). These together suggest that giving-as-inner-act equips the human for faithful creaturely existence: holding received goods appropriately (as gift, not possession), and offering the self in response to divine call. The gap: the data does not contain explicit creation-order giving — the 872-005 verses are drawn from fallen/covenantal contexts, not from an explicit pre-fall design statement. The purpose of human giving in the created order is not stated; it must be inferred from the functional descriptions in the classified verses.

Group 550-NEW-02 (righteous hatred, anchor Pro 8:13) shows this directly. "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil" — the verse makes hatred of evil constitutive of what it means to fear God. Psa 97:10 commands it: "O you who love the Lord, hate evil!" Psa 45:7 grounds the anointed king's authority in it: "you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God your God has anointed you." The evidence shows that hatred of evil is not an incidental response but a necessary function of the properly ordered inner life — the negative pole of moral orientation that makes love of the good coherent. A person who loves righteousness without hating wickedness has an incomplete and unstable moral orientation.

No verse in M06-B suggests contempt serves a created purpose. Unlike righteous hatred, there is no commanded or praised contempt in M06-B. The characteristic appears entirely as a disordering of the inner being — the inversion of reverence and honour-giving. Whether contempt could theoretically have a righteous form (appropriate disregard for what is genuinely worthless) is not addressed by the verse evidence. The corpus treats contempt as a characteristically fallen disposition.

Group 252-001 shows the created purpose. The abhorrence of falsehood (Psa 119:163) is the negative pole of the love of God's law. The commanded abhorrence (Deu 23:7 — "you shall not abhor an Edomite...you shall not abhor an Egyptian") treats the capacity as real and regulable — implying it serves a proper function when rightly directed. The created purpose of abhorrence is to mark what is genuinely repugnant to God's character and to maintain the inner being's separation from it.

No verse suggests cruelty serves a created purpose. It is defined by the absence of mercy, restraint, and fear of God — the condition produced when the inner governing framework that would limit destructive impulses is removed. Cruelty cannot be directed rightly because it is constitutively the absence of what directing rightly requires.

Reproach does not serve a created purpose in the sense of a positive inner capacity. It is a condition imposed from outside — the experience of being an object of public contempt and shame. Unlike righteous hatred or abhorrence, there is no commanded righteous reproach. Reproach is what happens to the person, not what they exercise.

The adversary relationship serves the purpose of justice and covenant advocacy. Isa 49:25: "I will contend with those who contend with you" — the contention serves the purpose of deliverance for the oppressed. Exo 23:22 shows God adopting the adversary posture in service of covenant protection. The created purpose of the adversary-facing structure is not the hostility itself but the relational structure that creates the context for appeal, justice, and covenant vindication.

No created purpose. Malice is the compound of enmity, contempt, and pleasure in destruction — all three of which represent the inversion or corruption of positive inner capacities. It has no righteous form and no created purpose.

Love equips the person to be the relational image-bearer — the creature whose fundamental inner orientation is directed attachment toward God and neighbour. The great commandment (Mat 22:37 — Group 1542) names love as the vocation for which the person is constituted.

Compassion equips the person to respond to suffering with a visceral inner movement that generates action — to be a source of relief for those who suffer. The compassionate hearts commanded at Col 3:12 (Group 1638) establish this as the vocation of the new humanity.

Mercy equips the person to participate in the mercy-economy that structures the divine-human relationship — to be a recipient and conduit of mercy: "blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy" (Mat 5:7 — Groups 1629, 1631).

Goodness equips the person to be a source of benefit toward others and toward creation — "created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand" (Eph 2:10 — Group 1098). Goodness is the vocation for which re-creation is purposive.

Gentleness equips the person to engage difficult situations — correction, opposition, reception of God's word, witness under pressure — without becoming coercive or destructive. It equips the person to be a restorer (Gal 6:1 — Group 1104) and a witness (1Pe 3:15 — Group 1262).

Comfort equips the person to become a channel of the comfort they have received — "so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2Cor 1:4 — Group 602). The purpose is the cascading of received comfort outward.

Fellowship equips the person to participate in the shared life that the gospel creates — "so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and his Son" (1Jo 1:3 — Group 1055). The purpose is vertical and horizontal participation simultaneously.

The cluster's characteristics collectively equip the person for the full range of relational engagement: in love (constitutive orientation), compassion (response to suffering), mercy (response to guilt/helplessness), goodness (moral expression), gentleness (response to provocation and conflict), comfort (response to grief), and fellowship (shared communal life). Together they constitute the relational equipment for life as an image-bearer in a world where suffering, guilt, conflict, grief, and broken fellowship are constant realities.
**[A1 — God Righteousness]** A1 addresses God's righteousness, not human created purpose directly. The created-purpose question is answered primarily in A2.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The verse evidence across A2's VSGs reveals that righteousness equips the human person for relationship with God, stability in life, and protective presence for others. The righteous person is "seen, tested, known, upheld" by God (VSG 3246-002); stands before God in prayer and petition (VSG 942-001); is guarded and established (VSG M26-A2-013). Community function: the presence of righteous persons carries protective power — Abraham's intercession for Sodom (Gen 18:23–28, VSG M26-A2-015) shows the righteous as a preservative force within their communities. The person is equipped to be: in right relation with God, stable in life, generative toward others, and aligned with the grain of how reality is structured.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** The B verses show uprightness equipping the person for honest speech, discernment, and recognition of what is right. "Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path" (Pro 2:9, VSG 1212-002). Uprightness enables the person to walk in ways that are not devious (Pro 14:2) — equipped for reliable, straight-dealing life.

**[C — Justification]** Justification equips the person for heir-status and new standing before God. "Being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life" (Tit 3:7, VSG 3194-001). The purpose is not merely forensic acquittal — it establishes a new relational position enabling participation in divine life.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The D verses suggest that the capacity for avenging justice equips the person to entrust retribution to God rather than executing it personally. "Leave it to the wrath of God" (Rom 12:19, VSG 6841-002) — the inner act of relinquishing personal vengeance is itself an act requiring conviction that God will rightly repay. The purpose: the human capacity to recognise wrong and desire its correction is real and good, but it is purposed to flow toward God (petition, trust) rather than self-execution.

**[E — Condemnation]** The E verses reveal that the capacity for condemnation serves a diagnostic and moral purpose. Self-condemnation (autokatakritos, Tit 3:11) shows that the person is built with an inner mechanism tracking moral failure. The condemning capacity — even directed outward (Mat 12:41–42, VSG 4846-001) — reveals a moral faculty oriented toward truth. The purpose: the capacity for condemnation equips the person to take moral distinctions seriously.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The F verses show the reckoning faculty equipping the person for sustained moral orientation. "Count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Rom 6:11, VSG 3410-001). The reckoning faculty enables the person to apply theological reality to inner experience — to treat as true what God has declared. The purpose: the reckoning faculty is needed to receive and live from justification. Without it, the declared status of justification would have no inner-life traction.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The G terms reveal created purpose by negation. "They do not know how to do right" (Amo 3:10, VSG 1214-001) names the failure of the capacity for moral orientation. The structural opposites reveal that the created purpose of righteousness is to enable the person to know and do what is right — a capacity that can be forfeited.

**[CLUSTER]** Across the cluster, righteousness equips the human person to: (1) stand in right relation with God (A2, C); (2) live stably and generatively in the created order (A2, B); (3) function as a moral agent who can recognise right and wrong (F, E); (4) serve as a preservative and redemptive presence for others (A2-015); (5) entrust retributive justice to God rather than executing it autonomously (D). The cluster reveals a comprehensive created purpose: the person made righteous is equipped for full participation in the moral order God has established.

findings.finding_value: In M01-A the created purpose of reverential fear is comprehensive: it equips the person to know rightly (Pro 1:7 anchor: "foundational inner disposition from which all knowledge begins"), act ethically (Lev 19:14 anchor: the operative moral restraint in situations of power over the vulnerable), receive divine guidance (Psa 25:14 anchor: reverential fear "positions a person for intimate covenant relationship"), and sustain life in covenant relationship (Deu 6:2; Ecc 12:13: "the whole duty of man"). Fear equips the person to be wise, just, covenant-faithful, and relationally aligned with God.

M01-B's acute fear serves a situational purpose: it produces immediate inner responsiveness to genuinely dangerous or genuinely divine realities. Gen 32:7 (anchor B-VCG-05, Jacob's fear driving strategic action) shows fear equipping the person for responsive decision-making. The "do not fear" pattern (B-VCG-06, anchor Isa 43:1) implies that acute fear's created purpose is not suppression but redirection — the person is equipped to release fear when its object is mastered by God.

M01-C's terror-as-force serves the purpose of establishing divine authority over human history. The Exo 23:27 material shows God's terror equipping Israel to occupy the land not through military strength but through a divine inner state in their enemies. The created purpose is to make human history legible as a domain governed by God, where resistance to his purposes collapses from within.

M01-D's dismay serves a created purpose as an inner signal of genuine catastrophe — it is the inner collapse that accurately registers the breaking of what cannot hold. The D-VCG-04 material (Jer 1:17 anchor) shows that dismay is something a person of God can resist when God has spoken — suggesting its created purpose is honest registration of threat, checked by divine word.

M01-E's trembling serves the double created purpose of: (1) registering divine holiness somatically (Exo 19:16 anchor: "whole-body fear response to divine presence") and (2) marking genuine reverence for God's word (Isa 66:2 anchor: "the trembling is located in the spirit and shows reverence that orients the whole inner person toward God's communication"). The person who trembles at God's word is specifically identified as the one God looks for (Isa 66:2). Trembling equips the person to receive divine communication with appropriate gravity.

M01-F's anticipatory dread serves the purpose of honest forward-looking engagement with consequences. Job 3:25 (anchor F-VCG-02) shows dread that corresponded accurately to what actually came — the dread was not irrational. The covenantal-curse form of dread (Deu 28:66-67, anchor F-VCG-03) shows fear serving as a covenant-consequence indicator. The pastoral anxiety material (2Cor 12:20 anchor F-VCG-05) shows anticipatory dread serving responsible concern for others.

M01-G's evidence defines the purpose of fear by negating timidity: the created purpose of the inner constitution is courage, faith, and trust — not cowardly shrinking. 2Ti 1:7 (anchor) specifies the spirit God gives: "power, love, and self-control." Timidity's absence equips the person to act faithfully under pressure (Mat 25:25; Mat 8:26).

Across M01, fear as a created capacity serves the following purposes: (1) orienting the person toward God as the supreme reality worthy of awe (M01-A); (2) enabling accurate inner registration of genuine threat and genuine holiness (M01-B); (3) establishing divine sovereignty over the inner states of peoples and nations (M01-C); (4) providing honest signal of genuine collapse (M01-D); (5) registering divine holiness in the body (M01-E); (6) enabling forward-looking moral responsibility (M01-F); and (7) establishing faith and courage as the created positive (M01-G). The capacity for fear is integral to the created inner life.

The verse evidence consistently shows anger equipping the person to respond to moral violation with action that defends what matters. Moses' anger at Pharaoh (Exo 11:8 / M02-B-VCG-04) drives the final confrontation of injustice. Nehemiah's anger at oppression (Neh 5:6 / M02-B-VCG-04) equips him to name and address economic exploitation. Samuel's anger at Saul's disobedience (1Sa 15:11 / M02-B-VCG-02) drives intercessory urgency. The functional purpose is a capacity for morally calibrated response: anger equips the person to take wrongdoing seriously and respond with energy proportionate to the violation.
