The indignation corpus reveals a further purpose: indignation as proof of inner moral seriousness. 2Cor 7:11 shows indignation arising from godly grief as evidence of genuine repentance — its presence proves the inner person has engaged the moral reality of the wrong. Indignation equips the person to be a genuine moral witness to themselves and to others.

The jealousy-toward-God corpus reveals a purpose of consuming devotion: Elijah (1Ki 19:10; 19:14) and the psalmist (Psa 69:9; 119:139) show jealous zeal for God's honour equipping single-minded prophetic and devotional identity. This sub-register of the characteristic equips the person for the kind of fierce, exclusive loyalty that covenant demands.

The cluster's verse evidence suggests anger serves as the inner-being energy that refuses indifference to moral violation. It equips the person to register injustice with weight, to pursue just response, and to protect what is covenantally claimed. The created purpose is a morally calibrated reactivity — the capacity to care enough about what is right and wrong that the inner being fires with energy when the moral order is threatened.

The verse evidence across M03 indicates that grief equips the person for four primary purposes. First, grief drives prayer: the dominant pattern of M03-D-VCG-01 (tsar/tsa.rah corpus — 56 verses) is distress → cry to God → divine answer; grief is the engine of Godward petition. Second, grief enables moral responsiveness: godly grief produces repentance, earnestness, zeal, and moral reformation (2Cor 7:9-11 — M03-C-VCG-02; Eze 9:4 — M03-E-VCG-01). Third, grief enables empathic solidarity: weeping with those who weep is commanded as an act of will and love (Rom 12:15 — M03-A-VCG-05); Job's soul wept for the needy (Job 30:25 — M03-A-VCG-04). Fourth, grief orients the inner person toward eschatological hope: sighing as the mark of exile is paired with its future displacement by everlasting joy (Isa 35:10, 51:11 — M03-E-VCG-03), and the new creation's abolition of mourning (Rev 21:4 — M03-B-VCG-04) reveals that present grief is the condition of a not-yet-redeemed world, fitting for now, but not for the fullness.

Weeping equips the person for empathic solidarity (Rom 12:15), for intercessory prayer (1Sa 1:10; Joe 2:17), and for penitential honesty before God (2Ki 22:19; Ezr 10:1). In M03-A-VCG-02, tears function as the evidence that drives God to respond, making weeping the somatic form of genuine inner petition.

Mourning equips the person for socially structured grief expression (M03-B-VCG-01), for communal solidarity under shared catastrophe (M03-B-VCG-02), and for the orientation of the whole inner person toward God in repentance (Jam 4:9 — M03-B-VCG-04). The wise heart chooses the house of mourning (Ecc 7:2, 7:4) because mourning confronts the person with mortality and truth.

Distress equips the person for prayer and for covenantal discipline. M03-D-VCG-01 (56 verses) repeatedly names distress as the state that activates the divine-human exchange: "call upon me in the day of trouble" (Psa 50:15). M03-D-VCG-03 shows distress turning the inner will back toward God (Deu 4:30; 2Ch 15:4; Hos 5:15).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence consistently shows exultation functioning as the appropriate inner response of the created person to the reality of God's reign, salvation, and presence. Psa 2:11 commands "rejoice with trembling" before the enthroned Lord; Psa 32:11 commands the upright in heart to be glad in the Lord and rejoice; Psa 97:1 calls the earth to rejoice because "the Lord reigns." The purpose exultation serves is alignment: it orients the whole inner being — soul (Psa 35:9), heart (Psa 13:5; 32:11; Zec 10:7), whole being (Psa 16:9) — toward God as its rightful object. Exultation is the inner-being mechanism by which the human person participates in the truth of God's sovereignty and goodness. It equips the person to live from a true account of reality.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence reveals multiple created purposes: (1) **Alignment with God's reality** — joy is the appropriate inner response to divine sovereignty and goodness; the commanded feast-rejoicings (Deu 12:7, 12, 18; 16:11, 14, 15; 26:11; 27:7; Lev 23:40) establish rejoicing before God as the designed posture of the covenant community in God's presence; (2) **Relational completion** — Deu 24:5 (the husband exempted from military service to make his wife glad) shows that joy serves the completion of human relational bonds; Pro 10:1; 15:20; 23:24–25; 29:3 (wise children gladding parents) show joy functioning as the inner fruit of right-ordered human relationships; (3) **Communal cohesion** — M04-D (sunchairo) shows joy functioning as the mechanism of communal solidarity — the body that co-rejoices is the body that is bound together; (4) **Worship** — joy is the inner quality that animates and is the purpose of worship; Deu 28:47 makes failure to serve with joyfulness and gladness of heart the root cause of judgment, revealing joy as the designed inner disposition of the worshipper; (5) **Sustained engagement with life** — the Ecclesiastes evidence (Ecc 8:15; 9:7; 11:8–9) shows joy commended as the inner companion of mortal life across its whole span.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The evidence presents Suffering-Joy as primarily a **response-to-fallen-condition** capacity rather than an original-creation capacity (see T0.2.2) — it equips the person to: (1) **Maintain inner-being coherence under persecution** — Mat 5:12 ("rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven") equips the persecuted to sustain their inner orientation despite suffering; (2) **Participate in Christ's own suffering-to-glory pattern** — 1Pe 4:13 ("rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed") — Suffering-Joy equips the believer to enter the same suffering-glory trajectory Christ entered; (3) **Produce proven character** — Jas 1:2 ("count it all joy when you meet trials of various kinds") frames Suffering-Joy as the inner faculty that enables the trials to accomplish their formative work; (4) **Ground the inner being in eschatological reality** — 1Pe 1:6 ("in this you rejoice, though now for a little while... grieved by various trials") — present suffering is contextualised by the eschatological inheritance; Suffering-Joy equips this recontextualisation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence reveals three created purposes: (1) **Moral orientation** — M04-L-VCG-02 shows Gladness-as-evaluation guiding decisions, conduct, and community life (Jethro's assessment of Moses, Exo 18:17; Naomi's assessment of Ruth's best course, Rut 2:22; the repeated "not good" verdicts on injustice in Proverbs). The evaluative faculty equips the person to navigate moral reality accurately; (2) **Relational assessment** — M04-L-VCG-02 includes comparative evaluations of relational worth (Rut 4:15 — Ruth's love surpassing seven sons; 2Sa 18:3 — David's worth ten thousand soldiers) — the faculty serves honest relational perception; (3) **Receptive recognition of circumstantial goodness** — M04-O shows Gladness as the soul's warm inner response to genuinely good news, beneficial states, and received blessedness (Pro 12:25 — good word counteracting anxiety; Pro 15:30 — good news refreshing bones; Neh 2:18 — God's good hand motivating communal action). The characteristic equips the person to recognise and receive the good when it is genuinely present.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence reveals four created purposes: (1) **Alignment of the will with what is genuinely good** — Psa 40:8 ("I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart") — the will directed by Delight toward God's law enables natural, willing obedience rather than reluctant compliance; 1Ch 28:9 — "a willing mind" as the right orientation for serving God; (2) **Sustaining the inner person through adversity** — Psa 119:92 ("if your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction") — Delight in God's word is a life-preserving inner resource; similarly Psa 119:77, 143 — delight sustains through trouble and anguish; (3) **Orienting the inner being toward its proper object** — Psa 37:4 ("delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart") — Delight in God aligns the will with his giving, restructuring what the heart desires; (4) **Equipping moral discernment** — Psa 1:2 ("his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night") — the delight-in-law faculty drives the sustained engagement that produces wisdom; the Preacher who "sought to find words of delight" (Ecc 12:10) names the inner faculty as a vehicle for discovering and expressing truth.

The characteristic is consistently framed as a departure from, and inversion of, designed inner capacities rather than as a designed function. Psa 119:133 (vc=38227 — VCG-04): "let no iniquity get dominion over me" — the prayer against dominion presupposes that iniquity's dominion is an unwanted deviation from a right inner state, not an intended capacity. The evidence contains no verse presenting active inner scheming as serving a positive original-design purpose.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The evidence does not address what purpose evil speech serves in the originally created human. The characteristic is entirely framed as a departure from and corruption of the designed speech-capacity: the evidence describes blasphemy as what the hardened will generates under judgment (Rev 16:9/11/21 — VCG-01), as what false accusation does to the innocent (1Pe 2:12 — VCG-03), and as what conduct-caused dishonour does to God's name (Rom 2:24 — VCG-02). No verse presents evil expressed through speech as serving a positive designed function. This is explicitly noted.

**[CLUSTER]** S — All six characteristics record the same finding: S (silent). No characteristic in the M10b cluster addresses a positive designed purpose for any of its six inner-being evil forms. This cluster-level unanimity is analytically significant: the six forms of evil covered by M10b — wickedness (Char 1), constitutional evil (Char 2), moral-character abomination (Char 3), idolatrous abomination (Char 4), iniquity-scheming (Char 5), and evil speech (Char 6) — are all exclusively failure-conditions, not designed capacities. The silence is not incidental but structural: the question of designed purpose is not posed by the evidence of any characteristic in the cluster because all six address conditions that presuppose and corrupt designed capacities rather than being designed capacities themselves. The cluster's unanimous S here is the strongest possible evidence that M10b names the inner-being failures, not the inner-being designs.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The ritual defilement-state in the created order equips the person to navigate the boundary between the sacred and the common, between death and life, with appropriate attention and discipline. Its purpose is formative: the discipline of managing the defilement-state — washing, waiting, presenting oneself for examination, maintaining the clean/unclean distinction (Lev 11:47, 10:10) — trains the inner person in watchful restraint, conscience-responsiveness, and sacral orientation. Lev 11:44 frames the purpose explicitly: the call not to defile oneself is the means by which the person participates in imitating divine holiness. The defilement-state, by being something that must be actively managed and resolved, equips the human person to be a creature whose bodily life is morally and sacrally ordered — not a merely biological entity but one whose bodily actions have inner and relational consequence.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The 26-verse corpus does not evidence a creational purpose for the moral-inner defilement-state. Unlike Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state), which has structural provisions built into the created order (bodily management, cleansing remedies), Characteristic 2 is consistently framed in the evidence as a departure from the divine calling rather than as a creaturely feature designed for formation. The evidence is entirely about the condition's negative impact and the call to leave it (Rom 6:19, 1Th 4:7, 2Cor 7:1). No verse in the 26-verse corpus frames the moral-inner defilement-state as something God created for human flourishing or formation. Its purpose, if it has one, is revealed only indirectly through contrast: what the person is called away from clarifies what they are called toward.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The 83-verse corpus does not evidence a creational purpose for the corporate/covenantal defilement-state. Like Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state), this characteristic is consistently framed in the evidence as a departure from the covenantal calling rather than as a created faculty serving human flourishing. The evidence is entirely about the condition arising through moral defection (VCG-01, -02, -03, -04) and being reversed through divine cleansing (VCG-05). No verse frames corporate/covenantal defilement as something designed for the community's formation or benefit. Its analytical significance is entirely through contrast with what the community is called to be.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The 21-verse corpus does not evidence a creational purpose for defilement by external spiritual agency. The characteristic is presented throughout as an affliction. Those troubled by unclean spirits are "cured" (Luk 6:18, VCG-02) — the language of cure presupposes a prior state of wholeness from which the condition is a departure. Mat 10:1 (VCG-03) frames the characteristic as something requiring "authority... to cast them out" — an opposition to be overcome. No creational purpose for the characteristic is evidenced.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals a sharp asymmetry in creational purpose across the four characteristics. Characteristic 1 is the only one with an evidenced creational purpose: the discipline of managing the ritual defilement-state — washing, waiting, examination, maintaining the clean/unclean boundary (Lev 11:47, 10:10) — is explicitly formative, equipping the person for sacral stewardship and training the inner person in watchful restraint and conscience-responsiveness (Lev 11:44 — "be holy, for I am holy"). Characteristics 2, 3, and 4 are each S on creational purpose: all three are consistently framed as departures from the divine calling or the proper creaturely state, not as designed features for human formation. The asymmetry reveals that within the M10c cluster, only the ritual-defilement register has a positive creational function — it is a feature of the created sacral order, not simply a fallen condition. Characteristics 2, 3, and 4 belong to the fall's domain (moral defection, covenantal betrayal, adversarial spiritual attack). The cluster thus shows the defilement concept operating across both creation (Char 1 as designed sacral structure) and fall (Chars 2, 3, 4 as conditions of departed or invaded humanity).

questions.section: T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
questions.question_text: Across the evidence, does the characteristic's role read as belonging to created design, to the fallen condition, to both, or as not determinable?

findings.session_b_note:
The tension is present but not resolved. Grace as unmerited giving presupposes a recipient who has no claim — consistent with both creaturely status before God (the creature always receives; it cannot give to God from its own resources) and fallen status. SD008 (Eph 2:1-5: grace addressing the dead) and SD032 (grace inhabiting weakness) both point toward the fallen condition as the primary context. But whether grace as the relational disposition of the greater toward the lesser belongs to the original created order is not directly resolved.

*Gap identified: the question of grace in the original created order — before the fall, by virtue of being a creature — is not addressed in the prior analysis. This is a genuine T0 gap.*

findings.session_b_note: The evidence supports both, distinguished by term. Gen 1:31 (884-007) establishes goodness as pre-fall and pre-relational — the Creator pronounces creation "very good" before any human moral life begins. This is goodness as original created quality, not a response to fallenness. The agathōsunē coinage (G0019, 885-001), however, is pneumatologically concentrated — a Spirit-produced fruit listed in Gal 5:22. The Spirit-production context implies the fallen condition: the natural human condition is characterised by complete absence of goodness (Rom 3:12), so Spirit-produced goodness is explicitly a redemptive response. H2896A in 884-002 (human moral character) and 884-003 (experiential good) could reflect both original design (the human created to be and experience good) and the ongoing challenge of maintaining that orientation under fallen conditions. The registry carries both registers: goodness as created design (Gen 1 ontological goodness, doxological goodness of 884-001) and goodness as restored/Spirit-produced capacity (885-001, 886-002). (OBS-067-OBS-036, OBS-067-OBS-046, OBS-067-OBS-048)

findings.session_b_note: The evidence strongly implies love is part of original created design — the great commandment assumes love as the constitutive purpose of the human person, not as a remedial response. Song of Songs presents love (ahavah, dod) in a creation-delight context without reference to sin or fall — erotic love as given, not remedial. The divine self-declaration (Exo 34:6) attributes love to God prior to and independent of the fall. However, the data also shows love operating distinctively in response to the fallen condition: agapē of enemies (Mat 5:44, OBS-103-143) presupposes enemies exist; racham/compassion (OBS-103-029) responds to suffering that is post-fall in character; forgiveness-love (Luk 7:47, OBS-103-020 via SD pointer) presupposes guilt. The data does not contain an explicit statement that love existed in creation before the fall — the gap in pre-fall love evidence is noted. Both dimensions appear present but the evidence is stronger for love as created design than as purely remedial response.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence is structurally ambiguous. The atonement/propitiation vocabulary (the largest cluster in R111) presupposes sin and guilt — it has no function in a sinless context. This suggests much of R111's vocabulary addresses mercy as response to the fallen condition. However, the compassion vocabulary (*racham*, *oiktirmos*) — which is etymologically connected to the womb (*rechem*) — suggests mercy as a created capacity prior to sin. 2Cor 1:3 names God as "Father of mercies" without restricting mercy to fallen contexts. The evidence does not resolve whether the created design includes mercy as a relational disposition that would express differently in a sinless world, or whether mercy is exclusively a redemptive response. This is a genuine gap — existing SD pointers do not capture it. OBS-111-009, OBS-111-068.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence points strongly toward contrition as a response to the fallen condition. Every anchor verse presupposes guilt, moral failure, or suffering as the context. The atonement-adjacent vocabulary and the penitential psalm context (Psa 51) situate contrition within the world of sin and divine holiness confronting it. However, the posture of lowliness before God (which underlies contrition) may be a created creaturely disposition — the creature before the Creator — that takes the specific form of contrition only in the fallen condition. This cannot be resolved from the available data. OBS-030-001, OBS-030-045.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence points toward fellowship operating across both original design and fallen condition. Existential fellowship (Ecc 9:4 — being-among-the-living) is a created given. Horizontal companionship fellowship (Ecc 4:10 — the friend who lifts) is a created structural good. The highest fellowship (2Pe 1:4 — divine nature participation) requires escape from corruption, implying the fallen condition as the frame from which this fellowship rescues. Fellowship therefore spans both: the created-design level (existential and companionship) and the redemptive level (divine nature participation requiring escape from corruption). OBS-062-019, OBS-062-045, OBS-062-058.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence positions forgiveness as primarily a response to the fallen condition. Every anchor verse presupposes sin, guilt, or offence as the context. The covenantal-objective mode (Lev 4:20 — sacrificial atonement) presupposes transgression. The NT pronouncements presuppose sin. Forgiveness is structurally dependent on a prior wrong — it cannot operate in an unfallen situation because there would be nothing to forgive. The divine attribute of forgiveness-readiness (sal.lach) is an eternal divine character quality, but its exercise awaits an offence. OBS-064-003, OBS-064-014.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence supports both elements but in different ways. The capacity for covenant-making (binding solemn relational commitment) is almost certainly part of the original created design — it reflects God's own nature (Q&A-002) and structures the relationship for which humans were created. The first covenant in Scripture is with Noah (Gen 6:18; 9:9-17 — OBS-034-038) — but this follows the fall and the flood. There is no explicit pre-fall covenant vocabulary in Genesis 1–2 in the programme's verse set. The Noahic covenant is a response to the fallen condition (God commits not to destroy again). What is missing from the data: whether the Edenic relationship contained covenantal structure (some traditions speak of a covenant of works, but this is theological inference, not programme verse evidence). The oath/curse vocabulary (H0423 — OBS-034-007) and the covenant-breach vocabulary (H3748 divorce, G0802 asunthetos — OBS-034-012, OBS-034-018) are clearly responses to or consequences of the fallen condition. Gap: the pre-fall covenantal design of the human person is not directly addressed by the programme's verse evidence. Naming this as S-adjacent — the data partially addresses this but the pre-fall dimension is genuinely absent from the evidence.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence shows both. (1) Peace as part of original design: Psa 85:10 ("righteousness and peace kiss each other") presents the eschatological restoration as a reunion of characteristics that belong together — implying they were originally united. The messianic reign of peace (Isa 9:6-7, Mic 5:5, OBS-117-147) is framed as the restoration of what was intended, not the creation of something novel. (2) Peace as response to the fallen condition: the "covenant of peace" structure (Num 25:12, Isa 54:10, Eze 34:25/37:26, OBS-117-145) presupposes a broken relationship being restored — covenant peace is given because natural peace has been ruptured. Isa 53:5 ("the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed") explicitly frames peace as purchased healing of a rupture. Gap: the evidence does not directly address the pre-fall condition — Scripture's earliest peace statements (Gen 28:21, Gen 37:4) already presuppose the fallen world. The precise relationship between created peace and covenant-restored peace requires Session D synthesis with other registries.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** A1's verse evidence addresses God's eternal righteousness. The divine attribute is prior to both original design and the fall.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Both. The OT assumes some persons are righteous — Abraham, Noah, Job — without specifying a restored or new state; the wisdom material speaks of the righteous as a recognisable category within the created order. The Ezekiel cluster (M26-A2-002) presupposes that persons can be righteous and then fall — implying original capacity. However, the NT explicitly reverses the OT assumption: "none is righteous, no, not one" (Rom 3:10). In the NT the primary mode is received through faith in Christ — a response to the fallen condition. Both streams present: the created design includes the capacity for righteousness; the fallen condition makes the reception-through-faith mode necessary.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Both. The B verses speak of uprightness as a path the person walks in or turns away from (Pro 2:13; Pro 14:2). This implies an original design — the path exists and can be taken. The effort required (teaching, leading, Pro 4:11) implies uprightness is not automatic — it requires formation. Both elements present.

**[C — Justification]** Specifically a response to the fallen condition. The terms all presuppose a prior moral deficit — a gap between actual and required standing. Job 4:17 ("Can mortal man be in the right before God?") frames the question that justification answers. Justification is not an element of original design — it is God's response to the condition in which persons find themselves unable to stand before him.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** A response to the fallen condition — it presupposes wrong done, harm inflicted, rights violated. In a world without injustice, there is no category for ekdikēsis or ekdikeō.

**[E — Condemnation]** A response to the fallen condition. Condemnation presupposes guilt — a departure from right standing. Self-condemnation (autokatakritos) presupposes that the person has acted in ways their own inner being recognises as wrong.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The reckoning faculty appears to belong to the original design — the capacity to weigh, count, and assess moral worth is part of how rational moral agents function. However, the specific content of reckoning in the verse evidence (counting oneself dead to sin, reckoning faith as righteousness, bearing accountable before God) is shaped by the fallen condition. The faculty is original; the specific reckoning tasks are responses to fallenness and redemption.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Wickedness and injustice are responses to the fallen condition — they name what has gone wrong. The presence of ra.sha as a recognisable category implies a departure from an original state.

**[CLUSTER]** A clear pattern: A2 and B belong to both original design and fallen response; C, D, and E are specifically responses to the fallen condition; F's faculty is original but its specific exercise is shaped by fallenness; G names the fallen state by opposition. The created person was designed with the capacity for righteousness; the fallen person requires justification (C), faces condemnation (E), and needs avenging justice (D) because that original capacity has been compromised.

findings.finding_value: Both, with temporal distinction. The ba.rakh blessing in Gen 1:22; 1:28; 2:3 is definitively pre-fall — God blesses creation and the Sabbath before any human failure. The creation-blessing is not remedial. However, much of the grace-vocabulary (particularly charis in the salvation register — Eph 2:8; Rom 3:24; Gal 2:21) is explicitly a response to the fallen condition: grace saves those who are dead in trespasses (Eph 2:5). The cha.nan supplication corpus (984-001) operates in contexts of affliction, distress, and need — overwhelmingly post-fall situations. The characteristic operates across both registers: blessing as created-design generativity (pre-fall), grace as saving response to guilt and need (post-fall), and ongoing favour as the continuing expression of the created relationship (both).

findings.finding_value: M01-A's reverential fear of God is presented as an original created purpose. Ecc 12:13 ("fear God, keep his commandments: the whole duty of man") presents this as constitutive of the human person without reference to the fall. The Deu 14:23 material ("cultivate an enduring inner reverence") and the Jer 32:40 material (God "pledges to implant the fear of himself") both treat it as a design feature capable of formation. The wisdom root (Pro 1:7) grounds knowledge itself in fear-of-God — this is not a fallen-condition repair but a created epistemological structure.

M01-B's acute fear engages both dimensions. Gen 3:10 (B-VCG-05: Adam's shame-triggered dread of divine presence) is explicitly post-fall: "I was afraid because I was naked." The fear of divine presence in naked shame is a fallen-condition response. However, the acute-fear capacity itself — the rapid inner response to threat — serves created purposes (Jacob's strategic response to Esau's approach, Gen 32:7) and cannot be attributed solely to the fall.

M01-C's terror-as-force (God sending terror as a weapon) operates within fallen human history as a covenantal instrument. No M01-C verse suggests this dimension existed before the fall; the Exo 23:27 material presupposes the conquest context, which presupposes human sin and displacement. M01-C is primarily a fallen-condition instrument of divine governance.

M01-D's dismay similarly operates in fallen-condition contexts: catastrophe, divine judgment, enemy threat, the hiding of God's face as covenant consequence. No M01-D evidence suggests dismay as an original creation design feature; it appears to be a response to the broken condition of the world and human sin.

M01-E's trembling spans both. The theophanic trembling at Sinai (Exo 19:16 anchor, E-VCG-01) and the "trembling at God's word" tradition (Isa 66:2 anchor, E-VCG-02) suggest that somatic reverence before God's presence and word is a created appropriate response — not fallen-condition damage. The fear-trembling of military crisis (E-VCG-04) operates in the fallen world but may engage a created capacity.

M01-F's chronic anxiety and dread are presented in primarily fallen-condition terms. Deu 28:66-67 (anchor F-VCG-03) names chronic unrelenting dread as a covenant curse — it is punishment, not design. Heb 2:15 (fear of death holding people in "lifelong inner slavery") names the fear of death as a condition Christ delivers from — implying it is a fallen state, not a created one. The pastoral anxiety of M01-F-VCG-05 (2Cor 12:20 anchor) is more ambiguous — concern for others is creational; the form it takes as anxiety may be fallen-condition.

M01-G's timidity is explicitly not from God (2Ti 1:7): "God has not given us a spirit of timidity." This implies it is a condition of the fallen inner constitution, not original design. The Rev 21:8 judgment on cowardice confirms it as a failure state, not a created purpose.

The evidence across M01 supports a differentiated answer: (a) The capacity for reverential fear of God (M01-A) and for somatic reverence before holiness (M01-E-VCG-01, E-VCG-02) appear to be original created design features. (b) Acute situational fear (M01-B) engages a created capacity but is shaped by fallen-condition contexts including shame-triggered dread of God (Gen 3:10). (c) Terror as a divine weapon (M01-C), dismay as inner collapse (M01-D), chronic anxiety as curse (M01-F), and timidity as constitutional failure (M01-G) are primarily fallen-condition phenomena.

The evidence indicates both, clearly distinguished. Divine anger and jealousy are presented as eternal divine attributes (Exo 34:14; Psa 7:11; Nah 1:2), not responses to the fall — they pre-exist and transcend creaturely conditions. Human anger appears in the narrative before and after the fall with no indication that its existence is a fallen condition: Cain's anger in Gen 4:5 (M02-B-VCG-02) is the first human anger in Scripture, and the verse does not present the anger itself as a product of the fall — rather, Gen 4:6 shows God questioning its source and moral legitimacy, treating it as a faculty subject to examination, not as an intrinsic disorder. Eph 4:26 ("be angry, and do not sin") explicitly acknowledges anger as a legitimate inner response whose persistence, not existence, is the problem.

The indignation corpus supports the both/and: divine indignation is constitutive and pre-fall (Psa 7:11; Mal 1:4), while the human anger that requires governance (Jam 1:19; Eph 4:31) reflects the fallen condition's distortion of the original capacity.

The cluster's evidence distinguishes between the capacity for anger (part of original design, reflected from God's own nature) and the disorder of anger (disproportionate, misdirected, self-serving anger as a product of the fall). The characteristic is not simply a fallen reality — it is a created capacity that the fall has distorted but not abolished.

The corpus gives evidence for both. The BOUNDARY sub-group includes the Genesis 3 toil-and-pain vocabulary (e.tsev H6089A at Gen 3:16; its.tsa.von H6093 at Gen 3:16, 3:17, 5:29 — M03-BOUNDARY-VCG-01), explicitly tying a dimension of the M03 register to the fall's consequences. The che.vel-B birth-pangs metaphor (Isa 13:8; Jer 13:21 etc. — M03-F-VCG-03) is embedded in the fall-curse frame of Gen 3. This argues that the acute pain and toil registers of M03 are at least partly responsive to the fallen condition. However, the core grief registers — mourning for the dead, distress that drives prayer, empathic weeping — are presented in the corpus without shame or judgment: Job's friends weep at his suffering (Job 2:12 — M03-A-VCG-01); Jesus is perilupos in Gethsemane (Mat 26:38 — M03-C-VCG-03); God himself grieves. The evidence suggests that the relational and responsive core of grief — the inner-being capacity to feel the weight of loss and to be moved by it — is part of the created design, while certain intensive and chronic expressions (groaning under slavery, the grinding toil of cursed existence) are responses to the fallen condition.

Penitential weeping (M03-A-VCG-02), God-governed mourning transformation (M03-B-VCG-03), NT mourning commanded as fitting inner response to sin (M03-B-VCG-04), Jesus's Gethsemane sorrow (M03-C-VCG-03), and the Spirit/creation groaning of Rom 8 (M03-E-VCG-02) together show grief operating within the fallen condition as a theologically proper and divinely honoured mode of the inner person. Grief is not the fall's product alone but the fitting response to living in a world where loss is real.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows exultation operating in both registers. Its function in the creation narrative is implicit in the cosmic-rejoicing passages (Psa 96:11; 97:1; 1Ch 16:31 — the heavens, earth, and coastlands called to rejoice because the Lord reigns), which presuppose exultation as part of the creation's designed response to its Creator's reign. Its operation in the fallen condition is most explicit in the salvation-exultation cluster (Psa 9:14; 13:5; 35:9; 61:10; Isa 25:9; 61:10; Hab 3:18) — where exultation arises specifically from divine rescue and deliverance. The eschatological exultation passages (Isa 65:18–19; 66:10; Zec 9:9; Jer 32:41; Zep 3:17) show the characteristic moving toward its fullest expression in the age of restoration. Exultation is therefore part of original design, given a particular form by the condition of redemption, and moving toward eschatological completion.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Both, with strong evidence for original design. The feast-commandments in Deuteronomy, Leviticus, and Numbers presuppose joy as the designed inner response of the covenant community before God. The cosmic-rejoicing passages (1Ch 16:31; Psa 96:11; 97:1) place joy as the appropriate response of all creation to divine sovereignty — not a fallen-condition remedy but the inherent response of the creature to the Creator's reign. The NT evidence adds the response-to-fallen-condition dimension: M04-C's emphasis on joy through suffering (Jas 1:2; 1Pe 1:6; 2Cor 6:10; Rom 5:3) and amid persecution (Mat 5:12; Luk 6:23) names joy specifically as the counter-intuitive inner posture required in the fallen world. The Ecclesiastes evidence (commending joy in the face of vanity and mortality) similarly frames it as the fitting inner posture amid creaturely limitation. Joy is both an original-design characteristic and one that takes particular forms in the fallen condition.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Primarily a **response to the fallen condition**. The M04-F corpus (ba.lag/mav.li.git — Job 9:27; 10:20; Psa 39:13; Jer 8:18) depicts fragile cheerfulness sought under extreme adversity that arises from the brokenness of creation under the curse: Job's suffering, the psalmist's mortality-distress, Jeremiah's grief over the people's ruin. None of these would arise in an uncorrupted creation. The M04-E-VCG-02 agalliao passages (Mat 5:12; Luk 6:23 — rejoicing under persecution; 1Pe 1:6; 4:13 — joy amid trials; 2Cor 6:10 implied by the adjacent characteristic-1 and 7 shared registers) arise from the conflict between the gospel community and a hostile world — again a fallen-condition context. That said, the characteristic anticipates its own eschatological resolution (1Pe 4:13 — "also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed") — suggesting it is a transitional capacity that serves the fallen condition while pointing toward the restoration where suffering-joy gives way to unqualified joy.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Strongly original design. The Gen 1 series (VCG-01) establishes the evaluative-gladness faculty as operating at creation itself — before the fall, God's own perception of the good in his work is the archetype. Gen 2:18's "not good" — the only negative in the creation narrative — shows the evaluative faculty precisely identifying a genuine lack (solitude) in an otherwise good creation. The M04-L-VCG-02 corpus in Proverbs, however, shows the evaluative faculty operating extensively in the fallen condition (assessing injustice, corruption, moral deficiency) — these uses are responses to the fallen world's moral complexity. M04-O's circumstantial Gladness similarly spans both: the soul's warm response to good news and blessing is a created-design capacity; its deployment in scenarios of exile, judgment, and adversity (Lam 3:26–27; Jon 4:3, 8; Hos 2:7) reflects operation in the fallen condition.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Both, with strong original-design grounding. (1) **Original design** — Pro 8:30–31 shows Delight operating before creation as Wisdom's daily pleasure before God and in the children of man — pre-fall, pre-human, grounding Delight as a created-design capacity anterior to the fall; Psa 37:4's promise ("delight yourself in the Lord… he will give you the desires of your heart") implies that properly directed Delight is what the person was constituted to experience; M04-H-VCG-03's volitional-preference idiom throughout the historical narratives shows human delight as a normal created capacity for personal judgment and preference; (2) **Response to fallen condition** — M04-P (corrupt delight — Eze 23:12; Hab 3:14; Isa 66:3) and M04-H-VCG-04 (negated and misdirected delight — Isa 65:12; 66:4; 2Th 2:12) are specifically fallen-condition phenomena — the misdirection of a created good toward wrong objects; M04-M (pleasing God as obedience orientation) in contexts of cultic correction (Lev 1:17; 1Sa 15:22; Hos 6:6) is also fallen-condition remedial; Delight-in-God's-word as a sustained life-preserving resource (Psa 119:92) is specifically operative in the fallen world's suffering.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Both, with strong original-design grounding: (1) **Original design** — Pro 3:17 ("her ways are ways of pleasantness") places wisdom's pleasantness in the created order; Psa 16:6 ("lines have fallen for me in pleasant places") describes a God-given inheritance of pleasant provision; Psa 36:8 ("river of your delights") is an attribute of God's house; the Song of Songs' celebration of bodily beauty and pleasantness (Song 1:16; 7:6) is original-design relational appreciation; (2) **Response to fallen condition** — the ni.cho.ach corpus (M04-K-VCG-01) is explicitly cultic and sacrificial, which is a fallen-condition institution addressing sin; Lev 4:31 (pleasing aroma alongside atonement) shows ni.cho.ach operating in a forgiveness-seeking context; M04-K-VCG-02's luxury-curse register (Deu 28:54, 56 — the delicate person's comfort destroyed) is entirely a fallen-condition phenomenon; (3) Pro 9:17 (stolen bread called pleasant) is the fallen-condition distortion of Pleasure: the same faculty that receives genuine pleasantness is deceived by illicit appearance.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Both, but with important distinctions by register: (1) **Original design** — M04-I-VCG-01's wonder at God's marvellous works (creation, redemption, providence) is an original-design capacity; Psa 139:14 ("I am fearfully and wonderfully made") — the wonder evoked by human embodiment itself is a created-design reality; (2) **Original design but fallen-context deployment** — most VCG-01 wonders are performed in the context of Israel's history (Exodus, wilderness, conquest) — these arise from God's redemptive responses to the fallen condition, but the wonder-capacity itself is original design; (3) **Fallen condition distortion** — M04-I-VCG-03's dark wonder (Job 10:16 — wonders worked against Job; Dan 8:24; 11:36 — the king's fearful destruction and astonishing blasphemy; Gal 1:6 — Paul astonished at the Galatians' defection; Rev 17:6 — wonder at the harlot) is specifically a fallen-condition phenomenon; wonder-as-dread, wonder-at-evil, and wonder-at-apostasy are not original-design states.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The seven characteristics distribute along a spectrum from most-original to most-fallen-condition-specific: (1) **Most strongly original design** — Gladness (Char 3): Gen 1's evaluative "God saw that it was good" is pre-fall; Pleasure (Char 5): the Song of Songs' celebration of bodily pleasantness and Pro 3:17's wisdom-pleasantness are original-design; Delight (Char 4): Pro 8:30–31's Wisdom-delight before creation is explicitly pre-fall; (2) **Original design but fallen-condition deployment** — Exultation (Char 1) and Joy (Char 2) have both registers: cosmic joy at God's reign (original design) and salvation-exultation following rescue (fallen-condition deployment); Wonder (Char 6): the capacity for Wonder is original design, but most VCG-01's wonders arise from God's redemptive-historical acts in the fallen world; (3) **Most strongly fallen-condition response** — Suffering-Joy (Char 7): Suffering-Joy as a phenomenon arises only in the fallen condition; it is by definition the characteristic of a person or community under suffering. The cluster as a whole therefore spans from the pre-fall foundation of creation's goodness (Gladness, Pleasure, Delight) through characteristics that are original in design but formed by the fallen world (Joy, Exultation, Wonder) to the characteristic that exists only because the fallen condition exists (Suffering-Joy). This distribution confirms that M04 is a cluster whose inner-being content is simultaneously created-design positive affect and fallen-world redemptive-positive affect — it cannot be reduced to either.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence positions shame as primarily a response to the fallen condition, not original created design. Gen 2:25 (vc=34835) explicitly names the pre-fall state as one without shame — the absence of shame is the positive mark of created wholeness. The fall produces the shame-condition. However, the capacity for shame — the inner moral apparatus that registers exposure, guilt, and relational brokenness — appears to belong to the image-bearing structure itself. The evidence from M07-C (Ezr 9:6; Jer 31:19; Eze 43:10-11) shows shame operating as the morally appropriate response to one's own sin, suggesting that the faculty which produces shame (moral consciousness, conscience) is part of the created design, while the experience of shame is a response to the fallen condition. Both dimensions are present: shame-as-experience is post-fall; shame-as-moral-signal depends on image-bearing moral awareness.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 is a response to the fallen condition. Social demotion (VCG-01), military defeat (VCG-02), and divine abasement-of-pride (VCG-03) all presuppose a world of human pride, violence, and political hubris. CHAR-2 is the corrective mechanism against fallenness rather than a feature of the unfallen design.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 as worth-denial is a response to the fallen condition — the failure of the worth-recognition capacity that belongs to the image. The failure takes two forms: active willful dishonour (VCG-01) and structural assigned dishonour (VCG-02). The created design included the worth-recognition capacity; its corruption produces CHAR-3.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence is ambiguous on whether CHAR-4 belongs to the original created design or is a response to the fallen condition. The shamefulness-of-conduct register (VCG-01) presupposes a moral standard against which conduct is assessed — this standard-sensitivity belongs to the created design (image-bearers are morally responsive). The inverted-conscience register (VCG-03 — Phili 3:19; Hos 4:18) is definitionally a fallen-condition phenomenon: the conscience that glories in what is actually shame is a corrupted conscience. CHAR-4 in its functioning form is part of created moral design; in its inverted form it is a fall-response.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 is a response to the fallen condition — contempt is a fallen-world mechanism, and the shame it produces arises because the fallen world denies worth to persons who genuinely have it. The VCG-02 evidence (the servants beaten by violent tenants; Herod mocking Jesus) is specifically about fallen-world contempt structures being enacted against innocent persons. The reversibility argument: Chars 1 (Eze 18:20-27 — reversal possible), 2 (Act 3:26 — transformation from wickedness through divine blessing), and 4 (Eze 37:23 — divine cleansing removes abominations; Jer 4:1 — removal possible) all show the characteristic as departing from an original state and reversible toward it — original design is not reversible. The faculty-inversion argument: Chars 2 (Mat 7:17-18 — diseased tree as fallen state not design), 5 (Job 15:35 — generative faculty designed for good now producing iniquity), and 6 (Jude 10 — regression to sub-rational instinct below designed rational-speech capacity) all show the characteristic as a corruption of a designed faculty, not a designed faculty itself. Char 3 contributes the conscience-design argument: the conscience that should register abomination with shame is the designed original capacity; its silencing is the fallen deviation (Jer 6:15 — VCG-04). The cluster's unanimous fallen-condition verdict rules out any original-design interpretation for any of the six forms of inner evil it names.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence does not resolve this directly, but signals point to the defilement-state as a structural feature of embodied creaturely existence rather than exclusively a consequence of the fall. The physiological defilement register (M10c-A-VCG-05: Lev 12 childbirth, Lev 15 menstruation) attaches defilement to natural bodily processes — reproduction, discharge — not to sin. Similarly, contact with death (M10c-A-VCG-07) is the most severe defilement category; death is a consequence of the fall, but the defilement arising from death-contact is treated as a structural given requiring management, not as moral failure. The Num 9:7 men grieve that their corpse-contact impurity was involuntary — "we are unclean through touching a dead body" — showing no moral fault but a bodily condition. This suggests the defilement-state as a category inhabits both: some sub-registers (bodily discharge, menstruation) may reflect the created order of embodied creaturely vulnerability; others (death-defilement) intersect with the fallen condition. The evidence does not permit a single clean answer here.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence strongly indicates the moral-inner defilement-state is a consequence of the fallen condition, not part of the original created design. Job 14:4 (M10c-C-VCG-01) — "who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one" — frames the condition as the constitutional reality of the human being as Job knows it: no clean thing emerges from this unclean origin. This is not a description of original design but of inherited human condition under sin. Rom 6:19 (M10c-C-VCG-02) describes the prior condition as "slaves to impurity and to lawlessness" — a slavery into which people fell, not a state they were created for. Rom 1:24 (M10c-C-VCG-02) frames the condition as God's judicial response to human rejection of him: "God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity" — the defilement deepens as a consequence of moral defection. Taken together, the evidence locates the characteristic as a condition of the fallen human being, not the originally created one.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence strongly indicates this characteristic is a response to the fallen condition operating in a covenantal context. The corporate register is the site of the characteristic's primary evidence: Psa 106:39 (M10c-D-VCG-02) — "thus they became unclean by their acts, and played the whore in their deeds" — describes the defilement as arising from specific acts of apostasy within a people who were already in covenant with God. 2Ch 36:14 (M10c-D-VCG-03) — "they were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the Lord" — frames the defilement as the corporate fruit of habitual defection from an existing covenant. The characteristic presupposes the covenantal relationship as prior; the defilement is what happens when that relationship is betrayed.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence strongly indicates this characteristic is a response to the fallen condition, not part of the original created design. The unclean spirits are "hostile, morally corrupting powers" (Mat 10:1 VCG-03) operating in opposition to divine order. Luk 8:29 (VCG-01): the spirit "had repeatedly seized the man, overpowering all human restraint" — the domination is experienced as an intrusion on the person's proper self-possession. The entire framework of the 21-verse corpus assumes that the defiled state is an aberration requiring correction. The characteristic belongs to the domain of adversarial spiritual opposition that operates in a fallen world.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's four characteristics distribute across a spectrum from created-order to fallen-condition with a nuanced middle position. Characteristic 1 sits at the ambiguous boundary: bodily-discharge defilement (Lev 12, 15 — VCG-05) attaches to natural physiological processes not marked as sinful, suggesting a created-order feature; death-defilement (M10c-A-VCG-07) intersects with the fallen condition since death is the consequence of sin. Characteristic 2 is clearly post-fall: Job 14:4 ("who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?") names the inherited condition of fallen humanity; Rom 6:19 describes slavery entered, not a created design. Characteristic 3 is clearly post-fall and covenantal: it presupposes the prior covenantal relationship as the context within which betrayal occurs — the defilement is the product of specific acts of apostasy by a community already in covenant. Characteristic 4 is clearly post-fall: the adversarial spiritual powers operate in the domain of opposition to God's order. The cluster as a whole thus positions defilement as (a) partially within the created-order at the embodied-ritual level (Char 1's physiological sub-register), (b) a consequence of the fall at the individual moral-inner level (Char 2), (c) a consequence of the fall at the corporate-covenantal level (Char 3), and (d) a consequence of the fall at the adversarial-spiritual level (Char 4).

questions.question_text: Across the evidence, is there any orientation toward a future fullness — something the person moves toward, not only what they currently are? Record it, or record none.

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides partial evidence.

**Eschatological signals present:** SD-012 identifies Rom 8:17 — "if we suffer with him (sumpaschō) we may also be glorified with him (syndoxazō)" — as placing compassion/fellow-suffering within an explicitly eschatological framework. Suffering-with-Christ is named as the condition of glorification-with-Christ. This is the clearest evidence in the data that the compassion vocabulary carries a future-orientation: present fellow-suffering is oriented toward future shared glory.

Jas 5:11 (polusplanchnos) connects divine deep compassion to the "purpose of the Lord" in the context of endurance and suffering, suggesting that the full expression of compassion belongs to a telos not yet reached.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not contain a verse that explicitly names compassion as moving toward eschatological fullness in the human person — as something the person is becoming, not only doing. The eschatological trajectory is more visible in the divine direction (God's everlasting chesed) and in the sumpaschō/syndoxazō frame, than in a direct statement about the human person's compassion moving toward completeness. This is a genuine gap; SD-012 partially addresses it but does not close it.

findings.session_b_note:
The evidence is partial. Psa 51:8 — "let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice" — presents the contrite person actively oriented toward a future state that is not yet possessed. The broken bones desire to rejoice: the contrite condition is explicitly a present state from which a future restoration is anticipated and sought. This forward orientation is present but not eschatologically specified in the data (no verse in the registry describes the fullness of contrition's trajectory in the new creation or final restoration).

The closest the evidence comes to a future orientation is the sequence: crushing → contrite posture → divine revival (Isa 57:15). The revival is presented as real and available, not eschatological in timing. The future fullness — whether contrition will be fully transcended in the restored creation, or whether creaturely lowliness before God remains — is not addressed in the verse evidence.

*Partial: forward orientation within the present experience is evidenced (Psa 51:8); ultimate eschatological trajectory is not addressed.*

findings.session_b_note:
The evidence carries a forward orientation, though it is not framed in explicit eschatological language.

**2Pe 1:4** — the construction *you may become partakers* is a future-oriented becoming, not a present possession. The divine nature participation is presented as a trajectory: the promises are given so that participation may be entered. This is forward movement.

**Phili 3:10** — Paul's formulation *that I may know him* is itself a reaching-forward structure. The fellowship of his sufferings and the conformity to his death are framed as means toward *the resurrection of the dead* (v.11, adjacent context). The fellowship trajectory in Phili 3:10 is explicitly incomplete in the present — it is being entered into.

**Ecc 9:4** — *he who is joined with all the living has hope* — fellowship with the living is identified as the ground of hope. The present condition (being joined with all the living) gives access to hope. This is not eschatological but it names fellowship as hope-enabling in the present.

**New finding:** The registry data, read as a whole, supports the observation that fellowship in its highest register (koinōnia vocabulary) is structurally forward-facing: it is entered progressively, it grounds hope, and its fullness is not yet possessed. This is a structural feature of fellowship that is not explicitly assembled in the existing findings. It has implications for T5.6 (Eschatological Trajectory).

Isa 54:4: "the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more." The eschatological future for reproach is not its completion but its total removal followed by permanent honour.

The adversary structure moves toward its own defeat. Job 22:20: "our adversaries are cut off." 1Pe 5:8's cosmic adversary has a terminus. The eschatological trajectory is the elimination of all adversarial opposition.

The eschatological trajectory is divine judgment. Eze 25:6-7, 25:15-17 — God's judgment of the nations' malice is the response. The characteristic that claimed perpetuity ("never-ending enmity," Eze 25:15) meets divine judgment. It does not move toward fullness but toward its own ending.

Every sub-group evidences an eschatological orientation. The cluster's characteristics are not only present realities but forward-pointing participations in what will be completed. The eschatological register varies by sub-group: love is permanent (M05-A); compassion gathers in great eschatological restoration (M05-B); mercy is awaited as eschatological grace (M05-C); goodness moves toward completion (M05-D); gentleness inherits the earth (M05-E); comfort is eternal (M05-F); fellowship participates in glory (M05-G).

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — Dan 9:24 — "to bring in everlasting righteousness" — and the eschatological acclamations in Revelation (Rev 15:3–19:2, VSG M26-A1-002) locate God's righteousness as the goal toward which history moves. **[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — "the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints" (Rev 19:8) — the bride's garment is the accumulated righteousness of the people, pointing to eschatological completion. **[B — Moral Uprightness]** The B verse evidence does not contain explicit eschatological language. Uprightness is presented as a current orientation and way of walking. Silence noted.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — "heirs according to the hope of eternal life" (Tit 3:7, VSG 3194-001). Justification establishes the person in new standing oriented toward future inheritance. The resurrection context in Rom 4:24–25 (VSG 3203-001) links justification to the risen Christ and the eschatological reality his resurrection inaugurates.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the cry of the martyrs in Rev 6:10 (VSG 944-001) is directed toward the final day of judgment. The "days of vengeance" (Luk 21:22, VSG 945-001) are eschatological. **[E — Condemnation]** Yes — the freedom from condemnation in Rom 8:34 (VSG 4846-002) is grounded in the risen and interceding Christ, pointing toward the final judgment. The "punishment of eternal destruction" (2Th 1:9, VSG 949-001) locates final condemnation in the eschatological future.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — "the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed" (Rom 8:18, VSG 3410-001). The reckoning faculty is explicitly applied to the eschatological future: counting present suffering against future glory is an act of inner orientation toward what is coming.

The eschatological crystallisation of moral identity — the future fullness is one in which the distinction between righteous and wicked is finalised and permanent.

**[CLUSTER]** Across the cluster, righteousness is oriented toward a future fullness that is both individual (the person becoming fully righteous) and cosmic (God's righteousness universally acknowledged and all wrongs addressed). M01-G's fullness is the full actualization of power, love, and self-control (2Ti 1:7 anchor) — the complete replacement of timidity with the spirit God gives. This is not a current possession fully realized but a trajectory.

The cluster as a whole points toward a future fullness that includes: perpetuated, deepened reverential fear of God (M01-A, confirmed by Rev corpus); release from all fear of threat, judgment, and death (M01-B, F, G); and the complete absence of terror-as-domination and trembling-as-threat (M01-C, D, E). The fullness is not the elimination of fear but its purification: what remains is the fear that is rightly placed — fear of God as the organizing inner posture of the fully redeemed person.

The eschatological-wrath corpus (M02-A-VCG-02) shows that divine anger has a future-oriented dimension: Rev 19:15 frames the wrath of God the Almighty as the force behind final judgment — the fullness toward which the enacted wrath of history has been moving. The human person's encounter with wrath in the present is oriented toward the day when all wrath is fully resolved in just judgment. For the believer, the future is deliverance from wrath (1Th 1:10; 5:9; Rom 5:9).

The jealousy corpus carries a restorative future: Joe 2:18 shows divine jealousy moving from judgment to pity and restoration; Isa 11:13 promises the abolition of inter-tribal jealousy in the messianic age. The future fullness for the human person is a freedom from destructive covetous jealousy and an entry into the divine jealousy's restorative mode.

The contentious-anger corpus (M02-F) points toward a future where strife is eliminated: 1Cor 11:16 names the dispute-loving disposition as incompatible with apostolic practice; Gal 5:20 identifies it as a work of the flesh that will be overcome in the life of the Spirit. The trajectory is toward a freedom from strife that anticipates the undivided community of the kingdom.

The cluster's eschatological content is concentrated in M02-A-VCG-02. The future fullness includes: complete just judgment resolving all unaddressed wrongdoing (Rev 19:15); deliverance of the redeemed from the wrath that hangs over the fallen order (1Th 5:9); and the transformation of covetous jealousy into devoted covenant fidelity. The present anger-and-wrath experience is oriented toward a future in which justice is fully enacted and destructive anger-expressions are fully healed.

The Isaianic exultation passages are concentrated around eschatological restoration: Isa 65:18 commands "be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create," grounding the exultation in a new creative act; Isa 65:19 places God's own rejoicing in Jerusalem in the new-creation context; Isa 66:10 calls all who love Jerusalem to rejoice with her at her vindication; Zec 9:9 directs Zion's exultation at the coming of her king. M04-C-VCG-04 extends this: Joh 16:22 ("your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you"); Rev 19:7 (commanded corporate rejoicing at the Lamb's marriage); Jude 24 (great joy at blameless presentation before God's glory); Heb 12:2 (the joy set before Jesus that sustained his cross). Within Characteristic 2 itself, fullness of joy is a recurring eschatological goal: Joh 15:11 ("that your joy may be full"); Joh 16:24 ("that your joy may be full"); 1Jo 1:4; 2Jo 12 (joy made complete). Present Joy is consistently experienced as partial and anticipatory.

The trajectory is toward accountability (leadership judged — 1Ki 16:2; 21:22) and structural reversal (the sin-transmitting institution demolished — 2Ki 23:15), not toward fullness in any positive sense.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The corpus orients political revolt toward sustained fracture rather than future fullness. 1Ki 12:19 and 2Ch 10:19 — "to this day" — name the ongoing persistence of the broken political relationship, with no resolution in view. 2Ki 8:22 and 2Ch 21:10 — "to this day" — similarly name Edom's revolt as a permanent fracture without restoration. The trajectory evidenced is toward continued division, not toward eschatological reunion. The characteristic does not point toward a positive future; it points toward an enduring political rift.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The corpus evidences two eschatological trajectories. (1) *Judgment for unforgivable blasphemy*: Mat 12:31 — "the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" — the unforgivable form carries forward permanently into eschatological consequence. (2) *The beast's blasphemy as eschatological-concentrated evil*: Rev 13:5/6 — the beast utters blasphemous words for "forty-two months" — a defined eschatological period. The beast's constitutive blasphemy is oriented toward the judgment that the Revelation context anticipates. The trajectory of sinful speech is toward eschatological consequence rather than any positive fullness.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence orients wickedness-as-settled-person-identity toward a future state, but that future state is one of judgment and termination rather than fullness. The Ezekiel corpus (M10b-A-VCG-07) repeatedly depicts wickedness as a "way" heading toward death (Eze 3:18; 33:8; 33:11). Psa 37:10 states "in just a little while, the wicked will be no more." Job 20:5 notes "the exulting of the wicked is short." Dan 12:10 describes the wicked acting wickedly and being unable to understand, while the wise are refined — pointing to an eschatological bifurcation. The trajectory of wickedness-as-settled-identity is therefore toward exhaustion and dissolution, not forward fullness. The one counter-note is the Ezekiel repentance sequence: Eze 18:21–27 and 33:12–19 show that the wicked person can turn from this trajectory, which opens a different future — but that future belongs to the characteristic's reversal, not its completion.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence orients evil as constitutional inner nature toward dissolution and termination rather than positive fullness. 2Ti 3:13 (vc=14451 — VCG-06) describes evil people moving "from bad to worse" — a downward trajectory, not a forward fullness. Mat 13:49 (vc=14459 — VCG-04) names the eschatological separation of the evil from the righteous — their future is separation from the righteous community, not a positive eschatological destination. The characteristic's future is anticipated only in terms of removal and judgment. The one counter-trajectory is in the evidence's consistent call for departure from the characteristic: Act 3:26 (VCG-05 — turning from wickedness), Jam 1:21 (VCG-05 — putting away rampant wickedness), Eph 4:31 (VCG-05 — putting away malice) — these envision a human future in which the constitutional inner evil is replaced, not fulfilled.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence orients the characteristic toward eschatological exclusion rather than forward fullness. Rev 21:27 (vc=22 — VCG-05): "nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life" — the eschatological end-state is one in which abomination is permanently excluded from the divine presence. The trajectory of the characteristic is toward final separation, not toward a positive fulfillment. Rev 17:5 (vc=65878 — VCG-05): the identity constituted by generating abominations ends in judgment. The one redemptive trajectory in the evidence is Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): restored memory producing self-loathing, which is the conscience-awakening that enables repentance — but that trajectory moves toward departure from the characteristic, not its fulfillment.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence orients idolatrous abomination toward eschatological judgment and removal rather than positive fullness. Dan 9:27 (vc=65914 — VCG-06): the abomination that brings desolation is an eschatological event leading to decreed judgment — "until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator." Dan 12:11 (vc=65916 — VCG-06): the abomination that makes desolate is set up at a specific apocalyptic moment pointing toward final judgment. The redemptive trajectory (Eze 37:23 — VCG-05: "they shall not defile themselves anymore… I will save them… and will cleanse them") points toward a future where the characteristic is entirely removed, not fulfilled. The eschatological trajectory is toward removal and restoration, not toward the characteristic's completion or fullness.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The evidence orients iniquity as active scheming toward eventual irrecoverable ruin rather than any positive fullness. Psa 36:12 (vc=38233 — VCG-04): "There the evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise" — the trajectory ends in total and permanent collapse. Psa 92:7 (vc=38246 — VCG-03): "though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever" — apparent flourishing precedes inevitable destruction. Psa 94:23 (vc=38249 — VCG-03): "He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out" — the iniquity returns on the schemer as judgment. The trajectory of the characteristic is toward its own undoing: the scheming generates ruin for the schemer. No verse presents the characteristic as moving toward a positive fullness.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The evidence orients the characteristic toward eschatological judgment and elimination rather than positive fullness. Rom 3:8 (vc=14358 — VCG-02): "their condemnation is just" — the slanderous misrepresentation carries a certain future condemnation. Rev 16:9-21 (VCG-01): the hardened blasphemers under eschatological judgment — scorched, in pain, struck by hailstones — with no repentance, only continued cursing: the trajectory terminates in destruction without reversal. 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): those who falsely accuse believers as evildoers "may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation" — the day of visitation brings the false accusation's end and the reversal of the defamation. The characteristic's eschatological fullness is judgment and exposure, not any positive future state.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics orient their evil-forms toward eschatological judgment and elimination, not positive future fullness. The cluster reveals a consistent eschatological pattern across all six: Char 1 (Psa 37:10 — the wicked seen no more; Dan 12:10 — wicked act wickedly and understand nothing at the end), Char 2 (Mat 13:49 — the evil separated from the righteous at the end of the age), Char 3 (Rev 21:27 — nothing abominable enters the holy city), Char 4 (Dan 9:27 → Mat 24:15 — abomination of desolation as eschatological culmination), Char 5 (Psa 92:7 — evildoers doomed to destruction forever; Psa 94:23 — wiped out), Char 6 (Rev 13:6; 16:9/11/21 — beast-blasphemy and population-blasphemy as eschatological events without reversal). The cluster's unanimous eschatological-judgment orientation reveals M10b as the inner-being cluster that defines the negative eschatological trajectory — what is excluded, eliminated, and judged at the end. Chars 3 and 4 have the most developed eschatological typology (abomination-of-desolation progression from historical desecration to cosmic culmination); Char 6 has the most extreme eschatological concentration (the entire Rev 16 corpus is eschatological judgment events). The cluster does not orient any of its six characteristics toward positive eschatological fullness — all six face the trajectory of elimination.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence within Characteristic 1's 133 verses points forward primarily through the elaborate cleansing provisions that accompany every defilement state: washing, waiting, priestly examination and clearance (M10c-B-VCG-02), the water of impurity (M10c-A-VCG-07). These prescribed remedies signal that the defilement-state is not permanent — it has a designed resolution. The fullness orientation is most explicit in Num 19:9 (VCG-07), where the red-heifer ashes are a "standing remedy" designated for the congregation as a "sin offering" — indicating that defilement management is not merely ritual maintenance but participates in a larger sacrificial-atoning economy pointing toward ultimate purity. The NT akathartos verses in M10c-B-VCG-05 (Act 10:14/28) show the defilement category itself being revised by divine revelation, signalling eschatological movement: the categories formed in the ritual order are not the final word. The future fullness is the state of unrestricted access to divine presence, of which the prescribed cleansing is a present anticipation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, through the positive-inverse register (M10c-C-VCG-05) and the call-to-cleansing register (M10c-C-VCG-03). Rev 3:4 (VCG-05): "people who have not soiled their garments... will walk with me in white, for they are worthy" — the future fullness is walking with Christ in white, which is the eschatological resolution of the moral-inner defilement's present struggle. Rev 14:4 (VCG-05): those who have not defiled themselves "follow the Lamb wherever he goes... redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb" — the orientation is toward eschatological consummation with the Lamb. The call at 2Cor 7:1 (VCG-03): "bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God" — the directional goal is the completion of holiness, a future fullness that the active cleansing from defilement serves. 1Th 4:7 (VCG-02): the divine call is "in holiness" — the fullness is holiness; the defilement-state is what stands between the person and that fullness.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, substantially. The VCG-05 corpus carries three eschatological-restorative texts. Eze 37:23 (VCG-05): "they shall not defile themselves anymore with their idols... but I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God" — a promise of permanent non-defilement as the mark of the restored covenant community. Isa 52:1 (VCG-05): "there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean" — the eschatological holy city excludes the defiling condition permanently. Zec 13:1 (VCG-05): "on that day there shall be a fountain opened... to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness" — the divinely provided fountain of cleansing addresses the corporate/covenantal defilement at a future eschatological moment. The characteristic is oriented toward a fullness in which the covenant community is permanently purified and the defilement-state is definitively ended.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. The expulsion-and-restoration register (VCG-02) consistently points toward the restored state as the positive fullness. Luk 6:18 (VCG-02): "those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured" — the healing points toward the wholeness that is the characteristic's structural opposite (M12). Luk 9:42 (VCG-01): "healed the boy, and gave him back to his father" — the restoration of the person to the family relationship pictures the positive fullness. Mat 12:43/Luk 11:24 (VCG-02): the spirit's post-expulsion restlessness implicitly points to a future state where such spirits find no access to any person — the eschatological fullness is a community in which the characteristic has no domain.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics are E on future-fullness orientation, but the form of the orientation differs significantly across them. Characteristic 1's orientation is the prescribed cleansing provisions themselves — the standing remedy (Num 19:9) and the NT's eschatological revision of the category (Act 10:14/28 — "what God has made clean, do not call unclean"), signalling that the ritual defilement categories point toward an unrestricted access to divine presence. Characteristic 2's orientation is explicitly eschatological: Rev 3:4 (walking with Christ in white), Rev 14:4 (firstfruits following the Lamb), 2Cor 7:1 (bringing holiness to completion) — each pointing toward the consummated holiness from which the defilement-state separates the person. Characteristic 3's orientation is the most extensively developed: three OT prophetic eschatological texts (Eze 37:23, Isa 52:1, Zec 13:1) each promise a future state of permanent non-defilement and covenant restoration. Characteristic 4's orientation is through the expulsion-and-restoration pattern, with Mar 9:25's command "never enter him again" pointing toward a final state of permanent exemption from the characteristic. The cluster as a whole is uniformly oriented toward M12 (purity/wholeness) as its eschatological fullness, but the specific form of that fullness varies: covenant-access completeness (Char 1), personal moral holiness (Char 2), corporate non-defilement in the restored covenant (Char 3), and communal freedom from adversarial spiritual inhabitation (Char 4).

questions.section: T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
questions.question_text: From the characteristic's God-relation (T0.1) and its role (T0.2), what aspect of the divine likeness, if any, does it instantiate in the person? Record the aspect, or record none.

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides the building blocks for this answer but does not assemble them into an image-bearer statement explicitly. Drawing from what is evidenced:

The divine image expressed through forgiveness operates on two levels:
1. **Structural:** The human act of forgiving mirrors the divine act structurally — releasing a legitimate debt-claim, cancelling an account of injury. OBS-064-026 notes the "shared act-structure between discipleship-leaving and forgiveness" through aphiēmi — the human volitional release mirrors the divine release. The human person, in forgiving, performs the same structural act that defines God's forgiveness-character.
2. **Dispositional:** The commanded disposition to forgive (Luk 17:3-4; Mat 18:35) calls the human person toward a readiness-to-pardon that mirrors the divine sal.lach attribute (Psa 86:5 — God is "forgiving" as a character description). The human person is called to embody what God is.

The aspect of divine likeness instantiated: the capacity to release a legitimate claim against another — to absorb the cost of wrong done and not exact payment — is the specific aspect of divine character that human forgiveness images. This is a *moral* and *relational* dimension of the divine image, not a structural (creative, rational) one.

What is not assembled in the data: an explicit statement of the divine image logic of forgiveness. This prompt surfaces the need for that synthesis at Session D.

findings.session_b_note:
When the human person exercises grace — in forgiving (5470-002: charizō carrying both giving and forgiving), in speech quality (charis as gracious words, Luk 4:22, Col 4:6), in character disposition (889-003: gracious disposition expressed in conduct) — they express the likeness of the one whose primary characteristic is to give freely to the undeserving. The image-bearing dimension is the capacity for uncaused giving: giving not triggered by the recipient's merit but by the giver's disposition.

*Adds structure: prior analysis addressed grace-as-human-act primarily in relational terms. The prompt frames it as an image-bearing capacity — a distinct T0-level claim.*

findings.session_b_note:
Compassion expresses the divine image in the human person through a specific and unusual mechanism: **the human body is the etymological ground of the divine attribute.**

The RACHAM root (H7355, H7356A, H7356B) names both the womb (anatomical) and compassion (abstract). The relationship is not the usual one where an abstract quality is later extended metaphorically to the body — it is the reverse. The abstract term (ra.cham, compassion) is named after the concrete anatomical reality (re.chem, womb). As the Pass 1 term analysis states: "the abstract (compassion) is named after the concrete (womb), not the other way around. This is unusual in Hebrew word formation and gives the compassion vocabulary a somatic grounding that is built into the language itself rather than being a later metaphorical extension."

This means that the divine image expressed in compassion is not a purely spiritual quality projected downward into the human — it is a quality named upward from the human body into the divine character. When Scripture says God is rachum (compassionate), it is drawing on the most intimate human bodily experience — the experience of carrying life from within — to describe what God is in his inner being.

The aspect of the divine image instantiated is therefore: **the capacity for interior, involuntary, body-grounded movement toward the other.** Compassion as image-bearer expression is not merely benevolent feeling — it is the quality of being moved from within, constitutively, toward those who need.
