findings.session_b_note:
As established at T0.1 Prompt 2, contrition is not shared between God and the human person. It is exclusively creaturely. There is, however, a creaturely analogue to something in God: the verse evidence consistently shows God as the one who produces the crushing (Psa 44:19; Psa 51:8) and responds to the crushed (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15). The divine analogue is not contrition but the **holy attention that makes contrition possible and meaningful**. God's holiness confronts the inner being; the inner being's right response is contrition. The divine version of this dynamic is the act of confrontation and subsequent reviving — God's own justice and mercy interacting with human brokenness.

The creaturely analogue relationship: contrition in the human corresponds to, and is response to, the holy-and-near character of God.

findings.session_b_note:
The evidence sits between the two options, and the data does not resolve this distinction clearly.

**For sharing:** 2Pe 1:4 suggests genuine participation in divine nature — not merely analogy. If the person *becomes a partaker of the divine nature*, the fellowship they enter is not merely analogous to something divine but a real participation in it. The language is ontological sharing, not merely imitation.

**For creaturely analogue:** The wound-fellowship vocabulary (H2250 groups), the companionship vocabulary (H2270 groups), and the joining vocabulary (H2266 groups) all operate at the creaturely level and carry no explicit claim to sharing in divine quality. They describe human-to-human relational realities.

**Gap:** Whether fellowship is shared (ontologically participatory) or analogous (structurally creaturely) depends on which register of fellowship is in view. The data establishes both registers but does not synthesise them. This is precisely the territory of DIM-62-SD001 and 062-SD002 — the ontological fellowship question is explicitly deferred to Session D.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence supports genuine sharing of the same lexical and moral category — tov names both God's goodness and human goodness without semantic differentiation in H2896A. Psa 119:68 addresses God as good and then asks God to teach statutes so the human can also know and do good — the same category of goodness applies to both. G5544 (chrēstotēs) is explicitly shared: it names God's inner disposition (886-001, Rom 11:22; Eph 2:7) and the Spirit-produced quality of the believer (886-002, Gal 5:22; Col 3:12) using the identical term. This is not merely analogy — the NT explicitly frames human chrēstotēs as Spirit-produced, meaning the divine goodness is the active source of its human expression (not merely the pattern for it). The relationship is participatory: human goodness participates in divine goodness rather than merely imitating it. However, Gen 1:31 (the creative-pronouncement group, 884-007) has no human analogue — only God can evaluate and declare creation good in that ontological-constitutive sense. (OBS-067-OBS-017, OBS-067-OBS-037, OBS-067-OBS-045)

G5544 (chrēstotēs) is explicitly shared: it names God's inner disposition (886-001, Rom 11:22; Eph 2:7) and the Spirit-produced quality of the believer (886-002, Gal 5:22; Col 3:12) using the identical term. This is not merely analogy — the NT explicitly frames human chrēstotēs as Spirit-produced, meaning the divine goodness is the active source of its human expression (not merely the pattern for it). The relationship is participatory: human goodness participates in divine goodness rather than merely imitating it. However, Gen 1:31 (the creative-pronouncement group, 884-007) has no human analogue — only God can evaluate and declare creation good in that ontological-constitutive sense. (OBS-067-OBS-017, OBS-067-OBS-037, OBS-067-OBS-045)

findings.session_b_note: The evidence strongly suggests love is shared, not merely analogical. The vocabulary is explicitly common: God's nephesh has a beloved using the same term as the human person's beloved (OBS-103-086); God's inner organs (me'eka) are moved using somatic vocabulary parallel to the human compassion-response (OBS-103-106, OBS-103-117); agapē is the term both for God's love toward persons and the commanded love of person toward God and others. The LXX use of agapē to translate chesed bridges the Testaments — the same vocabulary governs both divine and human love. DIM-103-002 (§N item) is precisely this question and is confirmed: the love vocabulary of R103 consistently attributes inner-being states to God with the same vocabulary used for human inner-being. This is not analogy but shared characteristic — love is the one characteristic in the programme where divine and human possession is most evidentially co-extensive.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence presents mercy as genuinely shared between God and the human person — not merely analogous. The same vocabulary (*eleeō/eleēmōn*) applies to both God (Rom 9:15 — God having mercy) and the human person (Mat 5:7 — the merciful). Christ's incarnation (Heb 2:17) takes on humanity specifically to become *eleēmōn* in the priestly sense — the divine mercy acquires human experiential content through solidarity. This suggests that mercy is not merely a creaturely analogue to a divine quality but a genuinely shared characteristic in which the divine and human poles are structurally interconnected. The image-sharing in mercy is constitutive: received mercy produces the capacity to extend mercy. OBS-111-030, OBS-111-033, OBS-111-052, OBS-111-055. *New finding: mercy is a genuinely shared characteristic — not merely analogical — in which the divine and human poles are interconnected through reception and extension.*

findings.session_b_note: The evidence supports that covenant is genuinely shared — both God and the human person make and keep covenants, and Scripture presents these as structurally analogous acts (though asymmetric in ground and reliability). God initiates covenants (OBS-034-046, OBS-034-052); humans enter and respond to God's covenants and also make their own person-to-person covenants (765-005, 3304-004 — OBS-034-042, OBS-034-049). The same Hebrew term (berit, karat berit) is used for both. The human instance is not merely an analogue — the human capacity to covenant is a genuine participation in the same type of act, though the human's faithfulness is contingent and fallible while God's is absolute and self-grounded. This distinguishes covenant from, for example, omniscience or omnipotence, which are exclusively divine and have no genuine human analogue.

findings.session_b_note: Shared — and with the unique feature that the sharing is constitutive rather than merely analogical. The evidence distinguishes: (1) God IS peace (YHWH-Shalom, 406-001, OBS-117-148) — divine ontological possession; (2) the human person receives peace from God and inhabits it (2508-001, OBS-117-144: soul bereft of peace; perfect peace for the trusting mind, Isa 26:3); (3) the messianic king IS peace (2508-004, Mic 5:5, OBS-117-147) — in the DHC structure, the divine-human boundary is breached in the direction of identification, not analogy. The peace that the human receives is not an analogue of divine peace but a participation in it — received from the same source (God), grounded in the same reality (covenant), moving toward the same telos (eschatological wholeness). This is a stronger connection than analogy; it is participation. The peace the human person bears is genuinely the same peace that God IS, received through covenant.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence supports shared characteristic with asymmetric form. God gives as the originating and sovereign giver: his giving constitutes covenantal reality (Gen 15:18), endows inner capacities (Neh 9:20, Job 38:36), and enacts eschatological transformation (Isa 61:3). The human gives in responsive mode: Job releases what God gave (Job 1:21); the Servant offers himself in trust of divine vindication (Isa 50:6). The characteristic is genuinely shared — both God and the human give from inner-being orientation — but the asymmetry is structural: God gives primarily and the human gives responsively. Human giving is always downstream of divine giving, either responding to it (Job 1:21) or participating in its pattern (Isa 50:6). This is not exclusively a creaturely analogue — it is a shared characteristic with a directional structure: God → human → God.

Shared. God hates (groups 3595, 3596 — extensively evidenced). The righteous person is commanded and praised for hating what God hates (group 550-NEW-02). Psa 139:21 shows the sharing is explicit and conscious: the psalmist's hatred is consciously derived from God's own orientation. This is not analogy but participation: the human person takes on God's own disposition as an act of alignment.

Not shared as an originating disposition. God's contempt-responses (Deu 32:19, Lam 2:6) are judicial and reactive, not expressions of an originating inner character. Contempt is a creaturely distortion — the inversion of reverence that belongs to the properly ordered creature before the Creator.

Shared. God abhors evil (Psa 5:6, Psa 106:40, Amo 6:8). The righteous person shares this abhorrence (Psa 119:163). The sharing is explicit in both the commands (Deu 23:7 regulates the direction, implying a shared capacity) and the psalmist's statements of alignment with God's own moral recoil.

Not shared. Cruelty is not a characteristic God possesses or shares with the image-bearer. It names the absence of what God has (mercy, restraint, purposive severity). It is exclusively a creaturely failure condition.

Not shared as a condition experienced. God removes reproach; he does not inhabit it. Christ's bearing of reproach (Psa 69:9 → Rom 15:3) is the redemptive exception — the Son entering the creaturely condition of being reproached in order to remove it.

Shared in the specific form of the adversary posture adopted in covenant faithfulness (Exo 23:22). God takes up the adversary relationship on behalf of his people. The capacity to stand in structured opposition as an act of advocacy is therefore shared — but only in its covenantal form, not in its hostile or adversarial form as directed against the person.

Genuinely shared across all seven sub-groups. The vocabulary is applied to both God and the human person without distinction of kind — the same Hebrew and Greek roots name the divine and human instances. The sharing is participatory and asymmetrical: the divine instance is the original, inexhaustible, and self-grounded; the human instance is derivative, creaturely, and dependent. But the sharing is real — the human does not perform an analogue to God's love; the human participates in the same characteristic that God is and has.
**[A1 — God Righteousness]** A1 is the divine instance. The question concerns the human instance's relationship to the divine.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Both genuinely shared and structurally analogical. The sharing is real: "born of him" (1Jo 2:29) implies genuine participation in the divine quality; "the righteousness of God" in 2Cor 5:21 is stated as the actual righteousness of God being constituted in the person. However, human righteousness can be forfeited (Eze 18:24, VSG M26-A2-002); God's cannot. The correct reading: the sharing is genuine but asymmetric — the human participates in a quality whose original and inexhaustible instance is in God.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** The uprightness vocabulary is used of both God and persons. The quality is shared — but directionally: God is the source and standard of what is straight; the person is the one who aligns with that standard. Analogue-with-genuine-participation is the correct framing.
**[C — Justification]** Justification as such is not a shared characteristic — it is a unidirectional act from God toward the creature. God does not receive justification; he performs it.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The commissioned human avenger shares the quality in a delegated sense — genuine but derivative. "Vengeance is mine" simultaneously attributes the quality exclusively to God while authorising its delegated expression. The sharing is real but bounded.

**[E — Condemnation]** The human capacity for condemnation is a creaturely analogue with genuine participatory elements. But self-condemnation (autokatakritos) is exclusively creaturely — it has no divine analogue because God's inner being does not work against itself.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The reckoning faculty is genuinely shared in its nature but asymmetric in its exercise. God's reckoning is omniscient and penetrating; human reckoning is instructed, partial, and effortful. The genuine participation is established by Paul commanding the human reckoning (Rom 6:11) as a real inner act with real consequences.
**[G — Structural Opposites]** Wickedness and injustice are not shared between God and humans.

**[CLUSTER]** The cluster evidence consistently points to a shared characteristic that is asymmetric: the human person genuinely participates in a quality whose perfect and inexhaustible instance is in God. The participation is not metaphorical — it is constitutive of what the human person is when righteous. But it is bounded, derivative, and dependent — the human instance cannot exist independently of the divine source.

The evidence across sub-groups consistently supports participatory sharing rather than mere analogy. The giving-structure (God gives wisdom: Jam 1:5; God places understanding: Job 38:36; Christ opens minds: Luk 24:45; God gives knowledge: Dan 2:21) shows divine attributes genuinely entering the human person, not merely being resembled. The human characteristic is a real participation in the divine, scaled to the creaturely constitution.

findings.finding_value: M46 has both genuinely shared and analogical elements. What is genuinely shared: God is plousios (rich), and Christ voluntarily became ptōchos (poor). The human acts of generous giving (M46-D) participate in the divine pattern established by 2Cor 8:9. The learned contentment of autarkēs may be an analogue to divine self-sufficiency rather than a direct sharing — God's autarkeia is ontological and unconditioned; Paul's is acquired through formation. The ordered reception of wealth (M46-C) is an analogue: God creates wealth and gives it; the human receives and stewards it. Inner closure (M46-A) and hardness (M46-B) are exclusively creaturely disorders — no analogues in the divine nature.

Reg 56 (envy) holds the full positive-negative dual register of the zeal/jealousy vocabulary. The evidence indicates genuine sharing rather than mere analogy. The Spirit grieves (Eph 4:30 — M03-C-VCG-02); Jesus's soul is perilupos in Gethsemane (Mat 26:38 — M03-C-VCG-03); God was afflicted in all Israel's distress (Isa 63:9 — M03-D-VCG-03). These are not merely analogical descriptions; they name grief as a real inner-being state of the Spirit and of Jesus-as-human-person. The evidence suggests that grief is genuinely shared between God and the human person at the level of the characteristic's relational core (being moved by loss, responding to the suffering of the beloved). What differs is the mode: divine grief does not involve bodily exhaustion (groaning, physical ache, bodily deterioration from weeping), which are creaturely somatic expressions of a grief that in God is real but expressed without creaturely limitation.

Jer 32:41 grounds God's rejoicing in "all my heart and all my soul" — constitutional language applied to God in a passage describing mutual restoration. The NT adds: God rejoices over the repentant sinner (Luk 15:7, 10) using the exact same register as human rejoicing. The most decisive evidence is Joh 15:11 — "my joy may be in you": Christ's own joy (chara) is to indwell the disciples, making their joy a participation in divine joy rather than a mere analogy to it. **[CHAR-7]** E — Genuinely shared, through Christ. This suggests that the capacity for moral revulsion at abomination (as opposed to being abominable) is a shared capacity between God and image-bearing humans, particularly those whose conscience is functioning rightly.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — God cannot be an idolater. The evidence confirms this by locating idolatrous abomination entirely in the human will's attachment to non-divine objects: Eze 11:21 (vc=1631 — VCG-05): the heart goes after detestable things; Isa 66:3 (vc=1633 — VCG-04): the soul delights in abominations — both are specifically human inner-being orientations. The divine position in the evidence is always that of the offended party (Deu 32:16 — VCG-02: God's jealousy provoked; Eze 5:11 — VCG-05: God's withdrawal). God has no analogue to false devotion — his devotion is always truthfully directed toward himself and toward his covenant people. The characteristic is exclusively a creaturely failure of the devotion-capacity.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic is exclusively creaturely. God is consistently positioned as the perceiver and judge of iniquity (Job 11:11 — VCG-04: "he sees iniquity, will he not consider it?"; Psa 5:5 — VCG-03: "you hate all evildoers"), never as its practitioner. The structural parallel that would be shared is the capacity for intentional inner generation — God devises plans (positive), the iniquity-schemer devises evil. But the iniquity-schemer's devising is entirely creaturely: Mic 2:1 (vc=38217 — VCG-02): "those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds" — the devising is human inner activity. The characteristic belongs exclusively to the creaturely sphere of misused generative faculty.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic is exclusively creaturely. God is the target of blasphemy (VCG-01 — Rev 13:6; 16:9/11/21) and the one whose name is dishonoured by others' speech and conduct (VCG-02 — Rom 2:24). The human person is both the agent of evil speech (Rev 16:9 — those who curse God's name) and the victim (1Pe 2:12/3:16 — VCG-03: falsely accused as evildoers; 1Cor 4:13 — vc=14351 — VCG-02: slandered). God has no analogue to the characteristic — he cannot blaspheme himself and he does not falsely accuse. The characteristic belongs exclusively to the creaturely sphere as the misuse of the creaturely speech-gift.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics are exclusively creaturely — confirmed unanimously across the cluster. The pattern is consistent: no M10b characteristic has a divine analogue. However, the cluster reveals important variation in how the exclusion operates. Chars 1, 2, and 5 are denied to God directly and absolutely (wickedness, constitutional evil, and iniquity-scheming are impossibilities for the divine nature). Chars 3 and 4 are denied to God as conditions while God's response-side is affirmed: God possesses the revulsion-response to abomination (Pro 8:7; Jer 44:4) but not the abominable condition itself — revealing a structural asymmetry in these two characteristics. Char 6 is denied through structural impossibility (God cannot blaspheme himself; he is the target of blasphemy, never its agent). The cluster's unified exclusively-creaturely verdict reveals M10b as naming the inner-being failures that belong entirely to the creaturely sphere — with no divine template or analogue for any of the six.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The evidence confirms this characteristic is exclusively a creaturely condition, with no divine counterpart. As noted at T0.1.2, God is not a subject of this characteristic in the 133-verse corpus. The characteristic has a structural analogue in God: God's holiness is the positive reality against which the defilement-state is measured. But the defilement-state itself — as condition, as vulnerability, as something acquired and managed — belongs to the creaturely domain alone. It is not a shared property between Creator and creature.

**[CHAR-2]** S — Exclusively a creaturely condition, as evidenced by the silence at T0.1.2. The moral-inner defilement-state is not shared with God. There is no divine analogue to the corrupted conscience (1Cor 8:7), the enslaved will (Rom 6:19), or the heart allegiance disorder equated with idolatry (Eph 5:5). The evidence uniformly frames the condition as what God is not and as what the divine call moves the person away from (1Th 4:7). The characteristic is exclusively creaturely — specifically, it is the condition of the fallen creature whose inner person has come under the dominion of desire, sin, and corrupted allegiance.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Exclusively a creaturely-covenantal condition, with the single judicial exception noted at T0.1.2. The corporate/covenantal defilement-state requires a community embedded in covenantal relationship with God — it is the condition of that community when it betrays the covenant. God as the covenant-giver and the holy One dwelling in the land does not share this condition; he is what the condition violates. Eze 5:11 makes this explicit: the people's defilement of the sanctuary provokes God's withdrawal — showing that God and the defilement-state are mutually exclusive realities.

**[CHAR-4]** S — Exclusively a creaturely condition. God is not inhabited, controlled, or defiled by unclean spirits; he is their sovereign authority before whom they bow (Mar 3:11, VCG-03). The characteristic presupposes a vulnerable creaturely person who can be invaded and dominated by an external spiritual force — a vulnerability that does not apply to God.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across all four characteristics, the cluster evidence converges on exclusively creaturely condition, with the single judicial exception at Characteristic 3 (Eze 20:26 — God deploying defilement as judgment, not possessing it). The pattern is uniform: God does not bear ritual defilement (Char 1 — he is the standard against which it is measured), moral-inner defilement (Char 2 — he is what the condition is not), corporate-covenantal defilement (Char 3 — he is what the betrayal violates), or spirit-agency defilement (Char 4 — he is the sovereign authority before whom the defiling spirits bow). The cluster as a whole positions the M10c domain as a specifically creaturely domain — the human person (and the covenant community) is uniquely susceptible to defilement across all four registers in ways that God is not. The unclean spirits' recognition of Christ's identity (Mar 3:11 — "You are the Son of God") is the most direct expression: even the adversarial agents who produce Characteristic 4 acknowledge that the divine person cannot be defiled by them.

questions.section: T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
questions.question_text: Where the characteristic is present or absent in a person, what does that indicate about the condition of the divine image in them — or is no such indication evidenced?

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides partial evidence on this, sufficient to ground an observation:

**Presence of forgiveness:** F-003 establishes that the person who has received divine forgiveness and extends it to others is functioning within the intended structural pattern — the vertical-horizontal interdependence is operating correctly. The love-orientation produced by received forgiveness (Luk 7:47; OBS-064-029) suggests a person in whom the divine-image capacity for relational generosity is actively expressed.

**Absence of forgiveness (withheld):** OBS-064-001 flags that "the absence of forgiveness poisons the inner life of the withholder." Mat 18:35 (the unforgiving servant) names the consequence: judgment falls on the one who received forgiveness but refuses to extend it. The refusal to forgive is treated as a structural incoherence — the divine image's relational-generosity capacity is present but deliberately suppressed.

**Outer limit — permanent absence:** Mar 3:29 (blasphemy against the Spirit) names the condition in which forgiveness becomes permanently inaccessible. OBS-064-024 connects this to the Spirit's role as the one whose work "creates and sustains the inner openness through which forgiveness is received." Permanent rejection of the Spirit's work = permanent closure of the forgiveness-capacity. This represents the most severe image-bearer condition: not merely the suppression of the capacity but its permanent foreclosure.

*New finding:* The data together implies a spectrum — from the person in whom the forgiveness-capacity is actively expressed (image functioning), through the person in whom it is suppressed (image distorted), to the person in whom it is permanently closed (image at its most extreme point of damage). This spectrum is not assembled in the existing observations but is implicit in the combined evidence of F-003, OBS-064-001, and OBS-064-024.

findings.session_b_note:
SD043 names acharistos (graceless, ungrateful) as the structural antithesis — the inner failure to register grace as grace. SD004 establishes pride as the counter-condition. SD033 (Eph 2:8) suggests surrender of self-contribution is the necessary inner condition for grace-reception. Together: where grace is absent, the image is impaired — the capacity for uncaused giving suppressed by pride, self-sufficiency, or ingratitude.

*Gap identified: the existing analysis addresses counter-conditions but does not frame them explicitly as image-impairment. The prompt surfaces this as a T0 observation not previously named.*

findings.session_b_note:
Two contrasting cases in the data address this directly:

**Presence — Lam 4:10:** The adjectival form ra.cha.ma.ni (compassionate) names the settled character quality of compassion. The verse describes compassionate women (ra.cha.ma.ni) doing something that violates the deepest expression of compassionate character — boiling their own children in the siege of Jerusalem. The data's observation is precise: "These are compassionate women — yet this is what they did. The term names the inner quality at the moment of its most catastrophic inversion." The verse reveals that compassion as a character quality is not indestructible — extreme external pressure can force its violation. This implies that the divine image, as expressed in compassion, can be damaged, distorted, or temporarily overwhelmed by circumstances of sufficient severity.

**Absence — Rev 3:17 (eleeinos):** The Laodiceans are described as pitiable (eleeinos) — the condition that ought to evoke compassion — without recognising their own condition. The data notes: "The word names the failure of the second condition. Compassion requires both the disposition (in the giver) and the recognition of need (in the receiver or an observer)." Self-deceived prosperity is identified as the inner state that prevents both the recognition of one's own pitiable condition and, by implication, the capacity to perceive and respond to the pitiable condition of others (SD-015). The absence of compassion-awareness signals a condition in which the divine image is obscured by self-sufficiency.

Taken together: the presence of compassion, even where it is violated, reveals that the image remains structurally in place. The absence of compassion-perception, particularly when masked by prosperity and self-deception, reveals an image condition that has been occluded at the level of inner orientation.

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence supports a clear answer to this, though it was not assembled in prior analysis in precisely these terms.

**Presence of contrition** reveals that the divine image is functioning in its creaturely-relational axis: the person knows themselves truly before God, is open to divine holiness, and is constituted to receive rather than assert. This is the inner-being condition of the genuine image-bearer — the creature that is genuinely creature before Creator.

**Absence of contrition** — attested in Jer 44:10 — reveals not the absence of the image but its distortion or closure. The people who have not humbled themselves, feared, or walked in God's law are not imageless — they retain their creaturely constitution — but they are operating in a posture of autonomy that is a distortion of right creaturely orientation. The divine image is present but functionally inverted: they are constituted to be low before God but have refused lowliness.

*New finding: the presence/absence of contrition functions as a diagnostic of whether the creaturely-relational axis of the divine image is functioning correctly. This is not destruction of the image but its functional distortion.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses what fellowship-absence implies, though not explicitly in image-of-God terms.

**What absence reveals:** 2Cor 6:14 presents the incompatibility of righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness — the person who is in fellowship with darkness is in a condition structurally incompatible with divine-nature fellowship. Hos 4:17 presents Ephraim *joined to idols* and abandoned — idolatrous fellowship is the replacement of the vertical fellowship orientation with a misdirected joining. The person joined to idols is not only morally compromised but relationally re-oriented away from God.

**What this implies for the image:** Idolatrous fellowship (joining to wrong objects) is the corruption of the participatory capacity that was designed for divine-nature participation. The image is not destroyed in Hosea's framing, but its orientation is entirely misdirected — the joining-capacity turns away from God and fastens to idols.

**Limitation:** This remains interpretive inference. The data does not explicitly frame this in image-of-God terms.

findings.session_b_note: The presence of goodness signals a person whose image-bearing capacity is functioning — oriented toward God, capable of moral assessment, and able to express relational and volitional goodness toward others. The absence or inversion of goodness is treated in the verse evidence as a diagnosis of image-condition. Rom 3:12 ("no one does good, not even one") names universal absence as the condition of fallen humanity — the image is present but the goodness-capacity is not operative. The three forms of goodness-absence in 884-006 (direct moral failure), Jer 6:16 (wilful refusal of the good way), and Jer 44:17 / Mal 2:17 (distortion — calling evil good) describe three modes of image-dysfunction: failure, resistance, and inversion. The most severe is inversion — calling evil good — because it corrupts the evaluative capacity that the image includes. The Haman instance (Est 5:9, 884-009) names a fourth mode: the appearance of well-being without genuine goodness — inner pleasantness not rooted in God, which is immediately fragile. (OBS-067-OBS-021, OBS-067-OBS-046, OBS-067-OBS-049)

findings.session_b_note: The data provides an unusually direct answer. Joh 13:35 (OBS-103-129) — 'by this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another' — makes love the externally legible mark of the divine image in the community. 1Jo 4:8 (via flag) — 'whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love' — states that lovelessness constitutes non-knowledge of God. The absence of love is not merely a moral deficiency; it is an epistemic and ontological condition: the person who does not love does not know God and therefore does not bear the divine image in its proper operation. Conversely, the presence of love — particularly love of enemies (Mat 5:44-45, OBS-103-144) — constitutes identity as a son/daughter of God. Love is thus the diagnostic marker of the divine image's condition: present and active = image bearing; absent or disordered = image distorted.

Absence of contrition (the hardened heart of Jer 44:10) reveals an image-bearer closed to this truth — self-sufficient, resistant to divine word. The hardened alternative is therefore an image-deficiency: the person who will not receive the divine verdict about their condition. OBS-030-028, OBS-030-047, OBS-030-062.

findings.session_b_note: The verse evidence provides clear indicators. Presence of covenant-faithfulness: in the human, keeping covenant is an expression of moral integrity (3308-002 — OBS-034-053), alignment with God's own character (Deu 7:9 — OBS-034-039), and is associated with knowing God and living under his blessing. Absence or corruption: G0802 (asunthetos — covenant-breaking as inner character defect — OBS-034-018, OBS-034-057) appears in Paul's catalogue of the debased mind (Rom 1:31) — the morally degraded human who has rejected God becomes incapable of covenant faithfulness. Dan 9:11 (OBS-034-036) frames collective covenant breach as the inner moral failure of a people. The pattern: covenant faithfulness indexes the health of the divine image in the person; covenant-breaking indexes its degradation. The person who cannot keep covenant is described in terms of inner moral collapse.

findings.session_b_note: The data provides clear evidence in both directions. Presence: the person who has shalom is in right orientation toward God (Isa 26:3 — mind stayed on God = perfect peace; Psa 119:165 — love of God's law = great peace; OBS-117-144). Mal 2:6 (OBS-117-146) — walking in peace and uprightness — is the portrait of the image-bearing priest. Absence: the absence of shalom is diagnostic of inner disorder. Three patterns emerge: (1) Moral disorder → absence of peace: Isa 48:22/57:21 ("there is no peace for the wicked"); the way of peace unknown to those in moral disorder (Isa 59:8); (2) False peace as image corruption: Deu 29:19 (2509-002, OBS-117-150) — the stubborn-hearted person who claims shalom without covenant ground; Jer 6:14/8:11 — prophets crying "peace, peace" when there is no peace; the corrupted image produces false shalom claims; (3) Somatic evidence: Psa 38:3 ("no health in my bones because of my sin") — the absence of shalom-wholeness has bodily expression. The image-bearing conclusion: shalom's presence is the marker of the person in right order with God; its absence (or false claim) reveals image-corruption at the deepest level.

The presence of rightly-directed hatred (group 550-NEW-02) reveals the divine image operating — the person's inner life is aligned with God's. The presence of disordered person-directed hatred (group 1601 — "you shall not hate your brother in your heart," Lev 19:17) reveals image-disorder: the capacity meant to oppose evil has been turned against a fellow image-bearer. Job 34:17: "shall one who hates justice govern?" — hatred of justice is the disqualifying inner disposition, the sign that the image is disordered at its governing level.

Its presence is a direct indicator of image-disorder. Isa 1:4: "they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged" — the contempt and the estrangement from God are sequential. Contempt of the sacred marks a person in whom the image's capacity for appropriate reverence and honour-giving has been inverted. The image is in disorder when the person despises what God values.

Righteous abhorrence reveals an image operating properly — the moral constitution is aligned with God's own. Inverted abhorrence (group 252-002 — abhorring justice) is among the clearest markers of a comprehensively reversed moral constitution: the capacity has been retrained to recoil from what it was made to receive and promote.

Psa 54:3's diagnostic is precise: "they do not set God before themselves." The image is in profound disorder when the person has removed God from their inner governing framework — when the consciousness of divine presence and accountability that would restrain destructive impulses is gone. Cruelty is the inner-being condition produced by the removal of God-consciousness from the person's operational centre.

For the one bearing reproach: the divine image in the bearer is not destroyed by reproach but assaulted, hidden, and temporarily eclipsed. The person can remain aligned with God even while their social status is destroyed — Psa 69:7: "for it is for your sake that I have borne reproach." For those imposing reproach: their contempt and hatred (M06-B, M06-A) reveal their image-disorder. God's restoration of honour to the reproached is an image-restoration act.

The capacity to stand in appeal before God when facing an adversary (Psa 35:1, Jer 15:15, Luk 18:3) reveals an image-bearing person who recognises their dependence and God's authority over all adversarial structures. The absence of this response — facing opposition without appeal — would indicate a form of self-sufficiency inconsistent with the creature's proper orientation.

Its presence reveals one of the most severe forms of image-disorder: the soul's rejoicing in destruction indicates that the image's deepest capacity (genuine joy in what is good) has been inverted into rejoicing in its opposite. All three constitutive elements of malice (enmity, contempt, pleasure in destruction) represent inversions of image-bearing capacities.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** A1 does not address the condition of the divine image in the human person.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The verse evidence is explicit: righteousness in the person reveals an image in alignment with its source; its absence reveals an image in disorder. "The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself" (Eze 18:20, VSG M26-A2-002) — the person's righteousness or wickedness is their own inner state. The presence of righteousness reveals a person whose inner being is rightly oriented toward God and neighbour. Its absence (M26-A2-003: distortion and counterfeit; M26-A2-004: far from righteousness) reveals an image that has been distorted, abandoned, or never formed.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** "They do not know how to do right" (Amo 3:10, VSG 1214-001) — the absence of uprightness reveals an image that has lost its orientation toward what is straight and true. The inner compass is broken. The presence of uprightness reveals a functioning moral compass, aligned with the divine quality of truth and straightness.

**[C — Justification]** Justification does not reveal the condition of the image in the present person — it transforms it. The person who receives justification passes from broken-image standing (guilty before God) to restored-image standing (righteous before God). Heb 11:7 — "an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith" — shows the justified person as one whose image has been rehabilitated through an act of grace.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The presence or absence of the avenging faculty does not in itself reveal the condition of the divine image. The image condition is revealed by how the faculty is exercised, not merely by its presence.

**[E — Condemnation]** The capacity for self-condemnation (autokatakritos, Tit 3:11) reveals an image that is self-aware enough to recognise its own failure — a genuine moral faculty functioning to expose departure from righteousness. The freedom from condemnation in Rom 8:34 reveals an image that has been restored — conscience no longer working against the self because the verdict of God has changed.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The reckoning faculty's presence reveals a person capable of engaging in the moral-theological work of assigning right standing and weighing moral worth. Its exercise in the right direction (counting oneself dead to sin, alive to God) reveals an image functioning in alignment with divine reckoning. Its misapplication (reckoning not from faith — Rom 14:23) reveals an image whose reckoning faculty is misdirected.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The presence of wickedness (ra.sha) and injustice (a.val) in a person reveals an image in profound disorder — a person who has turned against the moral order that the image is designed to instantiate. The ra.sha person is not merely imperfect — they are a person from whom the central quality of the divine image (righteousness) is absent or actively opposed.

**[CLUSTER]** The cluster reveals that righteousness is a load-bearing element of the divine image — its presence indicates an image in alignment with its source; its absence or distortion (A2-003, G) indicates an image in disorder. The cluster also reveals gradations: from the person in whom righteousness is stable and protected (A2-013), to the person in whom it is conditional and forfeitable (A2-002), to the person in whom it is absent (A2-004), to the person who actively opposes it (G).

findings.finding_value: In M01-A, the presence of reverential fear reveals a person whose inner life is rightly ordered — the image-bearing orientation toward God is intact. Psa 25:14 (anchor): fear positions the person for covenant intimacy. Pro 1:7 (anchor): fear grounds genuine knowing. Absence of fear reveals moral blindness: Psa 36:1 ("no dread of God before their eyes — a fundamental moral blindness that allows transgression to speak freely in the heart"); Rom 3:18 ("absence of fear of God in their inner orientation"). The 2Ki 17 corpus (M01-A-VCG-05) shows that syncretistic fear — fear of God mixed with fear of other gods — is not genuine fear but a persistent compromise that reveals a divided image. Jer 5:22-24 (anchor M01-A-VCG-05) shows that the failure to fear God is located specifically in the heart and expressed as failure to acknowledge God's gifts. The absence of fear marks a person whose inner orientation is fundamentally disordered.

M01-B's acute fear is not primarily a diagnostic of image-condition; its presence is involuntary and its absence (in the sense of not fearing what is genuinely threatening) can reflect either courage or foolishness. The B-VCG-06 "do not fear" pattern shows that the commanded absence of specific fears reflects faith, not image-damage.

M01-G is the most direct: timidity (deilia) is named as "not from God" (2Ti 1:7 anchor) — it reveals a spirit-level deficiency in the person, a departure from the inner constitution God gives. Rev 21:8 (cowardice listed alongside idolatry and murder) shows that persistent timidity-as-apostasy reveals a catastrophic failure of the inner life, not merely a temperamental weakness.

The condition of the divine image is most clearly diagnosed through M01-A (presence or absence of reverential fear), M01-G (presence or absence of courage over timidity), and M01-A-VCG-05 (whether fear is rightly directed toward God or displaced onto false objects). The image is intact when fear-of-God governs the inner person; it is disordered when fear is absent (Psa 36:1; Rom 3:18), misplaced (2Ki 17 corpus), or replaced by timidity under pressure (2Ti 1:7; Rev 21:8).

The righteous-anger corpus reveals that absence of anger at genuine wrongdoing is a moral failure, not a moral achievement. Nehemiah's anger at oppression (Neh 5:6) and Samuel's anger at disobedience (1Sa 15:11) are presented as appropriate moral responses — their absence would be moral indifference. Psa 37:1–8 warns against the fretting form of anger but does not endorse indifference to wrongdoing; the command is to relinquish incensed agitation, not to be indifferent.

2Cor 7:11 shows indignation as proof of genuine repentance — its presence evidences the condition of the divine image operating in the inner person. A person who encounters wrongdoing without any indignation may be evidencing image-suppression, not image-health.

The human-authority anger corpus (M02-A-VCG-04) shows the misuse of anger — officials' anger at Jeremiah (Jer 37:15) driving unjust violence, Naaman's anger at Elisha (2Ki 5:11) revealing wounded pride. When anger is self-serving, disproportionate, or directed at the messenger of God's word, it reveals the image distorted rather than expressed. Jam 1:20 names the structural limit: "human wrath does not produce the righteousness of God" — the divine image in this characteristic is only genuinely operative when the anger is truly oriented toward God's moral order.

The presence of rightly-ordered anger signals an operating divine image — a moral being who cares about what God cares about. The presence of disordered anger signals a distorted image — the capacity is present but misdirected. The absence of anger at genuine injustice may signal image-suppression or moral detachment.

The corpus contains striking evidence on this point. The absence of grief where grief is morally appropriate is named as a mark of moral failure or hardened inner state. The Corinthians' arrogance where mourning was appropriate shows a hardened or indifferent inner state (1Cor 5:2 — M03-B-VCG-04). The self-indulgent are condemned for not being grieved over Joseph's ruin, marking their moral failure (Amo 6:6 — M03-BOUNDARY). Babylon's boast that she will never see mourning marks her pride and spiritual self-deception (Rev 18:7 — M03-B-VCG-04). Conversely, Josiah's tender, humbled heart weeping before God moves God to hear him (2Ki 22:19 — M03-A-VCG-02). The presence of grief, particularly grief over sin and loss, signals a relational inner life that is functioning as the image demands; its absence in contexts that call for it signals a hardening or deadening of the image's relational responsiveness.

The most concentrated evidence for grief as image-indicator is M03-C-VCG-02 (godly grief producing repentance): 2Cor 7:9-11 shows grief producing the full range of morally restorative inner states. The one who is genuinely grieved by sin is demonstrating an inner life properly calibrated to the moral and relational seriousness that the image requires.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The inverted exultation passages (M04-A-VCG-02) provide the most direct evidence. Pro 2:14 shows those who "rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil" — exultation directed at evil is explicitly contrasted with wisdom's way, indicating that the characteristic's object determines whether it images God or distorts the image. Hos 9:1 commands Israel "rejoice not" because their joy is built on spiritual prostitution; Hos 10:5 shows idolatrous priests who rejoiced over a golden calf now mourning its departure — their exultation directed at an idol is now ended. The evidence shows that exultation directed toward God reveals the divine image functioning; exultation directed toward evil, idols, or another person's calamity (Pro 24:17; Psa 13:4) reveals the image distorted or corrupted. Absence of exultation before God — as in Job 3:6–7 (the wished-barrenness of the birth-night) — marks a state of such extremity that even the capacity for directed inner joy is temporarily overwhelmed.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The inverted and absent joy evidence (M04-B-VCG-06, M04-C-VCG-05 corrupt elements) is the most diagnostic: (1) **Image corrupted** — Pro 2:14 (those who "rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil"); Eze 25:6 (Ammon's joy arising from "malice within your soul" at Israel's ruin); Eze 36:5 ("wholehearted joy and utter contempt" of those who seized God's land) — joy directed at evil, at others' ruin, or at one's own pride reveals the image severely distorted; (2) **Image silenced by sin** — Psa 51:8, 12 (David's joy silenced by his sin, requiring restoration through confession and forgiveness); the loss of joy is a diagnostic of sin's damage; (3) **Image emptied by judgment** — Deu 28:47 (failure to serve with joyfulness as the root of covenant curses); Joe 1:16 (joy cut off from God's house under judgment) — the absence of joy before God reveals the covenant relationship broken; (4) **Image functioning** — Psa 97:11 ("joy for the upright in heart") — the presence of genuine joy in the uprightly-oriented inner being signals the image in its designed operation.

**[CHAR-7]** E — **Presence** reveals the image being renewed by the Spirit in the Christ-pattern: the person who genuinely rejoices amid suffering (1Pe 1:6–8; Jas 1:2) demonstrates that the Spirit is at work producing a quality of inner life that transcends circumstances — a deeply eschatologically-oriented inner being. **Absence / distortion** is most sharply evidenced in M04-F: Job 9:27 (Job considers attempting cheerfulness but immediately recognises he cannot maintain it — the image's capacity is there but overwhelmed by suffering's weight); Psa 39:13 (the psalmist's request for a little smile before death — the barely-flickering of the capacity under extreme mortality-distress). M04-F's fragile and barely-attainable cheerfulness shows the image's Suffering-Joy capacity as genuinely present but requiring the Spirit's enabling (M04-E-VCG-02) to function in its fuller form.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Presence reveals the image functioning: the person who accurately evaluates what is genuinely good (Mic 6:8's trio of justice, loving kindness, walking humbly; Naomi's wisdom in evaluating Ruth's best course; the Psalms' steady recognition of God's goodness as the ground of thanksgiving) shows the image in its designed operation. Distortion reveals the image degraded: the people who judged return to Egypt as "better than dying in the wilderness" (Num 14:3 — M04-O-VCG-02) are evaluating from fear rather than faith; the craftsmen who say "it is good" of their idol's soldering (Isa 41:7 — M04-L-VCG-02) show the evaluative faculty applied to a self-congratulating work that cannot respond or act; Jeremiah 44:17's people who attributed former wellbeing to idol-worship show the evaluative-gladness faculty seriously distorted by false memory. Absence reveals the image silenced: Eze 36:31 ("your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves") shows the evaluative faculty turned against the self in moral revulsion — the image partially restored through recognition of past failure, but accompanied by shame.

**[CHAR-4]** E — **Presence** of rightly directed Delight reveals the image functioning: Psa 40:8 (delighting to do God's will with the law within the heart — image functioning at its most direct, Heb 10:7 applies this to Christ); Psa 1:2 (delight in the law driving sustained meditation — the blessed person's image operating through will and mind); Rom 7:22 (delight in God's law "in my inner being" — even in the struggling person, the deepest layer of the image is directed toward God's law). **Misdirected Delight** reveals the image distorted: Isa 66:3 ("their soul delights in their abominations") — the same delight-capacity directed at the opposite of its proper object; Jer 6:10 (no pleasure in God's word — the image closed to its proper object); 2Th 2:12 (pleasure in unrighteousness — the image inverted). M04-F (fragile horizontal delight in beast-captivation — Rev 13:3; 17:8) shows the most complete image-distortion: the delight faculty captivated by an antichrist figure rather than by God. Jer 6:10's uncircumcised ear that takes no pleasure in God's word is the diagnostic of a heart sealed against its proper object.

**[CHAR-5]** E — **Presence of rightly directed Pleasure** reveals the image functioning: the person who finds wisdom genuinely pleasant (Pro 2:10 — "knowledge will be pleasant to your soul"), who appreciates the pleasantness of brotherly unity (Psa 133:1), who gazes on God's beauty (Psa 27:4), and whose worship genuinely soothes God's regard (M04-K-VCG-01) is an image-bearer receiving the world rightly. **Absence / distortion**: Neh 9:17 (Israel failed to register God's wonders — wonder absent); Pro 9:17 (stolen bread called pleasant — the Pleasure faculty deceived by wrong objects); Deu 28:54–56 (the delicate person's Pleasure destroyed by the curse — the image's receptive capacity collapsed under judgment); Job 20:18 (the wicked getting no enjoyment from his profits — the image's natural Pleasure capacity blocked by moral corruption). **[CHAR-5]** E — The presence of refusal to repent reveals the divine image in a condition of *persistent volitional capture*: the will that was designed to turn toward God is entrenched in a sinful direction and choosing not to reverse. 2Ki 10:31 — "not careful to walk in the law of the Lord... with all his heart" — the divided or entirely un-aligned heart is the image-condition. The image is present (the will exists, agency exists) but has been persistently directed away from God rather than toward him. The image's capacity for turning — and the sustained refusal to use it — is what makes refusal to repent a particularly revealing indicator of the image's compromised condition.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The presence of habitual defection reveals the divine image in a condition of settled misdirection: the will's habit-forming capacity has been trained in the direction away from God rather than toward him. Hos 8:11 — "altars multiplied for sinning, they have become altars for sinning" — shows how habitual sinning becomes self-perpetuating: the image's capacity to institutionalise and form patterns has been given to sinful worship, creating structures that reinforce the misdirection. 1Jo 3:6 — "no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him" — reveals that habitual defection indicates a fundamental absence of the saving knowledge of God that would redirect the image's volitional capacities. The image is present (habits are being formed, the will is active) but its directional orientation has been captured by the sinning pattern.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The presence of contagious sin in a leader reveals the divine image in a condition of *inverted authority*: the image's authority-bearing capacity is operating in the opposite direction to its design. 1Ki 16:2 — "I exalted you... and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin" — the contrast is stark: God elevated the person (image-bearing design) for their people's benefit; the person used the elevation to transmit sin (image-bearing capacity inverted). 2Ki 21:11 — Manasseh "committed abominations... more evil than all that the Amorites did... and has made Judah also to sin" — the image's capacity for moral formation of others has been deployed not merely neutrally but actively against the image's designed function. The more clearly the leader's authority is God-given (1Ki 16:2 — explicit elevation by God), the more severe the inverted use of that authority appears.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Political revolt reveals the divine image in a condition of broken covenantal loyalty. 1Ki 12:19 / 2Ch 10:19 — "Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day" — the ongoing rebellion names a condition in which the image-bearing community refuses the authority structure that God established. 2Ch 21:10's causal chain reveals the deepest dimension: the image-condition that produces political revolt is first a condition of having forsaken the Lord — the vertical loyalty broken before the horizontal political loyalty fractures. Political revolt is thus a surface manifestation of a deeper image-condition of broken loyalty, both toward God and toward his established order.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The presence of sinful speech reveals the image's condition across three levels. (1) *VCG-01 (slander from inner corruption)*: Mat 15:19 — "out of the heart come evil thoughts... slander" — sinful speech from inner corruption reveals the heart's own moral condition; the speech is a diagnostic of the heart's state. 1Ti 6:4 — slander arising from "conceit and unhealthy craving" — the image's inner moral centre is diseased. (2) *VCG-02 (divine-authority usurpation)*: when sinful speech claims divine authority (Mar 2:7; Joh 10:33), the image has inverted its relationship to God — instead of the image reflecting God, the creature is claiming to be God. (3) *VCG-03 (constitutive defiance — beast)*: Rev 13:1 — "blasphemous names on its heads" — the most extreme image-condition: the entire character constituted by defiance of God rather than by reflection of him.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The presence of wickedness-as-settled-person-identity reveals the divine image in a state of advanced corruption. The evidence from multiple VCGs maps this corruption: the wicked person excludes God from their mind (Psa 10:4 — VCG-02 — practical atheism), the transgression-voice displaces the God-voice in their heart (Psa 36:1 — VCG-02), their soul actively desires evil (Pro 21:10 — VCG-09 — "the soul of the wicked desires evil"), their moral compass is inverted (Pro 10:32 — VCG-08 — "the mouth of the wicked knows what is perverse"), and even their acts of mercy are cruel (Pro 12:10 — VCG-09). The image-bearing faculties — soul, heart, mind, will, moral perception — are all present but all maloriented. The absence of this characteristic (the righteous person) correspondingly reveals the divine image more fully functional — the Psa 1 contrast (VCG-04) structures the whole pattern. The presence of wickedness therefore maps the degree of image-corruption with granular precision.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The presence of evil as constitutional inner nature reveals the divine image in a state of deep structural corruption. Heb 10:22 (vc=14426 — VCG-06) names "an evil conscience" as the barrier that makes approach to God impossible — the image-bearer whose conscience is constitutionally defiled cannot access the God in whose image they were made. Luk 11:39 (vc=14407 — VCG-05) names the inner person as "full of greed and wickedness" while the outward appearance is clean — the image's inner core is corrupted while the exterior remains formally intact. The absence of this characteristic (when it is departed from through repentance and divine renewal) reveals the image becoming functional again: Act 3:26 (VCG-05 — "turning every one of you from your wickedness" through divine blessing) implies restoration of the image's correct orientation when the constitutional evil is addressed.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The presence of the abominable inner conditions (crooked heart, arrogant heart, silenced conscience, dishonest dealings) reveals the divine image in a state of severe corruption — specifically at the moral-relational interface with God. Pro 3:32 (vc=1686 — VCG-02) reveals the consequence: the devious person (whose inner character is abominable) is excluded from God's confidence — the relational intimacy of the image-bearing relationship is severed. The absence of abominable conditions (the upright, the blameless) reveals the image more functional: Pro 11:20 (vc=1677 — VCG-01) — "those of blameless ways are his delight" — the image in its intended orientation toward God produces delight rather than revulsion. Tit 1:16 (vc=27 — VCG-02): those who profess God but deny him by their works are "detestable" — the gap between verbal profession and inner/practical reality is the specific image-corruption this characteristic diagnoses.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The presence of idolatrous abomination reveals the divine image in a state of radical misdirection — the devotion-capacity that should orient the heart toward God is instead directing the heart toward idol-objects. Eze 11:21 (vc=1631/65982 — VCG-05): "those whose heart goes after their detestable things and their abominations" — the heart's directional faculty (the image-bearing centre) is perverted. Hos 9:10 (vc=1632 — VCG-04): "they became detestable like the thing they loved" — the image-formation principle is operative but producing a corrupted image of the idol rather than a true image of God. The absence of this characteristic (Eze 37:23 — VCG-05: restored people no longer defiling themselves with detestable things) reveals the image functioning as designed — the heart oriented toward God, the devotion-capacity correctly attached.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The presence of iniquity as active inner scheming reveals the divine image in a state of severe inner corruption at the generative level — the faculty designed to conceive and produce good from within is instead producing evil. Isa 32:6 (vc=38181 — VCG-02): "his heart is busy with iniquity" — the heart's busyness (its generative activity) is wholly occupied with scheming harm, revealing an image whose central productive faculty is inverted. Pro 6:18 (vc=38224 — VCG-02): "a heart that devises wicked plans" — the heart as the image-bearing productive centre devises wrongly. The absence of this characteristic — the person whose heart devises good, whose thoughts are righteous — reveals the image more functional and intact. Isa 55:7 (vc=38200 — VCG-02): returning to God and forsaking iniquitous thoughts is the movement toward image-restoration.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The presence of evil expressed through speech reveals the divine image in a state of severe speech-faculty corruption — the capacity for naming, testifying, and glorifying is inverted. Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): the hardened will curses God's name rather than glorifying it — the image's speech-faculty is entirely reversed in its orientation. Jude 10 (vc=14355 — VCG-01): blaspheming what is not understood shows the image's cognitive-speech capacity (to understand and name accurately) replaced by contempt filling the void of ignorance. The absence of the characteristic — speech that names God's glory, testifies truthfully, and represents moral reality accurately — reveals the image functioning more as designed. 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): honourable conduct that contradicts false accusation and eventually silences it through good deeds represents the image-functioning alternative.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals that each characteristic's presence discloses a specific dimension of image-corruption, and their collective presence would represent comprehensive image-failure. Char 1's presence reveals the image's moral-orientation corrupted (the inner person directed away from God). Char 2's presence reveals the image's constitutive generative nature corrupted (producing evil by constitutional output). Char 3's presence reveals the image's relational access to God foreclosed (exclusion from divine confidence). Char 4's presence reveals the image's devotion-faculty attached to wrong objects and constitutionally transformed toward their image (Hos 9:10 — "became detestable like the thing they loved"). Char 5's presence reveals the image's cognitive-generative faculty producing evil schemes rather than good. Char 6's presence reveals the image's speech-faculty blaspheming and defaming rather than naming, testifying, and glorifying. The cluster's six image-corruption signatures correspond inversely to six image-bearing functions — with the cluster's absence representing the image operating correctly: morally oriented toward God (Char 1's opposite), producing goodness by constitution (Char 2's opposite), in divine intimate confidence (Char 3's opposite), devotionally attached to God alone (Char 4's opposite), generating good through cognitive-generative faculty (Char 5's opposite), and speaking glory, truth, and honest testimony (Char 6's opposite).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The presence of the defilement-state does not, by itself, indicate damage to the divine image — because within Characteristic 1's register, defilement can be involuntary (Lev 5:2-3 VCG-01: hidden violation; Num 9:7 VCG-07: involuntary corpse-contact). The men at Num 9:7 who grieve their exclusion from Passover are fully image-bearing persons whose defilement was not moral fault. The image-condition is revealed more by the person's response to the defiled state: does conscience awaken (Lev 5:2-3), does the person seek cleansing (Num 19:19), does the will refuse to remain in the defilement (Num 19:20 — willful non-cleansing is the decisive moral fault)? The absence of the defilement-state — maintained purity — reveals a person actively ordered toward sacred access, exercising the sacral stewardship that the image-bearing vocation requires. The presence of defilement reveals vulnerability and finitude; the response to it reveals the condition of the image.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The presence of moral-inner defilement reveals disruption of the divine image at the most interior level — the conscience, will, and heart are not oriented toward God but toward corrupted desire and allegiance. The clearest evidence: Mat 23:27 (VCG-04) — "within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness" — the inner life that should reflect divine purity is instead marked by death and corruption. Eph 5:5 (VCG-04): the impure person is equated with an idolater — their interior has displaced God with corrupt desire, revealing the image's most fundamental disruption (misplaced allegiance). The absence of the characteristic — the positive-inverse state — reveals the image functioning toward its intended fullness: Rev 14:4 (VCG-05), those not defiled follow the Lamb, are called firstfruits for God — the image is expressed in the orientation of the whole inner person toward God.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The presence of the corporate/covenantal defilement-state reveals a specific failure of the image-bearing vocation: the community created to reflect divine holiness in the land, to maintain covenant fidelity, and to guard the divine name has instead become the source of the land's pollution, the sanctuary's desecration, and the name's defilement. Eze 36:17 (VCG-04): "their ways before me were like the uncleanness of a woman in her menstrual impurity" — the corporate conduct has become repugnant to divine holiness. The absence of the characteristic — the condition of the community before the defection begins, or after restoration — reveals the image functioning: land kept holy (Num 35:34), sanctuary guarded (Eze 44:23/25), covenant fidelity maintained. Eze 20:43 (VCG-02) reveals a distinctive image-bearing moment: the future community will remember its defilement and "loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed" — even the memory of the defilement serves the image-bearing vocation of repentance.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The presence of defilement by external spiritual agency reveals the divine image as disrupted and occupied by an alien power: will overridden (Luk 8:29), communicative faculties suppressed (Mar 9:25), person's proper selfhood dominated by the spirit's agenda. The image-bearing functions (willing, communicating, relating) are not destroyed but overridden. The absence of the characteristic — or its reversal through expulsion — reveals the image functioning: the person restored to their own will, faculties returned, and communal access restored (Luk 9:42 — "gave him back to his father").

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's four characteristics reveal the divine image's condition through different diagnostic lenses. Characteristic 1's presence does not automatically signal image-disruption — involuntary defilement (Num 9:7) does not indicate moral failure; the image-condition is revealed by the person's response (does conscience awaken? does the will seek remedy?). Characteristic 2's presence signals image-disruption at the most interior level — the conscience, will, and heart corrupted from within (Mat 23:27, Eph 5:5). Characteristic 3's presence signals image-disruption at the communal-vocational level — the community entrusted with land, sanctuary, and divine name has defiled what it was called to steward (Eze 36:17). Characteristic 4's presence signals image-disruption through occupation — the image-bearing capacities (willing, communicating, relating) are not destroyed but overridden by an alien agency (Luk 8:29, Mar 9:25, Mar 5:2). The cluster together reveals the divine image as a multi-dimensional reality that can be disrupted at the bodily-creaturely level (Char 1), the moral-interior level (Char 2), the communal-vocational level (Char 3), and the volitional-agency level (Char 4) — each register carrying its own diagnostic of the image's condition.

questions.question_text: Does this verse use the characteristic typologically — pointing beyond the immediate to a covenantal, eschatological, or christological reality; if so, which, and in which direction (the divine instance establishing the pattern, or the human pointing toward the divine)? Record the use and direction, or record none.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes. The typological use is multi-directional and well-evidenced in the data:

1. **Cultic-to-Christological:** Group 5379-001 (Lev 4:20 — priestly atonement → forgiveness) is the OT cultic mechanism. Eph 1:7 establishes the NT fulfilment: "in him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses." The OT sacrifice system types the atoning work of Christ. OBS-064-014 names this contrast: "OT grammar of received forgiveness — covenantally guaranteed by correct external action" vs. NT inner-being access-conditions (faith, repentance, confession).

2. **Covenantal-to-Eschatological:** Jer 31:34 (group 5379-003) is named as "God's promised and proclaimed forgiveness in the new covenant context." OBS-064-017 notes the permanent, irreversible quality of the forgiveness — "the debt is not merely cancelled but rendered non-recallable." This new covenant forgiveness participates in an eschatological reality — a future state already declared.

3. **Christological:** Mar 2:7 — "who can forgive sins but God alone?" — the scribes' question frames the typological claim that Jesus's act of forgiving names him as the divine forgiver. The human Jesus performing the divine-exclusive salach-class act is a Christological self-disclosure.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes. The data contains clear typological uses, operating in multiple directions.

**Christological typology:** The splanchnizō vocabulary in the Gospels functions typologically in that Jesus's compassion-movements enact what the Hebrew womb-vocabulary had named as God's character. The Synoptic pattern — Jesus "moved with compassion" before healing, feeding, and restoring — is not merely biographical detail. It is the embodied enactment of the divine character formula of Exod 34:6. Jesus's compassion-in-action is the Christological realisation of what the OT had named as God's inner disposition. The Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:33 — splanchnizō) deploys compassion typologically as well: the Samaritan's act of compassion answers the question "who is my neighbour?" in a way that points beyond the immediate story to the nature of covenant membership and the shape of the new humanity (SD-010).

**Covenantal typology:** The Exod 34:6 formula (rachum ve-channum) operates as a covenantal anchor — it is cited whenever the community's relationship with God is re-established or renewed (Neh 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jon 4:2). The compassion of God is the covenantal ground that makes return and restoration possible. In this usage, compassion is not merely a divine attribute — it is the character that holds the covenant open at the moment of its violation.

**Eschatological typology:** Rom 8:17 (sumpaschō → syndoxazō) places present fellow-suffering within an eschatological frame: suffering-with-Christ now participates in glory-with-Christ then. Jas 5:11 (polusplanchnos) connects divine deep compassion to the "purpose (telos) of the Lord" — present suffering is held within a divine compassionate purpose that is not yet fully disclosed.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes, with high confidence. The most significant typological use in the registry is Isa 53:5 (group 7552-002): "he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed." The Servant's crushing here is explicitly substitutionary — the crushing vocabulary is applied to the Servant's inner person in a way that produces peace and healing for the community. This is the contrition-vocabulary deployed typologically: the physical-to-inner crushing image points toward a christological reality (the Servant as the one crushed on behalf of others).

The typological direction is from the broader crushing vocabulary (which applies to human penitential experience) toward a unique instance of crushing that operates at the covenantal-redemptive level. The human experience of being crushed and contrite before God provides the conceptual vocabulary through which the Servant's substitutionary suffering is described and understood. The human instance provides the language; the divine Servant-instance provides the redemptive reality.

*New finding: the typological use of the crushing vocabulary in Isa 53 has not been explicitly named as typological in prior analysis. Group 7552-002 was identified as "Divine-Human Correspondence" dimension, and OBS-030-026 noted it as analytically distinctive, but the specifically typological direction of the text — that human contrition-vocabulary points toward and is fulfilled in the Servant's substitutionary crushing — was not assembled as a typological claim.*

findings.session_b_note:
Yes. The evidence establishes typological use in at least two directions.

**Christological:** Phili 3:10 (*that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death*) — fellowship with Christ's sufferings and death is explicitly oriented toward resurrection. The fellowship is not contained within the suffering moment; it points through suffering toward transformation. This is typological in the sense that the fellowship with Christ's death pattern images the death-resurrection pattern of the Gospel.

**Eschatological:** 2Pe 1:4 — divine nature participation is presented as an escape from corruption *in the world*. The trajectory of this participation points beyond present conditions. The fellowship with divine nature is a present entry into something whose fullness belongs to the age to come.

**Covenantal:** Eze 37:19 — the joining of Judah and Ephraim into one is explicitly an act of covenant restoration. The two sticks become one in God's hand — a physical/political sign pointing to the restoration of the covenant people. The fellowship of the restored community points to the covenant fulfilment.

**New finding:** The fellowship vocabulary across this registry carries typological weight in all three registers simultaneously (christological, eschatological, covenantal). This assembly has not been made explicitly in the prior findings, which addressed these dimensions individually.

findings.session_b_note: The covenantal typological dimension is present and clear: God's good word (884-005, Jos 23:14) and his chrēstotēs displayed supremely in Christ (Eph 2:7) both carry a Christological register — the fullness of divine goodness is displayed in Christ's person and work. Rom 2:4 names chrēstotēs as the mechanism through which God leads to repentance, which is structurally a Christological movement. However, the data does not contain an explicit typological argument (e.g., the good king who typifies the messianic king, or a creation-goodness → new-creation-goodness typology). The christological and eschatological dimensions are present in NT usage but not through formal typological structure. This is a partial finding — the direction is named but the full typological structure is not explicitly drawn in the verse evidence. (OBS-067-OBS-006, OBS-067-OBS-036)

findings.session_b_note: Yes — extensively. The dod vocabulary of the Song is the most concentrated typological deployment: human eros/marital love functions as the vehicle for God's love for Israel (Isa 5:1 OBS-103-083; Eze 16:8 OBS-103-083b) and in the prophetic-allegorical tradition as the figure of divine-human covenantal love. God's love for Israel is called 'the time of love' (Eze 16:8) using marital vocabulary. The father-son love (Mat 3:17, OBS-103-120) functions typologically: the Father's love for the Son at baptism is simultaneously the origin-point from which all love flows (SD-016) and the pattern of divine-to-human love in redemption. The parable of the prodigal son (Luk 15:20, OBS-103-057) deploys parental love typologically — the father's running, embracing, and kissing figure God's reception of the returning sinner. Typological use runs in both directions (OT human love → divine love type; NT divine love → human love pattern).

findings.session_b_note: Yes — mercy has explicit typological architecture. The *kapporet* (mercy seat, H3727) is the physical OT locus of divine-human meeting in mercy; *hilastērios* (G2435) names Christ as the fulfillment of the mercy seat (Rom 3:25). The typological movement is explicit: physical mercy seat → Christ as living mercy seat received by faith (OBS-111-066, OBS-111-067). The Day of Atonement (*kippurim*, H3725) similarly finds typological fulfillment in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (Heb 9–10, though the Heb 9:5 verse notes this trajectory). findings.session_b_note: Yes — covenant is used typologically throughout Scripture, and with unusual density. (1) The Noahic covenant and ark (G2787H, 1 Pet 3:20 — OBS-034-065) are deployed by Peter as a type of baptism: the saved-through-water structure of Noah's covenant-obedience prefigures the new covenant sign of baptism. (2) The Sinai covenant (blood of the covenant — Exo 24:8, echoed in Mat 26:28, Mar 14:24, Heb 9:20) is taken up into the new covenant in Christ's blood — the Eucharist is the new covenant's covenantal meal, explicitly structured after Sinai's blood ritual. (3) The Davidic covenant (everlasting covenant — OBS-034-041) is deployed typologically in the NT as pointing toward Christ's eternal kingship. (4) Gal 4:24 (OBS-034-071) explicitly allegorises the two covenants (Hagar/Sinai = slavery; Sarah/Jerusalem = freedom). (5) Hebrews systematically typologises the Mosaic covenant as a shadow of the new: the ark (OBS-034-064), the blood of bulls and goats (Heb 9:13 context), the tabernacle — all point beyond themselves to Christ. Covenant is the primary typological category of the OT in the NT's reading of Scripture.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — more explicitly than most characteristics in the programme.
